lead: Two stories of trust in God’s provision stand side by side. On Mount Moriah Abraham is asked for the one thing that holds all God’s promises, his son Isaac, and answers Isaac’s question with the words “God himself will provide”. In Capernaum a paralyzed man is carried to Jesus by friends, and Jesus, seeing their faith, offers first what the man did not ask for: the forgiveness of his sins. In both, God gives more than anyone dared to hope. The psalm, Psalm 115, gives the right answer: “Not to us, O Lord, but to your name give glory.”

r.h: God himself will provide
set: Abraham was a hundred years old when Isaac, the child of the promise, was born (Genesis 21:5), after many years of waiting. Only shortly before our passage Abraham had to send away his other son, Ishmael (21:8–21). Now God asks for Isaac. The ancient Jewish tradition calls this chapter the Akedah, “the binding” of Isaac, and it is one of the most reflected-on chapters of the Old Testament.

Background. Moriah is mentioned again only in 2 Chronicles 3:1, where Solomon builds the Temple “on Mount Moriah”, so the story was early linked with Jerusalem. Some neighbouring peoples practised child sacrifice, and the Law of Israel forbids it (Leviticus 18:21; Deuteronomy 12:31). Many readers see in the story’s ending a lesson that the God of Israel does not want it. The narrator tells us at the start what the reader must know and Abraham does not: “God tested Abraham”.
str: vv. 1–2: God’s call, “Abraham!”, and the command, with its four slow steps from “your son” to “whom you love”.
vv. 3–8: the three-day journey; the wood laid on Isaac; Isaac’s question and Abraham’s answer.
vv. 9–10: the altar, the binding, the raised knife.
vv. 11–14: the angel of the Lord stops him; the ram; the place is named.
vv. 15–19: God’s oath renews the blessing for all the nations.
kw: To test is to bring what is hidden in a person into the open, not to lead into sin. The Letter of James says that God tempts no one to evil (James 1:13). Here the test shows the depth of Abraham’s trust, and teaches Abraham himself.
Abraham says this three times: to God (v. 1), to Isaac (v. 7), and to the angel (v. 11). It is the answer of a man wholly available, to God and to his child alike.
Literally “the Lord sees” or “sees to it”. The name Abraham gives the place (v. 14) repeats his own answer in verse 8: God sees the need and supplies it.
vv: Take your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love
Each phrase tightens the cost. In the Hebrew the name Isaac comes last, as if God were holding back the word that hurts most. The command does not explain itself; it asks for trust.
God himself will provide the lamb for a burnt offering, my son.
Abraham neither lies to Isaac nor claims to understand. It is an answer of faith, and the Church hears in it a promise only Christ fulfils (John 1:29).
Do not lay your hand on the boy or do anything to him
God stops the sacrifice before it happens. Isaac is not given up to death; he is given back. The test was of Abraham’s heart, and God never willed the child’s death.
by your offspring shall all the nations of the earth gain blessing for themselves
The promise made at the first call (12:3) is sworn by God’s own oath. Paul reads the “offspring” as finally fulfilled in Christ (Galatians 3:16).
ch: The New Testament reads this chapter as a lesson in faith. The Letter to the Hebrews says that Abraham, offering Isaac, reasoned that God was able even to raise someone from the dead (Hebrews 11:17–19). The Catechism speaks of Abraham’s faith that did not weaken, “God himself will provide the lamb”, and sees him made like the Father who did not spare his own Son (CCC 2572; Romans 8:32). The Fathers saw Isaac carrying the wood as a figure of Christ carrying his Cross; Origen develops this at length (in substance, Homilies on Genesis 8). The first Eucharistic Prayer of the Mass, the Roman Canon, names “the sacrifice of Abraham, our father in faith” among the offerings that God has accepted. The Church does not read the chapter as approval of human sacrifice: God alone is Lord of life (CCC 2258).

r.h: Authority to forgive sins
set: Jesus has just crossed the Sea of Galilee after healing two men on the far shore (8:28–34). He comes to “his own town”, which is Capernaum, where he had made his home (4:13). Mark 2:1–12 and Luke 5:17–26 tell the same story with more detail, including the roof opened by the bearers. Matthew tells it briefly, so that attention rests on one question: who has authority to forgive sins?

Background. Many people in the ancient world linked serious illness with sin, and the man’s friends may have shared that view. Jesus never says here that his illness was caused by his sins. The scribes are right in one thing: only God forgives sins. What they do not yet see is that God is at work in Jesus.
str: vv. 1–2a: arrival in Capernaum; the bed carried to Jesus.
v. 2b: Jesus sees their faith and says, “your sins are forgiven”.
vv. 3–4: some scribes think “blasphemy”; Jesus knows their thoughts.
vv. 5–6a: which is easier? The Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins.
vv. 6b–8: “Stand up”; the man goes home; the crowds glorify God.
kw: A word of encouragement, used again in Matthew 9:22 and 14:27. Jesus first calls the man “son”, then strengthens him; the forgiveness comes as a father’s word.
To speak against God, or to claim what belongs to God alone. By the law, only God can forgive. The scribes reason well from a wrong starting point: they do not recognize who stands before them.
Not only power but the right to act. Matthew uses the word again of Jesus’ teaching (7:29) and at the very end of the Gospel (28:18).
vv: When Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic, “Take heart, son; your sins are forgiven.”
“Their faith” is the faith of the friends who carried him, and perhaps his own. Jesus answers the deeper need first; the healing of the body follows as a sign.
Why do you think evil in your hearts?
Jesus reads hearts, which Scripture attributes to God (1 Samuel 16:7). His question is not hostile; it opens a door to understanding.
so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins
An unseen forgiveness is proved by a visible cure. The “Son of Man” recalls the figure of Daniel 7:13–14, to whom dominion is given.
they were filled with awe, and they glorified God, who had given such authority to human beings.
The crowd says “human beings”, in the plural. The Church hears in this a hint of what Jesus will give to his apostles and their successors (John 20:21–23).
ch: The Catechism teaches that only God forgives sins, and that Jesus, as Son of God, says of himself that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive them (CCC 1441). Christ willed that the whole Church, in her prayer, life and work, be the instrument of the forgiveness he won, and he entrusted its exercise to the apostles and their successors (CCC 1442). So the priest in the sacrament of Penance speaks the words of absolution in the name of Christ. The friends who carry the paralyzed man are also a picture of intercession: since Abraham, standing before God for another has marked a heart that shares God’s mercy (CCC 2635).

qa: Did God really ask Abraham to kill his son?

The text says plainly that God “tested” Abraham, and the story ends with God forbidding the sacrifice. The Church reads it as a trial of faith and trust, not as approval of human sacrifice. God alone is the Lord of life (CCC 2258). The story teaches that Abraham held nothing back from God, and that God does not take what he asks us to be ready to give.
study: Abraham answered, “Here I am”, to God and to his son. When am I truly available to God and to the people closest to me?
The friends carried the paralyzed man to Jesus. Who is someone I can carry to him in prayer this week?

lead: Two tables and a tomb. In Genesis, Abraham buries Sarah in the only piece of land he ever owned in Canaan, and later his servant brings Rebekah to Isaac, who “was comforted after his mother’s death”. The promise of God continues through grief and through a marriage. In the Gospel Jesus calls a tax collector, Matthew, from his booth and sits at table with him and his friends. When he is questioned, he answers with a word from the prophet Hosea: “I desire mercy, not sacrifice.” Psalm 106 begins the response: “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good.”

r.h: Buried with honour, comforted by love
set: Sarah has died at Hebron, aged one hundred twenty-seven; she is the only woman in Genesis whose age at death is recorded. Abraham, who has lived as a wanderer for more than sixty years, now has to ask for land to bury her. The lectionary leaves out the long and courteous bargaining with Ephron the Hittite (23:5–18), and the long story of the servant at the well (24:9–61), and gives us the beginning and the end of each chapter.

Background. The cave of Machpelah was the first piece of the promised land that Abraham owned. Abraham himself, Isaac and Rebekah, and later Jacob and Leah were buried there (Genesis 25:9–10; 49:29–32). The servant in chapter 24 is not named; Jewish tradition identifies him with Eliezer, mentioned in 15:2. The oath with the hand “under the thigh” (24:2) was a solemn form of swearing in the patriarchal age.
str: 23:1–4: Sarah dies; Abraham mourns, then asks the Hittites for a burial place.
23:19: the burial in the cave of Machpelah.
24:1–8: Abraham, now old, makes his servant swear to seek a wife for Isaac among his own kindred, and not to take Isaac back to Mesopotamia.
24:62–67: Isaac meets Rebekah in the evening; he takes her into Sarah’s tent, loves her, and is comforted.
kw: The two words describe a foreigner without land rights. Abraham uses them of himself. The Letter to the Hebrews says that the patriarchs confessed themselves “strangers and foreigners on the earth” (Hebrews 11:13).

Found only here in the Old Testament and of uncertain meaning. The ancient Greek translation read “to meditate”, which is also how the Malayalam Bible understands it. Either way, Isaac is shown in quiet evening solitude when his bride arrives.
The verb of consolation. Rebekah does not replace Sarah; she is the sign that life and the promise go on.
vv: I am a stranger and an alien residing among you
Abraham has been in Canaan for decades and still owns no land. He asks politely, as a guest, and will insist on paying the full price (23:16).
he will send his angel before you
Abraham trusts that the God who brought him out of his father’s house will guide the servant. The same God who once demanded Isaac now provides for him.
Isaac went out in the evening to walk in the field
A textual note: the Hebrew verb is rare and its meaning uncertain. “Walk” and “meditate” are both ancient readings, and the second has made this verse a favourite picture of prayer.
He took Rebekah, and she became his wife; and he loved her. So Isaac was comforted after his mother’s death.
Marriage is shown as a place of love and consolation, not only of family planning. The tent of Sarah, empty since her death, is filled again.
ch: The Church treats burial as a work of mercy and an act of faith in the resurrection: the bodies of the dead are to be treated with respect and charity (CCC 2300). Abraham’s grief and his care for Sarah’s grave are a first example. The reading from Genesis 24 is one of those offered for the celebration of marriage in the Roman Rite, because it shows a marriage received from God’s hand, begun in prayer and ending in love. The Letter to the Hebrews sees the patriarchs, living in tents as strangers and looking for a city with foundations, as a sign of the Church’s pilgrim journey (Hebrews 11:9–10, 13–16).

r.h: I desire mercy, not sacrifice
set: Right after the healing of the paralyzed man (9:1–8), Jesus passes the tax booth at Capernaum and calls Matthew. Mark (2:14) and Luke (5:27) give the man’s name as Levi; the Church has always understood him to be the apostle Matthew, who is called “the tax collector” in Matthew 10:3.

Background. Tax collectors collected duties on goods and travellers on behalf of Herod Antipas or of Rome. They were widely resented as collaborators and often as extortioners. “Sinners” here means those regarded as living outside the law as it was taught, or openly bad. To eat with someone was to share fellowship, which is why the question is asked. The Pharisees are men who take holiness seriously; their question comes from that concern, not from simple hostility.
str: v. 9: the call: “Follow me”, and Matthew rises at once.
v. 10: a meal at the house, with many tax collectors and sinners.
v. 11: the Pharisees ask the disciples why their teacher eats with such people.
vv. 12–13: Jesus’ answer: the physician, the word of Hosea, and his mission.
kw: The ordinary word for a disciple following a teacher. In the Gospels it is also the call to share his way and, in the end, his Cross.
Greek for the Hebrew hesed in Hosea 6:6: faithful, loving kindness. Hosea sets it against sacrifice offered without it. Jesus does not reject sacrifice; he reminds the listeners what it is for.
Literally “those who have it badly”. The image of the physician is Jesus’ own description of his mission, and the Church has taken it up in many prayers.
vv: he saw a man called Matthew sitting at the tax booth; and he said to him, “Follow me.”
Matthew’s call is told in two verbs: he saw, and he said. Jesus sees the man behind the booth. Matthew’s response is equally brief: “he got up and followed him”.
Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?
The Pharisees ask the disciples, not Jesus. The question assumes that holiness means keeping apart. Jesus’ answer shows that his holiness reaches towards sinners to heal them.
Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick.
Jesus does not say that the Pharisees need no healing. He takes the common saying and makes it a statement of why he has come.
Go and learn what this means, ‘I desire mercy, not sacrifice.’
“Go and learn” was a teacher’s way of sending someone to study Scripture. Jesus quotes Hosea 6:6 to show that he stands within the prophets, not against them.
ch: The Catechism says that Jesus scandalized the Pharisees by eating with tax collectors and sinners as familiarly as with themselves (CCC 589), and that he invites sinners to the table of the kingdom (CCC 545). The Fathers delighted in the call of Matthew. Bede, in a homily on this passage, says that Jesus saw him with mercy and so chose him (in substance, Homilies on the Gospels 1.21). Pope Francis took the words of this homily as his episcopal motto. The Mass keeps the same pattern: the Church, a company of sinners, is called to the table of the Lord, and before Holy Communion confesses, “Lord, I am not worthy”.

qa: Does “I desire mercy, not sacrifice” mean that worship does not matter?

No. Hosea was criticizing worship that was offered without love of neighbour and fidelity to God. Jesus, who worshipped in the Temple and kept the feasts, quotes the verse to show that worship and mercy belong together. Sacrifice without mercy is empty; mercy is what God has always wanted at the heart of every offering.
study: Abraham called himself a stranger and still kept his hope. When have I felt a stranger, and what held my hope?
Jesus saw Matthew, and Matthew got up. What would it mean for me to rise from my own “tax booth” today?

lead: On the feast of St Thomas the Church reads two texts about foundations. Ephesians says that the household of God is “built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the cornerstone”, and the Gospel shows one of those apostles at the moment his faith is laid. Thomas, who refused to believe a report, meets the risen Lord and speaks the highest confession in the Gospel of John: “My Lord and my God!” Psalm 117, with its refrain “Go out to all the world and tell the Good News” (Mark 16:15), turns the apostle’s faith into a mission to all nations. According to tradition, that mission carried Thomas as far as India.

r.h: Built upon the foundation of the apostles
set: Ephesians is a letter about the Church as one body of Jews and Gentiles in Christ. Just before our passage Paul, or the author writing in his name, reminds Gentile believers that they were once “aliens from the commonwealth of Israel” and “strangers to the covenants of promise” (2:12), and that in Christ the dividing wall has been broken down (2:14). They are now brought near, to share in what God gave to Israel.

Authorship. The letter claims to be Paul’s, written from prison (3:1; 4:1), and the Catholic tradition receives it as his. Many scholars think it was written by a disciple in Paul’s name soon after his death. In either case the Church reads it as Scripture. Some early manuscripts omit “in Ephesus” in 1:1, which suggests that it may have been a circular letter for several churches.
str: v. 19: from outsiders to citizens: “no longer strangers and aliens”.
v. 20: the foundation: the apostles and prophets, and Christ as cornerstone.
vv. 21–22: the building grows into a holy temple, a dwelling for God in the Spirit.
kw: People living in a place without full rights. Paul says that the Gentile believers are no longer in that condition; they now belong to the household.
The stone at the corner that fixes the line of the walls. The image comes from Isaiah 28:16 and Psalm 118:22, which the New Testament applies to Christ (1 Peter 2:6–7; Mark 12:10).
The word naos means the sanctuary itself, where God dwells. The Church, built of living people, becomes his dwelling.
vv: you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are citizens with the saints and also members of the household of God
Gentile believers are not guests in someone else’s home. They are members of God’s household, the same household that includes Abraham, Moses and the prophets.
built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the cornerstone.

The apostles are witnesses to the Resurrection, and their testimony is the foundation. Most scholars take “prophets” here to be the prophets of the New Testament Church (compare 3:5; 4:11); others include the prophets of Israel. The cornerstone, Christ, holds the whole together.
In him the whole structure is joined together and grows into a holy temple in the Lord
A living building: it “grows”. The Church is not finished, and each generation is another course of stones.
you also are built together spiritually into a dwelling place for God.
“Together” and “spiritually”: the Spirit makes a community, not a collection of private believers, into God’s dwelling place.
ch: The Catechism quotes this passage when it calls the Church God’s building: the Lord compared himself to the stone which the builders rejected, and on this foundation the Church is built by the apostles (CCC 756). The Church is also apostolic because she is founded on the apostles, in three ways: built on their witness, kept by the Holy Spirit in their teaching, and guided by their successors (CCC 857). Thomas, on this feast, stands for all the apostles whose faith became the foundation of the faith of others.

r.h: My Lord and my God!
set: It is the evening of Easter Sunday, and the risen Jesus has appeared to the disciples behind locked doors, showed them his hands and side, breathed on them the Holy Spirit and given them power to forgive sins (20:19–23). Thomas, “one of the twelve”, was not there. John calls him Didymos, the Greek for “twin” (the Aramaic is te’oma). We have met him twice before in this Gospel: when Lazarus died he said, “Let us also go, that we may die with him” (11:16), and at the Last Supper he asked, “How can we know the way?” (14:5).

Background. A week later, which is the Sunday after Easter, the disciples are again together. From earliest times the Church has seen in this the beginning of her gathering for the Lord’s Day. The passage is the last of John’s appearance stories; verses 30–31 that follow give the purpose of the whole Gospel: “that you may come to believe that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God”.
str: vv. 24–25: Thomas is absent; he hears the news and refuses to believe on report.
v. 26: a week later Jesus comes through closed doors: “Peace be with you.”
v. 27: Jesus invites Thomas to touch his hands and side.
v. 28: Thomas’ confession.
v. 29: the blessing on those who believe without seeing.
kw: Both the Aramaic name Thomas and the Greek Didymos mean “twin”. The Gospel does not tell us whose twin he was. Tradition gives him the name Judas Thomas.

The Greek says, literally, “do not become unbelieving but believing”. It is not a rebuke only; it is a call to become a believer. The verb “believe” in the Gospel’s purpose statement (20:31) comes from the same root.
ho kyrios mou kai ho theos mou

Kyrios, Lord, is the word used for the God of Israel in the Greek Old Testament, and theos is God. The Gospel which began with “the Word was God” (1:1) ends its stories with a disciple saying it of Jesus.
vv: Unless I see the mark of the nails in his hands, and put my finger in the mark of the nails and my hand in his side, I will not believe.
Thomas wants no more than the others were given (20:20). He asks to see the Crucified. He is not the sceptic who asks for proof of just anything; he wants the wounds.
Although the doors were shut, Jesus came and stood among them and said, “Peace be with you.”
The same greeting as on Easter evening. The risen body is the same body that was crucified, and it is no longer bound by walls.
Put your finger here and see my hands. Reach out your hand and put it in my side. Do not doubt but believe.

Jesus answers Thomas’ words one by one. He knows what Thomas said in his absence. John does not say that Thomas actually touched him; many early readers supposed he did, but the text shows him moved to confession at the sight of the Lord.
My Lord and my God!
The highest confession in the Gospel, and Thomas is the one who says it. He does not say “you are like God”, but “my God”. The words are personal: my Lord, my God.
Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have come to believe.
The blessing looks beyond the apostles to every later believer. It does not scold Thomas for asking; it names the faith of all who rely on the apostles’ witness.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the disciples’ doubt before the risen Jesus is part of the Gospel record: Thomas himself went through the test of doubt, so the idea that the Resurrection was a product of the apostles’ credulity is untenable (CCC 644). The risen body is the same body that was crucified, and it still bears the marks of the Passion, yet it already shares in the glory of God (CCC 645). St Augustine says that Thomas saw and touched the man and confessed the God whom he could neither see nor touch (in substance, Tractates on John 121). St Gregory the Great taught that the Lord allowed Thomas’ doubt so that the believers who came after him would be strengthened (in substance, Homilies on the Gospels 26). Many Catholics say Thomas’ words silently as the Host and the chalice are raised at Mass.

qa: Was Thomas wrong to doubt?

Thomas wanted to meet the risen Lord for himself, as the other apostles had (20:20). He was not condemned: Jesus came back for him a week later and spoke to him with gentleness. The title “Doubting Thomas” is too narrow. The Gospel shows him earlier as loyal to the point of death (11:16) and here as the one who makes the most complete confession of faith in the Gospel.
Did Thomas really come to India?

Thomas’ journey to India is not told in the New Testament. It rests on a strong and ancient tradition. The Christians of India have always held that he preached on the Malabar coast, and an early third-century non-canonical work, the Acts of Thomas, places him in India at the court of King Gondophares. Historians discuss the details, but the Church honours the tradition, and the Christians of India of several Churches honour him as the apostle who brought them the Gospel.
What does it mean that the Church is built on the apostles, if Christ is the cornerstone?

There is no rivalry. Christ is the cornerstone who holds everything together; the apostles are the foundation because they were chosen and sent by him, and they are witnesses of his Resurrection. Their authority is his, given to them (compare Matthew 28:18–20; CCC 857).
rite: St Thomas is listed among the Twelve in all the Gospels, and the Gospel of John gives him the most memorable lines. The feast was kept on 21 December in the Roman calendar until the reform of 1969, when it was moved to 3 July, the day on which, according to tradition, his relics were brought to Edessa (present-day Urfa in Turkey). Tradition also holds that Thomas reached the Malabar coast in the year 52, founded communities there, and was martyred at Mylapore, near present-day Chennai, about the year 72, where his tomb is venerated. For Catholics in India the feast is of special joy, and Christians of several Churches there honour him. His words, “My Lord and my God”, are among the shortest and fullest prayers of the Church.
study: Thomas asked to see the wounds of the Crucified. What in my own faith needs to meet the real Jesus, wounds and all, and not an idea of him?
Thomas was away when Jesus came. How can I make sure I am present when my community gathers on the Lord’s Day?
“Blessed are those who have not seen.” Who passed the faith to me, and how can I pass it on?
Ephesians says the Church is still growing. What small stone can I add to it this week?

lead: All three readings ask how God’s word comes to us, and why we so easily miss it. Ezekiel is sent to a people who may not listen, with the promise that they will at least know that a prophet has been among them. In Nazareth, Jesus is the prophet, and his neighbours cannot see beyond the carpenter they know. Between them stands Paul, who prayed three times to be rid of a thorn and heard the Lord answer: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness.” In all three, God works through what looks small, ordinary or weak. Psalm 123 gives the prayer: “our eyes look to the Lord our God, until he has mercy upon us.”

r.h: A prophet among them
set: Ezekiel was a priest of Jerusalem, carried into exile in Babylon in 597 BC with King Jehoiachin and thousands of others. He received his call in the fifth year of that exile, by the river Chebar (1:1–3). Before our passage he has seen the glory of God on a moving throne (chapter 1), and has fallen on his face. Now God speaks to him, calls him “mortal” (literally “son of man”, the title God uses of him some ninety times), and sends him.

Background. The people to whom Ezekiel is sent are his own: Israel, in exile or still in Jerusalem. The prophets speak from within the covenant people, not against them, and their sharp words belong to Israel’s own Scripture. The book that begins with judgment also holds some of the Old Testament’s greatest promises of restoration (chapters 34 to 37). “A nation of rebels” describes a people who have broken faith, as Israel itself confesses.
str: v. 2: the Spirit enters Ezekiel and sets him on his feet.
v. 3: the mission: to Israel, to those who have rebelled.
v. 4: the messenger formula: “Thus says the Lord God.”
v. 5: whether they listen or not, they will know a prophet has been among them.
kw: The usual address to Ezekiel, a reminder that he is a frail human being. Jesus later uses the same expression of himself in the Gospels.
The one Hebrew word covers the Spirit of God and the breath that lifts Ezekiel to his feet. The prophet cannot stand to receive his mission until the Spirit stands him up.
A repeated phrase in Ezekiel for a people that has turned from God. It is spoken from within, by a prophet who loves his people.
vv: a spirit entered into me and set me on my feet
The call comes in two stages: God speaks, and the Spirit makes the prophet able to listen and to stand. God does not send anyone without giving them strength.
I am sending you to the people of Israel, to a nation of rebels who have rebelled against me
The mission begins with a hard truth. The prophet is not promised that his people will welcome him.
Thus says the Lord God.
The prophet’s authority is not his own. He is a messenger, and the word he carries is the Lord’s.
they shall know that there has been a prophet among them
The success of the prophet is not measured by whether people obey. The word will have been spoken, and Israel will not be able to say that God did not warn them.
ch: The Church teaches that God formed his people through the prophets in the hope of salvation and of a new and everlasting covenant (CCC 64). Jesus calls himself “Son of Man”, and the Letter to the Hebrews says that God, who spoke by the prophets, has spoken in these last days by a Son (Hebrews 1:1–2). Pope St Gregory the Great preached a series of homilies on Ezekiel in Rome during a time of great danger for the city, and pastors have found in this call a picture of their own task: to speak God’s word, whether it is welcomed or not.

r.h: My grace is sufficient for you
set: Paul has been forced into what he calls “foolish” boasting (11:1 to 12:13), because some newly arrived teachers at Corinth were claiming greater status than he had. He tells of an unnamed man in Christ caught up to the third heaven fourteen years before, and of things “that no mortal is permitted to repeat” (12:1–4). He now says why he does not boast of this. The thorn comes in at once.

Background. Paul never says what the thorn was. Interpreters through the centuries have suggested an illness, a temptation, a handicap, or the opposition of enemies. The Church has not defined it, and the silence may be intended: every reader can supply their own thorn. Paul calls it “a messenger of Satan”, but he also writes that it was “given” to him, which means that God permitted it for a purpose.
str: v. 7: the thorn, given to keep Paul from pride.
v. 8: his triple prayer for its removal.
v. 9a: the Lord’s answer.
vv. 9b–10: Paul’s response: gladness in weakness, and the paradox of strength.
kw: A sharp point such as a splinter or a stake. It suggests acute and continuing pain rather than a passing trouble.
God’s undeserved gift of his own life and help (CCC 1996). Paul’s answer is not a lesson in patience but a promise: the Lord’s own grace is enough.
The same word is used of illness and of human frailty in general. In this chapter it becomes the very place where the power of Christ shows itself.
vv: a thorn was given me in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to torment me

The verb is passive: the thorn “was given”. Paul recognizes that God allowed it, while its torment is evil. He does not say that God wished him to suffer; he says that God used it to guard him from pride.
Three times I appealed to the Lord about this, that it would leave me
Paul prays as Jesus prayed in Gethsemane, asking three times that the cup pass (Mark 14:32–42). Even an apostle’s prayer does not always receive the answer he asks for.
My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness.
Textual note: many manuscripts read “my power”, others omit “my”; the sense is the same. The Lord’s word is not an explanation but a presence: his grace is enough.
whenever I am weak, then I am strong
Not a boast of weakness for its own sake, but trust that when Paul has nothing of his own to lean on, the strength he relies upon is Christ’s.
ch: The Catechism says that only faith can embrace the mysterious ways of God’s almighty power, and that this faith “glories in its weaknesses in order to draw to itself Christ’s power”, with the Virgin Mary as its supreme model (CCC 273). St Augustine, writing on prayer, held that when God does not give what we ask for, it can be mercy: Paul was not granted the removal of the thorn, because what he received was better (in substance, Letter 130). The passage is also often read at the Anointing of the Sick and in prayer with those who suffer: it does not say that suffering is good, but that God’s grace does not leave the sufferer.

r.h: A prophet without honour
set: Jesus has just worked two great signs: the calming of the storm and the raising of Jairus’ daughter, with the healing of the woman who touched his cloak (4:35 to 5:43). Now he comes to “his hometown”, which Mark does not name but which is Nazareth, with his disciples. In Mark’s account it is his first return since leaving to begin his mission, and on the Sabbath he teaches in the synagogue.

Background. The people of Nazareth are Jesus’ own neighbours and kin, a small village where everyone knew everyone. They are not villains; they are astonished by his wisdom and works. Their trouble is a human one: it is hard to see someone great in a person you have known all your life. Jesus and his family and disciples are themselves faithful Jews of Galilee, and Mark’s story is of the village’s struggle to believe, not of a nation.
str: vv. 1–2a: Jesus comes to his hometown and teaches in the synagogue on the Sabbath.
vv. 2b–3: astonishment and offence: where does he get all this?
v. 4: Jesus’ saying about the prophet.
vv. 5–6a: few miracles; his amazement at their unbelief.
v. 6b: Jesus goes on teaching in the surrounding villages.
kw: A strong word, “struck out of themselves”. Mark uses it elsewhere for the crowd’s reaction to Jesus’ teaching (1:22; 11:18). Astonishment is not yet faith.
A craftsman in wood, and perhaps in stone as well. This is the only time Mark calls Jesus a carpenter. Matthew (13:55) says “the carpenter’s son”.
From skandalon, a stumbling block. What trips them is the ordinariness of the one who teaches, and their own sense that they know where he comes from.
vv: On the sabbath he began to teach in the synagogue, and many who heard him were astounded.
Jesus teaches in the synagogue as a faithful Jew, and the people recognize authority in him. The question is not whether his words are good, but where they come from.
Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary and brother of James and Joses and Judas and Simon

Villagers are usually identified by their father’s name; “son of Mary” is unusual. “Brother” here and “sisters” later are used in the Old Testament sense of close relatives (CCC 500). Mark gives them as an ordinary family, to make the point that Jesus’ origins seemed to the neighbours quite unremarkable.
Prophets are not without honor, except in their hometown, and among their own kin, and in their own house.
Jesus applies a proverb to himself and places himself among the prophets such as Ezekiel who were not welcomed. He also shows the loneliness of the Son who is not recognized by his own.
he could do no deed of power there, except that he laid his hands on a few sick people and cured them.

Mark’s language is strong: “could do no deed”. It does not mean that his power failed, but that miracles are signs offered to faith, not shows to compel it. Matthew softens it to “he did not do many” (13:58).
he was amazed at their unbelief
Jesus is amazed here and, in Matthew and Luke, at the faith of the centurion (Matthew 8:10; Luke 7:9). The one who astonishes everyone is himself astonished, once by faith and once by its lack.
ch: The Catechism says that during the greater part of his life Jesus shared the condition of the vast majority of human beings: a daily life spent without evident greatness, a life of manual labour (CCC 531). The scandal of Nazareth is the scandal of the Incarnation itself: God comes in what is ordinary. Preachers have long seen in the neighbours’ question a warning to every believer: familiarity can dull wonder, even before the Eucharist, which seems so plain. The same question is asked of the Church: how can God’s power and wisdom be present in people, words and bread that are so familiar?

qa: What was Paul’s thorn in the flesh?

Paul does not say, and the Church has not defined it. Illness, temptation, persecution and opposition from rivals have all been proposed. The unnamed thorn lets every reader hear the Lord’s answer for their own suffering: “My grace is sufficient for you”.
Why does Mark say that Jesus “could do no deed of power” in Nazareth?

Mark does not suggest that Jesus’ power failed, but that miracles are signs that call for faith, not tricks to compel it. Where people are closed to him, the sign cannot do its work. Even so, Jesus heals a few, and goes on teaching. The same Gospel shows him giving power to others in the next verses (6:7–13).
Who are the “brothers and sisters” of Jesus?

The Greek adelphos and the Hebrew word behind it can mean close relatives such as cousins. The Catholic Church holds that Mary is ever virgin. James and Joses, named here, are described elsewhere as sons of another Mary who was a disciple (CCC 500; compare Mark 15:40).
rite: This is the Fourteenth Sunday in Ordinary Time, in Year B of the Sunday cycle, the year of Mark. Mark is the shortest Gospel and cannot fill a whole year, so for five Sundays from 25 July the Church reads the Bread of Life discourse of John 6. The Sunday Mass is where the prophet’s word is still proclaimed: the Church hears the readings as spoken to her now, and the homily is meant to open them (CCC 1154). The Sunday Mass is also the place where the ordinary is the carrier of Christ’s presence, as it was in Nazareth: simple bread and wine, a priest the parish knows, a congregation of familiar faces.
study: Ezekiel is told that the people may not listen. When have I spoken a word of faith and not been heard, and how did I respond?
Paul’s thorn was not taken away. What is my own “thorn”, and what would it mean to hear “my grace is sufficient” about it?
The people of Nazareth could not see beyond what they knew. Where does familiarity dull my wonder at Jesus: in the Eucharist, in my parish, in my own family?
Psalm 123 prays with eyes fixed on the Lord “until he has mercy upon us”. How do I wait on God when I am treated with contempt or when I feel small?

lead: A man on the run, a stone for a pillow, and the first thing he learns about God: the Lord is in this place, and Jacob did not know it. In the Gospel a synagogue leader and a nameless woman, one asking for a daughter’s life and the other for her own health, find that the same Jesus meets both. Psalm 91 gives the prayer of both: “My God, in whom I trust.”

r.h: The house of God and the gate of heaven
set: Jacob is fleeing. He has taken his brother Esau’s blessing by deceit (chapter 27), and at his mother Rebekah’s urging he sets out for Haran, to her brother Laban, to escape Esau’s anger and find a wife (27:41–45; 28:1–5). It is the first night of his life away from home, and he is alone, with nothing but a staff (32:10).

Background. Bethel, “house of God”, was an ancient holy place in the hill country north of Jerusalem, called Luz before. Later Israel remembered it as a place of worship (Judges 20:18; 1 Kings 12:29). The ladder, in Hebrew sullām, appears only here in the Bible. It is probably a stairway, like those that led up the temple towers of Mesopotamia, linking earth to heaven.
str: vv. 10–12: the night, the stone, the dream of the stairway and the angels.
vv. 13–15: the Lord stands beside Jacob and renews to him the promise made to Abraham and Isaac.
vv. 16–17: Jacob wakes in awe.
vv. 18–22a: the pillar, the oil, the name Bethel, and Jacob’s vow.
kw: The only occurrence in the Bible. The angels first go up and then come down: heaven’s messengers are already at work on earth before Jacob even knows it.
Jacob renames the place. A site that was just “a certain place” has become the house of God, because God has made himself known there.
A standing stone set up as a memorial of a meeting with God. Jacob pours oil on it, as a sign of consecration.
vv: Know that I am with you and will keep you wherever you go
God’s promise to a runaway. Jacob has done nothing to deserve it, and the promise comes before any change in him. God is with him on the road, not only at the shrine.
Surely the Lord is in this place
The next words are “and I did not know it”. The lesson is that God is present even where we are not aware of him, and prayer is often a waking up to a presence already given.
How awesome is this place! This is none other than the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven.
Awe, not comfort, is Jacob’s first response. The Church uses these words in the rite of dedicating a church, because every church is meant to be a house of God and a gate of heaven.
If God will be with me, and will keep me in this way that I go
Jacob’s vow is bargaining and trust together. It is the first prayer of a man who is still learning, and God does not rebuke it.
ch: In the Gospel of John, Jesus tells Nathanael that he will see heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man (John 1:51). The Fathers saw in this that Christ himself is the ladder, the one place where heaven and earth are joined, and Bethel is where God has met humanity. St Augustine saw in the stone anointed with oil a figure of Christ, the Anointed One, which is what the word “Christ” means (in substance, City of God 16.38). Jacob’s vow of a tenth is an early mention of tithing in the Bible (Abraham had already given a tenth, Genesis 14:20), which Israel later made part of its worship.

r.h: The hand, the cloak and the sleeping girl
set: Jesus is still at the table of Matthew in Capernaum, speaking about the new wine of his teaching (9:14–17), when a synagogue leader comes in and kneels. Matthew tells the story briefly: the girl has “just died”. Mark (5:21–43) and Luke (8:40–56) give the man’s name, Jairus, and tell that the girl was still alive when he first came. The healing of the woman is set inside the story of the girl, so that the two miracles meet.

Background. The woman had suffered bleeding for twelve years, which according to Leviticus 15:25–27 kept her from the Temple while it lasted. This was a state of ritual impurity, not a moral fault, but a long illness would have meant a long separation from worship and from many in the community. She touches the “fringe” of Jesus’ cloak: the tassels that every observant Jewish man wore at the corners of his garment (Numbers 15:38–39). Jesus himself keeps this practice.
str: vv. 18–19: the leader’s request; Jesus goes with him.
vv. 20–22: on the way, the woman touches the fringe of his cloak and is healed.
vv. 23–25: at the house: flute players and the crowd; Jesus takes the girl by the hand and she gets up.
v. 26: the report spreads.
kw: The tassel at the corner of the garment, commanded in Numbers 15:38–39 as a reminder of God’s commandments. The woman reaches for the very place that tells of obedience to God.
The Greek verb sōzein means both to heal and to save. Jesus’ words to the woman are about her body and about her whole person.
she got up, she was raised
The verb used for the girl rising is the same one the New Testament uses for Jesus’ Resurrection. Matthew makes the first rising a sign of the last.
vv: If I only touch his cloak, I will be made well.
Her faith is quiet and secret, and it is real. She does not ask; she reaches. Jesus does not let her go unnoticed: he turns and sees her.
Take heart, daughter; your faith has made you well.
He calls her “daughter”, which restores her to the family of Israel in the sight of all, and the same word “take heart” that he said to the paralytic (9:2).
the girl is not dead but sleeping
Death is called sleep because it will not have the last word. They laugh, because they know she is dead; Jesus speaks as the one who will wake her.
he went in and took her by the hand, and the girl got up.
The gesture is simple and the result complete. Jesus does not stand at a distance; he takes the dead girl’s hand.
ch: The Catechism says that Jesus often asked the sick to believe, and that the sick tried to touch him, for power came out of him and healed them all; in the sacraments Christ continues to “touch” us in order to heal us (CCC 1504). The raising of Jairus’ daughter, the widow’s son and Lazarus are signs that foreshadow his own Resurrection, though these did not yet bring the final victory over death (CCC 994). The Church has long read the two miracles together: the woman, whom no one could help, and the girl, whom no one could save, are both given to Jesus’ power, and it is the woman whom he calls “daughter” (9:22).

study: Jacob said, “the Lord is in this place, and I did not know it.” Where might God be present in my ordinary day without my noticing?
The woman reached out to touch only Jesus’ cloak. What is the smallest act of faith I can make today?

lead: Two portraits of compassion and struggle. In the dark at the river Jabbok, Jacob wrestles with a mysterious stranger until dawn, refuses to let go until he is blessed, and leaves limping with a new name, Israel. In the Gospel Jesus sees crowds “harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd”, and tells his disciples to pray for workers; in the next verse he will send them. Psalm 17 gives the hope of both: “I shall behold your face in righteousness.”

r.h: I will not let you go unless you bless me
set: After twenty years with Laban, Jacob is going home, and he learns that Esau is coming to meet him with four hundred men (32:6). He is afraid. He prays one of the great prayers of Genesis (32:9–12), sends gifts ahead, and on the last night divides his family and possessions across the ford of the Jabbok. Then he is left alone.

Background. The Hebrew carries a play on three words: the river Jabbok (yabbōq), Jacob (ya‘ăqōb), and “wrestled” (ye’ābēq). The mysterious opponent is called simply “a man”. Jacob later says he has “seen God face to face”, and the prophet Hosea speaks of the same story as a struggle with God and with the angel (Hosea 12:3–4).
str: vv. 22–24a: Jacob sends everyone across the ford and stays alone.
vv. 24b–26a: the night wrestling; the wound at the hip.
vv. 26b–29: “I will not let you go unless you bless me”; the change of name; the stranger will not give his own name.
vv. 30–32: Peniel; Jacob limps into the sunrise; the custom about the thigh muscle.
kw: The text explains the name as “you have striven with God”. Scholars note that it more likely means “God strives” or “God rules”, but the biblical explanation is what shapes the story. The people of Israel inherit a name that means struggle and blessing together.
The place where Jacob saw God’s face and lived. The next chapter returns to this when he meets Esau and says that seeing his brother’s face is “like seeing the face of God” (33:10).
Jacob’s demand. After a life of seizing a blessing by trickery, he now asks for it openly, in the dark, from one who holds it.
vv: Jacob was left alone; and a man wrestled with him until daybreak.
The stranger comes when Jacob is alone and at the end of his own resources. In the Bible, encounters with God often come in such places.
I will not let you go, unless you bless me.
Wounded, Jacob will not give up. His persistence is not arrogance but need: he knows that his future depends on the blessing.
You shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel, for you have striven with God and with humans, and have prevailed.
A new name is a new identity. Jacob, “the heel-grabber”, becomes Israel, and the people who bear his name will carry the same story of struggle, blessing and survival.
For I have seen God face to face, and yet my life is preserved.
In the Old Testament, to see God and live is a wonder (Exodus 33:20; Judges 13:22). Jacob’s limp is the sign that the encounter was real.
ch: The Catechism says that from this account the spiritual tradition of the Church has kept a symbol of prayer as a battle of faith and as a triumph of perseverance (CCC 2573). The story does not teach that we can force God’s hand, but that God invites honest, persistent prayer from those who truly need him, and that such prayer changes the one who prays. Jacob receives both a blessing and a wound: an encounter with God leaves a mark. The Jewish custom still kept of not eating the thigh muscle (gid hanasheh) remembers this night; the Church honours Israel’s faithfulness to the memory of its own story.

r.h: The harvest is plentiful
set: Here ends the section of Matthew’s Gospel that shows Jesus’ works of power, chapters 8 and 9: ten miracles, as they are usually counted. Together with the Sermon on the Mount (chapters 5 to 7) they show the Messiah in word and deed. The final scene is the healing of a man who could not speak, brought to Jesus by others, followed by Jesus’ summary of his whole ministry, which is almost word for word the same as 4:23. The passage prepares the sending of the Twelve in chapter 10.

Background. The crowds respond with wonder: “Never has anything like this been seen in Israel.” Some Pharisees answer with an accusation, that his power comes from the prince of demons. This charge is repeated in 12:24. Matthew’s Gospel was written when his community, Jewish believers in Jesus, was in painful disagreement with other Jewish leaders; the harsh words belong to that family argument and are not a judgment on the Jewish people.
str: vv. 32–33: the mute man speaks; the crowds are amazed.
v. 34: the accusation by some Pharisees.
v. 35: the summary: teaching, proclaiming, healing.
v. 36: Jesus’ compassion for the crowds.
vv. 37–38: the harvest and the call to pray for labourers.
kw: From splanchna, the inner organs, the seat of deep feeling. It is a word in the Gospels used almost only of Jesus (and of characters in his parables who represent God). His compassion moves him, in the body, to act.
Literally “worn out and thrown down”: people battered by life and left without anyone to lead them. The picture of the shepherdless sheep recalls Numbers 27:17 and Ezekiel 34.
A common biblical image of God’s final gathering. The harvest here is not a threat but a promise: God’s people are ready to be gathered, and the workers are few.
vv: Never has anything like this been seen in Israel.
The crowds recognize the newness of what they see. In Matthew they speak in the name of Israel; they are not an enemy of Jesus.
he had compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd
Jesus sees what the crowds need before they say it. He sees them as a flock; he is the shepherd whom Israel was promised (Ezekiel 34:23).
The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few
Jesus is not complaining about the harvest but about the shortage of workers. The field is ripe; those who will gather it are few.
therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest.
The first response to need is prayer. The disciples who are told to pray are in the next verse the ones sent (10:1), so that the praying and the going belong together.
ch: The Catechism says that Christ’s compassion toward the sick and his many healings are a resplendent sign that God has visited his people (CCC 1503). The Second Vatican Council, drawing on this passage, taught that the duty of fostering vocations belongs to the whole Christian community, which must do so above all by a fully Christian life (Optatam Totius 2). That is why the Church keeps a day of prayer for vocations on the Fourth Sunday of Easter, Good Shepherd Sunday. Every Christian is both asked to pray for labourers and called to be one.

qa: Who was the man who wrestled with Jacob?

The text calls him “a man”, and Jacob concludes that he has seen God. Hosea 12:4 speaks of an angel. The story keeps the identity veiled: the opponent is God’s own messenger, speaking with God’s authority, who will not give his name (32:29). Christian readers have often seen in him a figure of God drawing close to humanity. What matters is the outcome: Jacob is blessed and renamed Israel.
study: Jacob would not let go until he was blessed. What blessing am I asking God for, and am I willing to persist in asking?
Jesus saw the crowds with compassion. Who around me looks “harassed and helpless”, and what can I do for them or pray for them?

lead: This week the weekday Mass begins the last great story of Genesis, the story of Joseph and his brothers, and at the same time the mission discourse of St Matthew, chapter 10. Today the famine reaches Egypt and Pharaoh sends the hungry to Joseph, the brother who was sold. In the Gospel Jesus names the Twelve and sends them out with his own authority to proclaim that the kingdom of heaven has come near. Psalm 33 gives the thread: the eye of the Lord is on those who fear him, to deliver them from death and keep them alive in famine.

r.h: Go to Joseph
set: The story of Joseph begins in chapter 37, where the favourite son of Jacob is thrown into a pit by his brothers and sold to traders. In Egypt he rises from slavery and prison to be governor under Pharaoh, after he has interpreted Pharaoh’s dream of seven good years and seven lean years (41:1–36). The lean years have now come.

Background. The reading joins two scenes. First, Egypt is hungry and Joseph opens the storehouses, so that “all the world” comes to him for grain. Then Jacob’s sons come from Canaan, where the famine has also reached, and bow to the ground before the brother they sold, who is now a stranger in Egyptian dress. The dream of Joseph’s boyhood, of sheaves bowing down (37:7), is fulfilled, but Joseph does not use his power for revenge. The passage skips the middle of chapter 42, in which the brothers are accused as spies.
str: 41:55–57: Pharaoh sends the starving to Joseph; he opens the storehouses and the whole world comes to him.
42:5–7: the sons of Israel come to buy grain and bow to Joseph, who recognizes them and speaks harshly.
42:17–20: three days in prison, and then the condition: one brother stays, the others bring the youngest.
42:21–24: the brothers speak of their guilt, Reuben reminds them, and Joseph, who understands, turns away and weeps.
kw: From the verb to break. Genesis 41–42 uses this one word again and again for grain, as if to say: the bread that breaks the hunger.
The brothers’ own word in 42:21. After more than twenty years, a hard word from a stranger makes them remember what they did, and say it aloud.
In 42:23 the brothers do not know that Joseph understands them, because an interpreter stands between them. The man whose language they think he cannot follow hears every word of their remorse.
vv: Go to Joseph; what he says to you, do.

Nine words in English, and a pointer for the whole story. Pharaoh sends the hungry to the one who was rejected. Christian readers have often heard in these words an echo of Mary’s word at Cana, “Do whatever he tells you” (John 2:5).
And Joseph’s brothers came and bowed themselves before him with their faces to the ground.
The reader remembers the dream of chapter 37. The brothers do not know whom they bow to, but Joseph knows.
Alas, we are paying the penalty for what we did to our brother; we saw his anguish when he pleaded with us, but we would not listen.
A new detail: only now do we learn that Joseph pleaded with them. Guilt that was buried for more than twenty years is brought up by hardship, and this is the beginning of their change.
He turned away from them and wept;
The harsh governor weeps in secret. His severity is not hatred. Joseph is testing the brothers, as the following chapters show, and he longs for the family to be whole.
ch: Since early times Christians have seen in Joseph a figure of Christ: the beloved son who is handed over by his brothers, falls low, and then becomes the one who feeds the world. Preachers have often heard in Pharaoh’s word “Go to Joseph” a call to go to Christ, the bread for the hungry. Remember that the story is first the Jewish people’s own story of how Israel came to Egypt and was preserved there by God; Christians read it as part of the one history of salvation (Nostra Aetate 4). The Catechism teaches that God is Lord of history and is able to draw good even from the sin of men (CCC 312, quoting Genesis 50:20).

r.h: The Twelve are sent
set: Matthew has gathered Jesus’ teaching into five great discourses. The second is the mission discourse of chapter 10, which we read this week. It is introduced by Jesus’ compassion at the sight of the crowds, “harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd”, and his word that the harvest is plentiful and the labourers few (9:36–38). Chapter 10 is the answer: the Twelve are the labourers.

Background. The number twelve is not accidental. It recalls the twelve tribes of Israel; Jesus is gathering and renewing Israel. The mission is first to “the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (v. 6), as the first stage in the history of salvation, before the Gospel goes to the nations after Easter (Matthew 28:19). The list of names is one of four in the New Testament (compare Mark 3:16–19; Luke 6:14–16; Acts 1:13), and each names Peter first.
str: v. 1: Jesus calls the twelve disciples and gives them authority over unclean spirits and every sickness.
vv. 2–4: the names of the twelve apostles, in pairs.
vv. 5–6: the mission is first to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.
v. 7: the message: the kingdom of heaven has come near.
kw: From the verb to send. Matthew uses this noun only here (10:2). The apostles do not act on their own authority but on that of the one who sends them.
Not their own power but a share in Jesus’ authority over evil spirits and sickness, which Matthew has just shown in chapters 8 and 9.
The same message as that of John the Baptist (3:2) and of Jesus himself (4:17). The kingdom is not only coming; it is at the door.
vv: Then Jesus summoned his twelve disciples and gave them authority
Authority is given, not taken. The disciples go out as those who were first with him.
Simon, also known as Peter,
Matthew writes “first, Simon”, and so places Peter at the head of the list. Matthew himself is named in v. 3 as “the tax collector”, a reminder that Jesus calls the unlikely.
Judas Iscariot, the one who betrayed him.
The Gospel does not hide that a traitor stood among the Twelve. Even a call from Jesus must be answered every day.
As you go, proclaim the good news, ‘The kingdom of heaven has come near.’
The disciples’ task is simple: to proclaim. The healings and the freedom from evil (v. 8) follow the word as signs of the kingdom.
ch: The Catechism teaches that from the beginning of his public life Jesus chose twelve men to be with him and to share in his mission, giving them a share in his authority (CCC 551), and that the Lord endowed his community with a structure that remains until the kingdom is fully achieved, beginning with the choice of the Twelve with Peter at their head (CCC 765). The kingdom was first announced to the children of Israel and is meant to receive people of all nations (CCC 543). Bishops are sent in the line of the apostles, and priests share in their ministry (CCC 861).

qa: Why did Jesus first send his disciples only to Israel?

In the plan of God, Israel was the people to whom the promises had been given, and the Messiah was sent first to them (compare Romans 15:8). The mission of the Twelve to Israel is the first step; after the Resurrection the risen Lord sends the same disciples to all nations (Matthew 28:19). The earlier command does not close the door on others; it follows the order of God’s revealing.
study: Joseph wept in secret over the brothers who had harmed him. What does this teach me about dealing with a wrong that was done to me?
To whom has Jesus sent me, in my family, my parish or my work, and what is the simple message I am to carry?

lead: Today the story of Joseph reaches its climax. Judah, who once proposed selling Joseph, steps forward and offers himself in place of Benjamin; and Joseph can no longer hold back. “I am your brother, Joseph, whom you sold into Egypt.” In the Gospel Jesus goes on instructing the Twelve: heal, raise, cleanse, “You received without payment; give without payment.” Both readings are about gift. Joseph gives his brothers a life they did not deserve, and the disciples are to give as a gift what they have received as a gift. Psalm 105 sings the same story from God’s side: he sent a man ahead of them, Joseph, who was sold as a slave.

r.h: I am Joseph, your brother
set: On their second journey to Egypt the brothers brought Benjamin, the youngest, as the governor demanded. Joseph then had his silver cup hidden in Benjamin’s sack and had the brothers arrested on the road, saying that the one in whose sack it was found would become his slave (44:1–17). This was the last test: would they again abandon a favoured brother of Rachel, as they once abandoned Joseph?

Background. Judah’s plea is one of the longest speeches in Genesis. The Lectionary gives it in part, leaving out vv. 22, 23a and 30–34. In the part left out Judah says that he will remain as a slave in Benjamin’s place so that the boy may go home to his father. It is the same Judah who once said, “Come, let us sell him” (37:27). Years ago he spoke of selling a brother; now he offers to be sold himself. The brothers have changed, and this is what Joseph needed to know.
str: 44:18–21, 23b–26: Judah begins humbly and recalls how the governor asked about a father and a brother, and how the brothers refused to leave Benjamin behind.
44:27–29: he quotes the words of old Jacob: one son lost, and the loss of the other would send him to the grave in sorrow.
45:1–3: Joseph cannot control himself; he sends the Egyptians out, weeps aloud and reveals himself, asking first: “Is my father still alive?”
45:4–5: he calls the brothers close and tells them not to be distressed, for God sent him ahead to preserve life.
kw: Judah calls himself “your servant” over and over in this speech, and calls Jacob “your servant my father”. The humility of the word shows how far Judah has come from the man who sold his brother.
Joseph could no longer hold himself back in front of all those who stood by (45:1). The verb means to restrain. Long hidden love breaks through.
Joseph interprets the whole story with this word (45:5). What the brothers meant as death for him, God turned into life for many.
vv: Then Judah stepped up to him and said,

Judah steps forward as spokesman and advocate. In Jewish tradition he becomes the one who takes responsibility, and from his tribe David and, as Matthew’s genealogy says, Jesus will come (Matthew 1:2–3).
his father loves him.
The brothers once hated Joseph because their father loved him more (37:4). Now Judah speaks for the favoured child with love, not envy.
Then Joseph could no longer control himself before all those who stood by him,
The man who has been hard and strange for two chapters breaks. His heart was never closed.
I am your brother, Joseph, whom you sold into Egypt.
He names the wrong plainly, without hiding it, and in the next breath he forgives. Forgiveness does not pretend that nothing happened.
for God sent me before you to preserve life.
This is a reading of history in faith: not that the crime was good, but that God was able to use it for life. Verse 8 adds that it was God who sent him.
ch: The Church has read the scene of the discovery as a picture of reconciliation, in which the one who was wronged takes the first step. The Catechism teaches that it is not in our power not to feel an offence, but the heart that offers itself to the Holy Spirit turns injury into compassion and purifies memory by turning hurt into intercession (CCC 2843). The Fathers also saw in Judah, who offers himself in place of Benjamin, a figure of Christ, who gave himself in our place; this is a reading in the tradition, not the sense of the text itself.

r.h: Give without payment
set: The mission discourse continues. In yesterday’s verses Jesus named the twelve apostles and began the instructions; today he says what they are to do, what they are to take, and how they are to be received. The setting is the Galilee of the early ministry, where the disciples go out to the villages around them.

Background. The disciples are to travel light: no money in the belt, no bag, no second tunic. The point is not hardship but trust. In Jewish custom a hosting household was a duty of hospitality, and the messenger of a teacher was received as the teacher himself. The greeting of peace (shalom) was the usual greeting on entering a house; here it becomes a gift that can rest or return.
str: vv. 7–8: proclaim the kingdom; heal, raise, cleanse, cast out; what was given as a gift is to be given as a gift.
vv. 9–10: no gold, no bag, no second tunic: the labourer deserves his food.
vv. 11–13: look for a worthy house; greet it; let your peace rest on it, or return to you.
vv. 14–15: if a town will not receive you, shake off the dust; its fate is grave.
kw: The same Greek word is used in Romans 3:24 for the grace by which we are justified, a gift that cannot be earned. Everything the apostles have is gift, so they must not trade on it.
The Greek translates shalom: wholeness, well-being and a right relation with God and neighbour. The disciples carry it with them, and it is not lost if it is refused.
Used for the house, in vv. 11–13. It means a house ready to welcome, not one that has earned the right by merit.
vv: Cure the sick, raise the dead, cleanse the lepers, cast out demons.
The disciples continue the works of Jesus in chapters 8 and 9. The kingdom is announced in word and in deed.
You received without payment; give without payment.
The root of the apostolic ministry: the gift of God cannot be sold. The Church has always taken this word as a warning against making money from sacred things.
for laborers deserve their food.
Those who serve the Gospel may rightly be supported by the community. A similar saying is echoed in 1 Timothy 5:18, and Paul gives the same principle in 1 Corinthians 9:14.
let your peace come upon it; but if it is not worthy, let your peace return to you.
The disciples’ peace is not wasted if it is refused; it returns to them. They carry it as a gift they never lose.
shake off the dust from your feet as you leave that house or town.
A sign of leaving without taking anything away, and without any anger of revenge. The disciples are not to curse a town; they leave its fate with God.
ch: The Catechism, on the sin of simony, recalls that spiritual things cannot be bought or sold, and quotes Peter’s answer to Simon the magician (CCC 2121). The Church applies the word “You received without payment” above all to the sacraments, which are given as gifts of Christ and are not sold. The faithful, for their part, are to provide for the needs of the Church and her ministers, following the word “laborers deserve their food”. The Church has also read the apostles’ lack of means as a call to evangelical poverty and simplicity in every ministry. The warning about Sodom and Gomorrah is a warning to take the word of God seriously; it is not a reason for contempt toward any people.

qa: Does “shake off the dust” mean we should leave anyone who rejects the Gospel?

No. The gesture belongs to the first mission of the Twelve, who were to go on quickly to the next village, and it says that they are not responsible for the choice of those who refuse. Jesus himself never stopped loving those who rejected him, and he told the disciples to forgive (Matthew 18:21–22). Dialogue and patient witness remain the way of the Church.
study: Joseph named the wrong and forgave in the same breath. Is there a wrong I have been unable to speak of, or to forgive?
What gift have I received from God that I am meant to hand on as a gift to others this week?

lead: The family of Jacob goes down into Egypt. At Beer-sheba, on the edge of the promised land, the old patriarch is afraid, and God speaks to him in the night: “Do not be afraid to go down to Egypt … I myself will go down with you.” In the Gospel Jesus sends the Twelve out “like sheep into the midst of wolves”, and promises that the Spirit of their Father will speak through them. Both readings are about being sent into a place that is not safe, with God going along. Psalm 37 gives the quiet confidence: the salvation of the righteous is from the Lord, their refuge in time of trouble. Some places keep today the optional memorial of St Augustine Zhao Rong and his companions, the martyrs of China; the readings are those of the weekday.

r.h: I will go down with you to Egypt
set: Joseph has revealed himself and Pharaoh has invited Jacob’s whole household to come and live in Egypt (45:16–20). Jacob, now called Israel, sets out with all that he has. In this chapter the text moves between his two names: Jacob, the name he was born with, and Israel, the name given after the struggle at the Jabbok (32:28).

Background. Beer-sheba is the southernmost place of the promised land, where Abraham planted a tree and called on the name of the Lord, and Isaac built an altar (21:33; 26:25). To go further is to leave the land God promised. Isaac had been told not to go down to Egypt in a famine (26:2), so Jacob’s hesitation is understandable. The words of God in v. 3 answer his fear. The reading leaves out the list of the seventy persons of Jacob’s house who came into Egypt (46:8–27).
str: vv. 1–4: at Beer-sheba Israel offers sacrifices, and God speaks in the night: do not be afraid; I will go down with you and bring you up again.
vv. 5–7: Jacob’s sons carry him, their families and their livestock into Egypt in Pharaoh’s wagons.
vv. 28–30: Judah leads the way to Goshen; Joseph meets his father, weeps on his neck, and Israel says he can die now.
kw: The word of God to the patriarchs and the prophets at moments of great decision (15:1; 26:24; Isaiah 41:10). Faith begins where fear is answered by a promise.
The promise first made to Abraham (12:2) is renewed in a place that seems the opposite of promise. Israel will become a people in Egypt, not in Canaan.
to go up, to bring up
God promises that he will “bring you up” again. In the Bible this is the language of the Exodus and of the pilgrimage to Jerusalem. The descent to Egypt already carries the hope of a return.
vv: God spoke to Israel in visions of the night, and said, “Jacob, Jacob.”
God calls by name, twice, as he did to Abraham (22:11) and to Moses (Exodus 3:4). The old man hears the name of his beginning.
do not be afraid to go down to Egypt, for I will make of you a great nation there.
God does not avoid Egypt; he goes into it. The place of danger becomes the place of growth.
I myself will go down with you to Egypt, and I will also bring you up again;
Two promises: presence and return. The same God who goes down with Jacob will later go down to see Israel’s affliction in Egypt (Exodus 3:7–8).
Joseph’s own hand shall close your eyes.
A tender promise: Jacob will die in the presence of the son he thought dead.
I can die now, having seen for myself that you are still alive.
Jacob’s words recall Simeon in the Temple, who was ready to depart in peace after seeing the child (Luke 2:29–30). A long grief ends in joy.
ch: The Church reads the descent of Israel into Egypt in the light of the Exodus and of the flight of the Holy Family into Egypt, where Matthew sees Hosea’s words fulfilled: “Out of Egypt I called my son” (Matthew 2:15). The word of God to Jacob, “I myself will go down with you”, is read as a promise of God’s nearness. The Catechism teaches that the Son of God came down from heaven for us and for our salvation (CCC 456), so that God has gone down to share our condition. When the Church prays for migrants and refugees, this text gives a warm reminder: God does not leave those who are sent into another land.

r.h: Sheep in the midst of wolves
set: The mission discourse now turns from the instructions to the cost. After the details of the journey, Jesus is open with the Twelve: they will meet hostility. Matthew writes for a community, probably Jewish-Christian in origin, that already knew rejection and persecution, and the words of Jesus are placed where his readers could recognize their own experience.

Background. The first disciples were all Jews. When Jesus warns that they will be handed over to councils and flogged in the synagogues (v. 17), he speaks of conflicts inside the Jewish world of the first century, between a Jewish teacher’s followers and other Jewish authorities. This must never be turned into a charge against the Jewish people. The warnings also reach to governors and kings and to the Gentiles (v. 18), and to families (v. 21).
str: v. 16: sheep among wolves; be wise as serpents, innocent as doves.
vv. 17–18: they will be handed over to councils, flogged in synagogues and brought before governors and kings, as a testimony.
vv. 19–20: do not worry about what to say; the Spirit of your Father will speak through you.
vv. 21–23: betrayal even within families; hatred for the sake of Jesus’ name; the one who endures will be saved; flee to the next town.
kw: The word for practical wisdom, the sense of the one who builds his house on rock (7:24). The serpent’s cleverness in the story of Genesis is here turned to good use.

Literally unmixed, as of pure metal or undiluted wine. The disciple is to be simple and without double dealing. Prudence without simplicity becomes cunning; simplicity without prudence becomes naivety.
Not only to put up with, but to remain under: the staying power of those who keep faith under pressure.
vv: See, I am sending you out like sheep into the midst of wolves;
The sender is Jesus, “I am sending you”. The disciples are not sent to be safe but to be faithful, and the Shepherd goes with the sheep.
so be wise as serpents and innocent as doves.
Both together. Jesus does not call for naivety, and he does not call for cleverness that lies.
do not worry about how you are to speak or what you are to say;
The promise is not that there will be no trial but that the Spirit will give the word at the hour. It does not forbid preparation for teaching; it speaks of the hour of testimony.
it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you.
The martyrs have often recalled this. The words of witness are a gift of God, and so the witness is not a matter of eloquence.
But the one who endures to the end will be saved.
Salvation is God’s gift and also asks for perseverance. The Church speaks of final perseverance as a grace that we ask for (CCC 1821).
When they persecute you in one town, flee to the next;
Flight is not cowardice. Jesus himself withdrew when his hour had not yet come, and the Church has never required anyone to seek martyrdom.
ch: The Church sees in this Gospel the pattern of all Christian witness. The Catechism teaches that the disciple must not only keep the faith but profess it and bear witness to it with confidence (CCC 1816), and that martyrdom is the supreme witness given to the truth of the faith (CCC 2473). The last words of v. 23, “before the Son of Man comes”, have been understood in several ways, as referring to the Resurrection and Pentecost, to the fall of Jerusalem in the year 70, or to the continuing mission to Israel until the end; the Church does not settle the question by a definition. The Church’s own history confirms the warning: in every century Christians in many lands have been hated for the name of Jesus, and she prays today for all who suffer for the faith, and for those who wrong them.

qa: Does Jesus want his disciples to run away from persecution?

He allows it. “When they persecute you in one town, flee to the next” shows that prudence is part of discipleship. The Church honours the martyrs who stood firm when flight was not possible or when faith itself was at stake, but she has never taught that anyone should seek suffering for its own sake.
rite: Today the Roman Calendar gives the optional memorial of St Augustine Zhao Rong and his companions, the 120 martyrs of China canonized in the year 2000, who died between the seventeenth and the twentieth century. Zhao Rong was a soldier who guarded a bishop under arrest, was moved by his witness, became a Christian and later a priest, and died in prison in 1815. Their story shows how Jesus’ words, “the Spirit of your Father speaking through you”, have been lived.
study: Where in my life do I feel “like a sheep among wolves”, and how can I be wise and innocent there at the same time?
Jacob was afraid to leave the promised land, and God said, “I myself will go down with you.” What fear of mine can I put before God in prayer today?

lead: Today the Book of Genesis ends, and the Gospel of the week keeps its theme: do not be afraid. After Jacob’s death the brothers fear that Joseph will take his revenge, and Joseph answers, “Do not be afraid! Am I in the place of God? You intended to do harm to me, but God intended it for good.” In the Gospel Jesus tells the Twelve three times not to fear: not the opposition, not those who kill the body, for the Father counts every sparrow and every hair of your head. Psalm 105 calls the people to seek the Lord and his strength, and to remember the wonderful works he has done. Where it is kept, the Saturday memorial of the Blessed Virgin Mary may be celebrated; the readings are those of the weekday.

r.h: God intended it for good
set: Genesis 49 gives the last words of Jacob, who blesses each of his twelve sons. Today’s reading begins with his final charge: to be buried with his fathers in the cave at Machpelah. Chapter 50 tells of the great funeral in Canaan (50:1–14). When the brothers return to Egypt, the fear they had put aside comes back.

Background. Joseph had forgiven his brothers seventeen years earlier (45:5; 47:28). But the brothers cannot believe forgiveness is real once their protector is gone. The reading ends the book with the death of Joseph in Egypt, in a coffin, and with a promise: God will come and lead the people up to the land he swore to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Genesis ends in a coffin and in hope. The Lectionary leaves out 49:33 and 50:1–14, the death and burial of Jacob.
str: 49:29–32: Jacob’s charge: bury me with my ancestors at Machpelah, the field Abraham bought.
50:15–18: the brothers fear that Joseph will repay them; they send a message in Jacob’s name and fall down before him.
50:19–21: Joseph weeps, says “Do not be afraid! Am I in the place of God?” and promises to provide for them.
50:22–26: Joseph lives one hundred ten years; he foretells that God will come, makes the Israelites swear to carry up his bones, and dies.
kw: The same verb is used twice in v. 20: you “intended” evil, God “intended” it for good. The same event has two authors: human sin and divine providence, and God’s purpose wins.
“God will surely come to you” (v. 24). The verb is used again in Exodus 3:16, when God visits his people in their slavery. It means a coming with power to save.
The Hebrew of v. 21 says Joseph “spoke to their hearts”. It is the language of tenderness (Hosea 2:14). Forgiveness here is not only a verdict but a tender word.
vv: There Abraham and his wife Sarah were buried; there Isaac and his wife Rebekah were buried; and there I buried Leah
Jacob lists the graves of his family. The only piece of the promised land the patriarchs own is a tomb, and Jacob wants to lie there in hope that the land will one day be his people’s.
What if Joseph still bears a grudge against us
Guilt does not believe in forgiveness easily. The brothers judge Joseph by their own hearts.
Do not be afraid! Am I in the place of God?
Joseph refuses to take the place of the judge. Vengeance belongs to God alone (Deuteronomy 32:35).
Even though you intended to do harm to me, God intended it for good, in order to preserve a numerous people, as he is doing today.
The summit of the Joseph story. It does not say that the wrong was right. It says that God is greater than evil and can bring good out of it.
