In this way he reassured them, speaking kindly to them.
Forgiveness is shown by both providing and speaking tenderly. Joseph promises food and he comforts.
you shall carry up my bones from here.

Joseph’s hope looks beyond Egypt. His bones were carried out at the Exodus (Exodus 13:19) and buried at Shechem (Joshua 24:32). The Letter to the Hebrews names this as an act of faith (Hebrews 11:22).
ch: The Catechism uses the words of Joseph to teach that God can bring good out of evil: it is one of the great examples in Scripture (CCC 312, quoting Genesis 50:20). The Church also reads the end of Genesis as a sign of hope against the grave. Joseph, who forgave and fed those who had harmed him, has long been seen as a figure of Christ, who prayed for those who crucified him and who gives himself as bread. Christians, as the Catechism says of forgiveness, ask for the grace to do what Joseph did (CCC 2843). The reading is also, first of all, the Jewish people’s own story of the end of the patriarchs and the beginning of the people of Israel.

r.h: You are of more value than many sparrows
set: The mission discourse of chapter 10 now comes to its centre: three times in vv. 26, 28 and 31 Jesus says “do not fear”. The disciples will be maligned as their master was. Matthew places this teaching just after the warning of persecution, to show that fear is answered by trust in the Father.

Background. In Jewish households a slave or pupil was bound to his master or teacher. “Beelzebul” in v. 25 is the name the opponents gave to the prince of demons when they accused Jesus (12:24; compare 9:34). To call the master of the house this is to call his whole household the same. A sparrow was the cheapest food in the market, sold for a small coin; in Luke the price is five sparrows for two coins (Luke 12:6).
str: vv. 24–25: the disciple is like the teacher; if they malign the master, they will malign his household.
vv. 26–27: do not fear: what is hidden will be revealed; proclaim from the housetops what you hear in secret.
vv. 28–31: do not fear those who kill the body; the Father knows each sparrow and counts each hair; you are of more value.
vv. 32–33: whoever acknowledges Jesus before others, Jesus acknowledges before the Father; whoever denies him, he denies.
kw: Perhaps “Baal the prince”, from the name of a pagan god (the origin of the name is debated); the Gospels use it for the prince of demons (12:24). The opponents of Jesus used it to belittle his power over evil spirits.

The verb appears with and without “not” in vv. 26–31. The Bible distinguishes the fear that paralyses from the reverent fear of God, which is the beginning of wisdom (Proverbs 1:7) and delivers us from every other fear.
Literally “to say the same thing”: to speak out for Jesus, as he speaks for us. The word later becomes the word for a confession of faith.
vv: A disciple is not above the teacher, nor a slave above the master;
Discipleship means sharing the master’s way, including its cost. The disciple is not exempt from what the Master meets.
What I say to you in the dark, tell in the light; and what you hear whispered, proclaim from the housetops.
Jesus taught his disciples in private, but the teaching is for all. The flat roofs of Palestine were a natural place for a public announcement.
Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell.

Most Fathers and commentators understand “him who can destroy” as God, the true judge (compare Luke 12:5). The sense is that nothing human is to frighten the disciple more than the loss of fellowship with God.
Yet not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father.
God’s care reaches the smallest of creatures. Not “without his knowledge” only, but within the knowledge and love of the Father.
And even the hairs of your head are all counted.
A picture of the attention of a father’s love. There is nothing about you that is overlooked.
So do not be afraid; you are of more value than many sparrows.
The argument from lesser to greater: if the Father cares for sparrows, how much more for his children.
ch: The Catechism quotes vv. 29–31 when it teaches about divine providence: Jesus asks for a childlike abandonment to the care of our heavenly Father, who looks after the smallest needs of his children (CCC 305). Verses 32–33 are the root of the Christian duty to confess the faith openly; the Catechism teaches that the Christian must not be ashamed to bear witness to the Lord (CCC 2471). The Church also teaches that the one who confesses Christ before others is acknowledged by Christ before the Father, and the one who denies him is denied; this is a call to fidelity and not a threat to the weak, for Peter who denied was forgiven (John 21:15–17).

qa: Does Jesus tell us to fear God, or not to fear?

Both, but in two different senses. We are never to fear in the sense of terror at a God who wants our harm: “do not be afraid” runs through the whole passage, and the Father numbers the hairs of our head. But the Bible keeps a holy fear of God, a reverent awe and a horror of losing him through sin, which is the beginning of wisdom. The Catechism teaches that the fear of the Lord is a gift of the Holy Spirit (CCC 1831).
study: The brothers could not quite believe in Joseph’s forgiveness. Where do I find it hard to believe that God has really forgiven me?
Which of my fears is the Father’s word “you are of more value than many sparrows” speaking to today?

lead: The three readings of this Fifteenth Sunday of Year B are about being chosen and sent. In the first, Amos is a herdsman and a dresser of sycamore trees whom the Lord took “from following the flock” and sent to prophesy to Israel; the priest of the king’s sanctuary orders him home, and he answers that he did not choose this work, God did. In the Gospel Jesus calls the Twelve, sends them out two by two with authority over unclean spirits, tells them to take almost nothing for the road, and they go out to proclaim repentance, to cast out demons and to anoint the sick with oil. Between the two, the opening of the Letter to the Ephesians tells us why: before the foundation of the world God chose us in Christ and destined us to be his children, so that the whole plan of his will might gather all things in Christ.

Psalm 85, the Sunday’s psalm, is the prayer of the listener: “Let me hear what God the Lord will speak, for he will speak peace to his people”, and “Steadfast love and faithfulness will meet; righteousness and peace will kiss each other.” The word that sends the prophet and the apostles is a word of peace. The memorial of St Benedict, abbot and patron of Europe, falls on this Sunday and is not kept this year; the Mass is of the Sunday.

r.h: The Lord took me from following the flock
set: Amos prophesied in the northern kingdom of Israel around the middle of the eighth century before Christ, in the time of King Jeroboam II (about 790–750). It was a time of peace and prosperity, and of injustice: the rich sold the poor for a pair of sandals (2:6; 8:6). Amos was not from the north. He came from Tekoa, a village in Judah, south of Bethlehem (1:1), and he spoke harshly against the sins of the powerful. “Let justice roll down like waters” is his best known word (5:24).

Background. Bethel was one of the two royal sanctuaries of the northern kingdom (1 Kings 12:29). Its priest Amaziah heard Amos announce that Jeroboam would die and Israel would go into exile, and he reported it to the king (vv. 10–11, left out of the reading). The reading is Amaziah’s order and Amos’s answer. Amaziah speaks like a state official: go home and earn your bread there. This is one of the earliest accounts we have of a prophet explaining where his authority comes from.
str: vv. 12–13: Amaziah tells Amos, the “seer”, to flee to Judah, earn his bread there and never again prophesy at Bethel, because it is the king’s sanctuary.
v. 14: Amos answers that he is no prophet by profession, but a herdsman and dresser of sycamore trees.
v. 15: the Lord took him from following the flock and sent him to prophesy to his people Israel.
kw: Amaziah’s word for Amos. Seers could be paid for their service at sanctuaries; he tells Amos to take his gift elsewhere and “earn his bread”.

One who speaks for God. Amos distances himself from the professional bands of prophets (“prophet’s son” means a member of such a guild). The Hebrew has no verb, so it can be read “I am no prophet” or “I was no prophet”; either way, Amos says his authority is not from his profession but from God’s call.
“The Lord took me” (v. 15). The same verb is used when God takes a person for his purposes, as he took Abraham (Joshua 24:3) and David (2 Samuel 7:8). It is God who begins, not Amos.
vv: O seer, go, flee away to the land of Judah, earn your bread there, and prophesy there;
Amaziah does not deny that Amos has a message; he says it belongs in a place where no one will be disturbed by it. Religion tied to the king’s favour becomes unable to hear a word of God.
but never again prophesy at Bethel, for it is the king’s sanctuary, and it is a temple of the kingdom.
“The king’s sanctuary”: worship at Bethel had become part of the royal order. The prophet’s word is a challenge to the idea that God belongs to the state.
I am no prophet, nor a prophet’s son; but I am a herdsman, and a dresser of sycamore trees,

Amos names his ordinary work. A sycamore fig tree gave cheap food for the poor, and the dresser nipped the fruit so that it would ripen. He was a working man of Judah, not a member of a religious class.
and the Lord took me from following the flock, and the Lord said to me, ‘Go, prophesy to my people Israel.’

The call came in the midst of work, as it did for David (2 Samuel 7:8), and for the fishermen of Galilee (Mark 1:17). Notice also “my people Israel”: the one who sends him from Judah calls the northern kingdom his people.
ch: The Church confesses in the Creed that the Holy Spirit “has spoken through the prophets” (CCC 702). Amos stands for the prophet who does not choose his mission and cannot be silenced by those in power, and for the link between worship and justice that runs through the prophets: God does not accept sacrifices from a people who trample on the poor (Amos 5:21–24). The Church teaches that all the baptized share in Christ’s prophetic office, to bear witness to the truth (Lumen Gentium 12 and 35). The scene also invites us to remember that all who are sent, in every age, are sent by God and not by the favour of the powerful.

r.h: He chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world
set: Ephesians is a letter in the name of Paul, written from prison (3:1; 4:1; 6:20). Many scholars think it was written by a disciple of Paul who developed his thought, others hold that Paul himself wrote it; the Church receives it as inspired Scripture in the apostolic tradition either way. Some early manuscripts omit “in Ephesus” in the first verse, and some think it was a circular letter for the churches of Asia Minor. Its first part (chapters 1–3) praises the plan of God, and the second (chapters 4–6) draws out the life of the Church.

Background. In the Greek, vv. 3–14 are a single sentence, a hymn of blessing in the manner of the Jewish prayer “Blessed be God”. It moves through the work of the Trinity: the Father who chooses and destines (vv. 3–6), the Son in whom we have redemption (vv. 7–12), and the Holy Spirit who seals the believers (vv. 13–14). The refrain “to the praise of his glory” closes each part (vv. 6, 12, 14). The shorter form ends at v. 10.
str: v. 3: blessing of the Father, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing.
vv. 4–6: the Father chose us in Christ before the world, to be holy, and destined us for adoption as his children.
vv. 7–10: in Christ we have redemption and the forgiveness of sins; the mystery of his will: to gather up all things in Christ.
vv. 11–14 (full form): the inheritance; those who first hoped in Christ, and “you also”; the seal of the Holy Spirit, the pledge of our inheritance.
kw: The Greek translation of the Jewish blessing bārûk. We bless God because he first blessed us (v. 3). The word begins the letter’s long hymn.
God’s plan is not only to forgive but to make us children, by sharing in the Son (Galatians 4:5–6; Romans 8:15). The word is from the Roman legal practice of adoption.
to gather up, to sum up

Literally to bring under one head. All things in heaven and on earth are to be united under Christ as head (compare 1:22). St Irenaeus of Lyons, in the second century, built his teaching on this idea that Christ recapitulates, or sums up, all things in himself (in substance).
A commercial word for a down payment that guarantees the rest. The Holy Spirit is God’s first gift, the guarantee that the full inheritance will follow.
vv: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places,
The letter begins with praise, not a request. The blessing is already given, “in Christ”: this phrase and its cousins appear again and again in vv. 3–14.
just as he chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world to be holy and blameless before him in love.
God’s choice comes before the world was made. It is a choice for holiness, for a life lived in love. The Church reads it as God’s call to all in Christ, not as a choice of some for hell.
He destined us for adoption as his children through Jesus Christ,
The goal is a family. We are not servants only, but sons and daughters in the Son.
In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses, according to the riches of his grace
Redemption was paid for by Christ’s blood, and the measure is the riches of grace. The Church sees here the offering of Christ on the Cross, made present in the Mass.
as a plan for the fullness of time, to gather up all things in him, things in heaven and things on earth.
The great vision of the letter: the division between heaven and earth, between Jew and Gentile, and the brokenness of creation are all to be gathered up in Christ.
were marked with the seal of the promised Holy Spirit;
A seal marks ownership and security. Baptism and the gift of the Spirit mark the believer as belonging to Christ.
this is the pledge of our inheritance toward redemption as God’s own people,
The Spirit is the guarantee. Our life now is a beginning, and the inheritance is to come.
ch: The Church places Ephesians 1:3–6 at the head of her teaching on the liturgy: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ” is the opening of the Catechism’s section on the blessing of the Father (CCC 1077). Christ’s whole life is a mystery of recapitulation, by which all things are summed up in him (CCC 518). On predestination the Church teaches that God’s eternal plan includes each person’s answer to his grace (CCC 600), and that God predestines no one to hell (CCC 1037). The reading also has a place for Israel: “we who were the first to set our hope on Christ” (v. 12) is generally understood as the Jewish believers, and “you also” (v. 13) as the Gentiles who join them. The Gentiles are brought into a hope that began with Israel.

r.h: Sent out two by two
set: This passage follows the rejection at Nazareth (6:1–6), when Jesus “was amazed at their unbelief” and went about the villages teaching. Mark then shows him sending out the Twelve, whom he had called to be “with him” and “to be sent out” (3:14). The mission of the Twelve in Mark is shorter than in Matthew 10, and tells what the disciples did rather than a long discourse.

Background. The disciples are sent “two by two”, which made their witness valid under the Jewish law (Deuteronomy 19:15) and gave them company. Mark allows a staff and sandals, which Matthew 10:10 does not, and the difference is a good example of how the evangelists adapt the tradition. The point in all of them is the same: dependence on God and on the hospitality of those who receive them. After the mission, the Twelve return and report all they did and taught (6:30).
str: v. 7: Jesus calls the Twelve, sends them out two by two and gives them authority over unclean spirits.
vv. 8–9: they take only a staff and sandals: no bread, bag, money or second tunic.
vv. 10–11: stay in the house where they are received; if a place will not welcome them, shake off the dust as a testimony.
vv. 12–13: they proclaim repentance, cast out demons and anoint many sick people with oil.
kw: The same root as apostolos, apostle. In 3:14 Jesus called them to be with him and to be sent: first the company, then the mission.
From metanoia, a change of mind and heart, a turning to God. The message of the disciples is that of Jesus himself in 1:15.
In the ancient world oil was used as medicine (Luke 10:34) and as a sign of the Spirit. Here it is joined with the proclamation and the casting out of demons as a sign of the coming of the kingdom.
vv: He called the twelve and began to send them out two by two, and gave them authority over the unclean spirits.
Jesus does not send them alone, and he does not send them empty. The authority is his, shared with them.
He ordered them to take nothing for their journey except a staff; no bread, no bag, no money in their belts;
The disciples must look like pilgrims. They carry the message and nothing else, and learn to depend on the Father.
but to wear sandals and not to put on two tunics.
Mark records even what they wore. The rule is plain: a traveller’s simplicity.
shake off the dust that is on your feet as a testimony against them.
The gesture is a sign that the disciples have done their duty and that the responsibility passes to the one who refuses. It is a sad warning, not an act of anger.
So they went out and proclaimed that all should repent.
The first mission of the Twelve is a mission of the word. The call to repent is a call to turn toward the God who is near.
They cast out many demons, and anointed with oil many who were sick and cured them.
The only mention in the Gospels of anointing the sick with oil in the ministry of the disciples; it is the root of the Church’s practice in James 5:14–15.
ch: The Church sees in this scene both the mission of the whole Church and the roots of a sacrament. The Church has recognized in the anointing of the sick in Mark 6:13 and James 5:14–15 a rite instituted by the Lord (CCC 1510). The whole Church is sent: the Church is missionary by her very nature, because she is sent by the Father through the Son and the Spirit (Ad Gentes 2, CCC 850). The pairs recall the communal character of witness. Jesus shows that mission is not heroism but obedience: the disciples take what he gives and go where he sends. The Church also keeps the Gospel’s gentleness: when a place refuses the Gospel, the disciples go on, and the Church prays for those who refuse.

qa: Does Ephesians say that God chose some people for heaven and others for hell?

No. The Church teaches that God desires all to be saved (1 Timothy 2:4) and predestines no one to hell (CCC 1037). In Ephesians 1 the choice is “in Christ”, for holiness and adoption, and Paul speaks to a community of believers, giving thanks for their calling. The mystery of how God’s eternal plan and human freedom work together is held in faith, with the Catechism’s assurance that God’s plan includes each person’s response (CCC 600).
Why does Mark allow a staff and sandals when Matthew does not?

The Gospels have the same core instruction: travel light and trust God. The differences in detail show that each evangelist wrote for his own community and handed down the words of Jesus with some freedom of expression, while keeping their sense. The Church reads the four Gospels together and does not need to make them agree in every detail to hear the single message of simplicity.
rite: On this Sunday the Latin Church would keep the memorial of St Benedict, abbot, patron of Europe, but a Sunday in Ordinary Time takes precedence, so the Mass is of the Sunday. The Gloria and Creed are said. The anointing of the sick, which is rooted in the Gospel of today, is celebrated in parishes and at the bedside, and in some parishes also in a communal celebration for the elderly. In the monsoon season it is fitting, especially in Kerala, to remember in this Sunday’s prayers the farmers and the families affected by the rains, and the Church prays also for all who suffer from floods and storms in many lands.
study: Amos did not choose to be a prophet, but he did not refuse. What is the ordinary work in which God may be calling me?
Ephesians says God chose us “before the foundation of the world”. How does this change the way I think of my worth and my vocation?
Jesus sent the disciples two by two and with few things. Who is my companion in the mission, and what do I need to put down in order to travel lighter?
When the Gospel is not welcomed, how can I “shake off the dust” without anger and still pray for the people?

lead: From today the first reading is the Book of Exodus. The family that Joseph saved is now a people, and “a new king arose over Egypt, who did not know Joseph.” Gratitude is forgotten, and a fear of the foreigner turns into slavery and the killing of newborn boys. In the Gospel Jesus closes the mission discourse of Matthew 10 with words that are hard to hear: he has not come to bring peace but a sword, and whoever loves father or mother more than him is not worthy of him. Yet the discourse ends with a promise: whoever welcomes the disciples welcomes Christ, and even a cup of cold water given to a disciple will not lose its reward. Psalm 124 holds the two readings together: “Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth.”

r.h: A new king who did not know Joseph
set: The Book of Exodus takes its Greek name from the departure (exodos) of Israel from Egypt; in Hebrew it is called by its opening words, “These are the names”. It opens with a list of the sons of Jacob who came into Egypt (1:1–5), and a first note of fulfilment: “the Israelites were fruitful and prolific; they multiplied and grew exceedingly strong” (1:7). The language recalls the blessing of the creation of humankind (Genesis 1:28) and the promise to Abraham.

Background. The king is not named. Many scholars place the oppression in the thirteenth century before Christ, under the Pharaohs of the Nineteenth Dynasty, since the store cities Pithom and Rameses are in the eastern Delta; the Bible gives no name, and the date is debated. The text keeps its focus on the theme: a power that forgets the good done to it and fears the people who live in its land. The reading skips the story of the midwives Shiphrah and Puah, who refuse to kill the boys (1:15–21).
str: vv. 8–10: a new king who does not know Joseph fears the growth of the Israelites and proposes to “deal shrewdly” with them.
vv. 11–14: taskmasters, forced labour, store cities, bitter lives; yet the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied.
v. 22: Pharaoh commands that every Hebrew boy be thrown into the Nile.
kw: In the Bible “to know” means more than to have heard of: to recognize, to acknowledge. The king did not acknowledge what Joseph had done, and so did not recognize the people’s place in his kingdom.
The word for the forced labour in vv. 13–14 is the same word used later for the worship of God. The question of Exodus is: whom shall Israel serve? Pharaoh, or the Lord (Exodus 4:23)?
“They made their lives bitter” (v. 14). The memory is kept in the Passover meal, where bitter herbs are eaten as a sign of the bitterness of slavery.
vv: Now a new king arose over Egypt, who did not know Joseph.
Chapter 1 stands in contrast with the end of Genesis. There, Pharaoh honoured Joseph; here, the memory of the benefactor is lost. Gratitude can be forgotten within a generation.
Come, let us deal shrewdly with them,
The new policy is presented as prudence. Fear is turned into a plan that treats a whole people as a danger. The Bible uses the account to show how oppression begins in fear and calculation.
But the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied and spread,
The blessing of God cannot be stopped by oppression. It is the first sign in Exodus that the Lord is at work behind the scene.
and made their lives bitter with hard service in mortar and brick and in every kind of field labor.
The picture of bricks and mortar is well known from Egyptian paintings and texts. For Israel it is the memory of the house of bondage.
Every boy that is born to the Hebrews you shall throw into the Nile, but you shall let every girl live.
From forced labour the king moves to the killing of children. The Church’s memory of the slaughter of the innocents at Bethlehem (Matthew 2:16) hears an echo of this verse.
ch: The Church reads the Exodus as the great foundation of Israel’s faith, first of all the story of the Jewish people’s liberation, which Jews remember each year at Passover; Christians read it as the first stage of the history that leads to Christ. The Fathers saw in the slavery of Egypt a figure of the slavery of sin, and in the crossing of the sea a figure of Baptism. The Catechism recalls this in the liturgy of Baptism (CCC 1221). The slaughter of the boys, and the Child who is saved, prepare the reader for Moses, and for Jesus, who like him was saved from a king’s decree (Matthew 2:13–15). The Catechism also teaches that the seventh commandment forbids every enterprise that leads to the enslavement of human beings (CCC 2414). Today the Church prays for those who are held in forced labour or trafficked in many lands, and for those who do such wrong.

r.h: Not peace, but a sword
set: These are the last verses of the mission discourse. After the warning of persecution (10:16–23) and the call not to fear (10:24–33), Jesus now speaks of the cost within the household. The verses alternate between warning and promise. The discourse closes in 11:1 with the formula Matthew uses at the end of each of the five great discourses: “when Jesus had finished…”.

Background. The sword is a figure of division, as the parallel in Luke makes clear (12:51: “No, I tell you, but rather division”). Jesus is not calling for violence; he forbids Peter to use the sword in the garden (26:52). The words of vv. 35–36 come from the prophet Micah (7:6), who spoke of the breakdown of trust in a time of trouble. Jesus says that the call to follow him will split even families, as it did in the early Church, where a convert could be rejected by his house.
str: vv. 34–36: Jesus has come not to bring peace but a sword, to divide even members of one household.
vv. 37–39: whoever loves father, mother, son or daughter more than Jesus is not worthy of him; take up the cross; lose your life to find it.
vv. 40–42: whoever welcomes the disciples welcomes Jesus and the Father who sent him; the reward of the prophet, the righteous and the cup of cold water.
11:1: when Jesus had finished instructing the Twelve, he went on to teach in their cities.
kw: The short sword of the soldier or the knife of the sacrificer. As used here, it is a figure for division and decision, not for war.

This is the first mention of the cross in Matthew, long before the Passion. For his hearers it was the Roman punishment of the condemned, who carried the beam to the place of execution. The disciple is asked to follow the Master on the same road.
The word means life, soul and self. To “find” one’s life by clinging to it is to lose it; to give it up for Christ is to receive it back from God.
vv: Do not think that I have come to bring peace to the earth; I have not come to bring peace, but a sword.
The Christ whom the angels announced as bringing peace on earth (Luke 2:14) says that peace which avoids the truth is not what he brings. Following him divides, because it demands a choice.
and one’s foes will be members of one’s own household.
Taken from Micah 7:6. For first-century disciples, faith in Jesus could cost them the favour of their families. The verse describes a pain that the Church has seen in every age.
Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me;
Not a denial of family love, which God commands (Matthew 15:4–6), but the order of love: Christ first, and every other love in him.
and whoever does not take up the cross and follow me is not worthy of me.
The cross is not a general name for any trouble; it is the path of following Jesus, even to the point of giving up one’s life.
Those who find their life will lose it, and those who lose their life for my sake will find it.
A saying found in every Gospel. Life is a gift that is kept by being given, and lost by being clutched.
Whoever welcomes you welcomes me, and whoever welcomes me welcomes the one who sent me.
The chain of sending: Father, Son, apostles, and those who receive them. To welcome a messenger of Christ is to welcome God.
whoever gives even a cup of cold water to one of these little ones in the name of a disciple
The smallest act of kindness, given for Christ’s sake, has its reward. In Palestine, a cup of cold water was a precious courtesy in the heat.
ch: The Catechism, speaking of the fourth commandment, teaches that the bonds of family, though important, are not absolute: the call of Christ takes precedence, as Jesus says in v. 37 (CCC 2232). It teaches too that the way of perfection passes by way of the Cross, and that there is no holiness without renunciation and spiritual battle (CCC 2015). The saints are those who took these words literally, and found that the love of Christ makes love of family deeper, not smaller. The closing verses on welcome underlie the Church’s works of mercy, and the promise that a cup of water will not lose its reward is the “small way” of every Christian. The Church also prays for families divided over faith, that the peace of Christ may reach them.

qa: How can Jesus say he came to bring a sword when he is the Prince of Peace?

He speaks of the division that his call causes, not of violence. The peace he gives is real, but it is a peace that does not come by ignoring the truth or the demands of discipleship. Matthew puts these words beside Jesus’ refusal of the sword in Gethsemane (26:52). The Church does not read this verse as a justification for violence in the name of Christ, and she reminds us that the first to bear the cost of discipleship are the disciples themselves.
study: Where does following Jesus ask me to put him before something or someone I love, and how can this make my love of them deeper?
Who is “one of these little ones” to whom I can give a cup of cold water today, in the name of Christ?

lead: Today the Church tells two stories of towns and people who were given a great gift. In Exodus a baby is drawn out of the Nile by an Egyptian princess, and grows up to be the one who will draw Israel out of Egypt. In the Gospel Jesus speaks sorrowfully to the Galilean towns of Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum, where he did most of his mighty works, because they did not change their hearts. The first reading shows how God quietly saves; the Gospel shows how much is asked of those who have seen his work. Today the Church also remembers St Henry, the emperor who ruled in the early eleventh century and died in 1024; the Mass of the weekday is kept.

r.h: Drawn out of the water
set: The book of Exodus opens with the Israelites multiplying in Egypt and with a king who feared them. Pharaoh set them to forced labor (1:11–14) and then ordered that every Hebrew boy be thrown into the Nile (1:22). Chapter 2 begins with a family from the tribe of Levi who will not obey that decree. Their names are not given here; the Bible names them later as Amram and Jochebed (6:20).
str: vv. 1–4: a Levite mother hides her son for three months, then places him in a basket among the reeds, with his sister watching.
vv. 5–10: Pharaoh’s daughter finds him, takes pity, and unknowingly hires his own mother as his nurse; she names him Moses.
vv. 11–15a: the grown Moses sees the forced labor of his people, kills an Egyptian, and flees from Pharaoh to Midian.
kw: The same rare word is used for Noah’s ark (Genesis 6:14). In both stories a vessel of wood or reed carries life safely through the waters of death.
The mother “saw that he was a fine baby”. The Hebrew is the word of Genesis 1, “God saw that it was good”. A quiet echo of creation: a new life, a new beginning.

The name sounds like the Hebrew verb māšâ, “to draw out”, which the princess uses in her explanation. Many scholars note that the name may also be Egyptian, meaning “born of” as in the name Thutmose. Either way, the story says that this child is the one who will draw out a people.
vv: when she saw that he was a fine baby, she hid him three months.
The parents act in faith. The Letter to the Hebrews says that it was by faith that Moses was hidden by his parents, because they were not afraid of the king’s edict (Hebrews 11:23).
He was crying, and she took pity on him.

The one who saves the child is not an Israelite but a daughter of the very house that threatens him. God works through the compassion of a woman who disobeys her father’s decree. Her pity opens the way.
She named him Moses, “because,” she said, “I drew him out of the water.”
Moses grows up in Pharaoh’s palace but is nursed by his own mother, so he knows who he is. God prepares his servant in two worlds.
Who made you a ruler and judge over us?

Moses acted for his people but by his own anger and his own authority, and they refused him. Stephen later recalls these very words in Acts 7:27 and 35. God’s call will come, but at God’s hour and in his way.
ch: The Church has always read the life of Moses as a shadow of Christ. Matthew tells of the infancy of Jesus in a way that recalls this story: a wicked king orders the death of children, the child is saved, and he is brought out of Egypt (Matthew 2). The Letter to the Hebrews praises the faith of Moses’ parents and says that Moses chose to share the ill-treatment of God’s people rather than enjoy the pleasures of Pharaoh’s house (Hebrews 11:23–25). The water that carries and saves is also a sign the Church has loved: the Catechism recalls that the ark of Noah and the crossing of the Red Sea foreshadow the saving water of Baptism (CCC 1219–1221).

r.h: Woe to you, Chorazin!
set: After sending out the Twelve (chapter 10), Jesus answered the question of John the Baptist’s disciples and spoke of John and of “this generation” (11:2–19). Now he turns to the towns where he had done most of his deeds of power. Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum lay close together on the northern shore of the Sea of Galilee. Capernaum was the town Jesus made his home (4:13; 9:1), and Bethsaida was the home town of Philip, Andrew and Peter (John 1:44). All these hearers were Jews, and Jesus speaks as a prophet to his own people, as Amos and Jeremiah did before him.
str: v. 20: the reproach: the towns did not repent.
vv. 21–22: Chorazin and Bethsaida are compared with Tyre and Sidon.
vv. 23–24: Capernaum is compared with Sodom.
kw: The Gospel’s word for miracles. They are not meant to impress but to call people to turn to God.
Literally to change one’s mind and direction. Repentance is not only sorrow but a new way of living.
The cry of the prophets (Isaiah 5:8–23). It is as much a lament as a threat, like the cry of someone at a funeral: how sad that it should come to this.
vv: Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida!
Tyre and Sidon, pagan cities of the Phoenician coast, had been denounced by the prophets (Isaiah 23; Ezekiel 26–28). Jesus says that even they would have repented if they had seen what Galilee saw.
on the day of judgment it will be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon than for you.
Responsibility is measured by the light received. The more we have been given, the more is asked (compare Luke 12:48).
will you be exalted to heaven? No, you will be brought down to Hades.

These words echo Isaiah 14:13–15, where the proud king of Babylon wants to climb to heaven and is cast down to the pit. Capernaum, honored by the presence of Jesus, is warned not to make that kind of pride its own.
ch: The Church reads these words as a call to conversion, not as a curse on any town. The Catechism teaches that Jesus’ warnings about judgment are urgent calls to conversion and that God wishes no one to be lost (CCC 1036; 1037). The Fathers often taught that the more of God’s gifts we receive, in the word and in the sacraments, the more we are accountable for them (in substance). For us the question is whether the Gospel, heard every Sunday, really changes us.

qa: Does Jesus condemn the people of Capernaum and the other towns for ever?

The passage is a prophetic warning, spoken with sorrow. It does not say that every person in those towns was lost; many of Jesus’ closest followers came from them. Jesus compares the towns with Tyre, Sidon and Sodom to show how serious it is to receive God’s gifts and not respond. The goal of every woe in the Bible is repentance.
study: Moses’ mother and Pharaoh’s daughter each did a small act of courage and mercy. What small act could I do for a child or a family in danger?
Jesus says that more is asked of those who have seen more of God’s works. What have I been given that I have not yet answered?

lead: In the first reading God calls Moses out of a burning bush and sends him to deliver his people: God has seen their misery and will be with Moses. In the Gospel Jesus thanks his Father for hiding these things from the wise and revealing them to infants, and tells of the knowledge that only the Father and the Son share. Both readings show a God who comes down to the lowly. He reveals himself to a shepherd in a wilderness and to the little ones of Galilee. Today the Church also remembers St Camillus de Lellis (died 1614), founder of the Ministers of the Sick; the weekday readings are kept.

r.h: The bush that was not consumed
set: Moses, rescued as a baby and raised in Pharaoh’s house, fled to Midian after killing the Egyptian (2:11–15). There he married Zipporah, the daughter of the priest of Midian, and became a shepherd for his father-in-law. The call at the bush comes in the middle of ordinary work. The Lectionary leaves out vv. 7–8, in which God says he has seen the misery of his people and has come down to deliver them; v. 9 repeats the same message.
str: vv. 1–3: Moses leads the flock to Horeb and sees a bush burning that is not consumed.
vv. 4–6: God calls him by name, tells him to take off his sandals, and says who he is.
vv. 9–10: God has heard Israel’s cry and sends Moses to Pharaoh.
vv. 11–12: Moses objects, “Who am I?”, and God answers, “I will be with you.”
kw: A thorn bush of the desert. Many scholars see a play on the name Sinai, the mountain where Israel will later worship (v. 12).
What belongs to God and is set apart from ordinary use. The ground is holy not because of the place but because God is present there.
The verb is the same as in the divine name of v. 14. God does not answer “Who am I?” with a list of Moses’ gifts. He answers with his own presence.
vv: the bush was blazing, yet it was not consumed.
Fire in the Bible is a sign of God’s presence (Genesis 15:17; Exodus 19:18). A fire that burns without destroying shows a God who is near, yet does not consume those who come before him.
God called to him out of the bush, “Moses, Moses!” And he said, “Here I am.”
God calls by name, and the answer is the answer of every prophet: hinnēnî, “Here I am”. It is the readiness of Abraham (Genesis 22:1) and of Samuel (1 Samuel 3:4).
Remove the sandals from your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground.
The one who comes near God does so with reverence. Joshua will be told the same near Jericho (Joshua 5:15). Holiness is not frightening for those who come as invited.
The cry of the Israelites has now come to me;
God is not far from suffering. He hears the cry of the enslaved, and he chooses a human being to carry out his rescue.
Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh
The humility of Moses is real. God does not argue it away. He gives the one promise that is enough: “I will be with you” (v. 12).
ch: The Church sees in this scene a revelation of God’s holiness and nearness. The Catechism teaches that before the burning bush Moses learns that God is the Holy One, and it speaks of the prayer of Moses that begins here (CCC 205; 2575). Jesus himself uses the words of v. 6 when he teaches the resurrection: God is not the God of the dead but of the living (Mark 12:26–27). Early Christian writers, including St Gregory of Nyssa (in substance), saw in the bush that burned without being consumed a figure of the Virgin Mary, who carried the divine fire of the Word in her womb and remained a virgin; this reading is still honored in the liturgical hymns of the East and the West.

r.h: Revealed to infants
set: The prayer of Jesus follows his warning to the towns that did not repent (11:20–24). At such a hard moment he does not complain; he gives thanks. He prays in the same chapter where John the Baptist’s doubts and Galilee’s hardness of heart have been described. The prayer is short, but scholars often call it the “Johannine thunderbolt” in the Synoptic Gospels, because it speaks of the Father and the Son with the language we know best from the Gospel of John.
str: v. 25: Jesus thanks the Father who hides these things from the wise and reveals them to infants.
v. 26: “Yes, Father, for such was your gracious will.”
v. 27: all things have been handed over to the Son; the Father and the Son know each other, and the Son reveals the Father to whom he chooses.
kw: The word means to acknowledge openly. It is the praise of the psalms, a confession of what God has done.
Babies, the little ones who cannot speak. In Matthew these are the humble disciples, the ones who need God and know it. The “wise and intelligent” are those who trust their own wisdom.
God’s good pleasure. The mysteries of the kingdom are given not because of human cleverness but because the Father chooses to give them.
vv: you have hidden these things from the wise and the intelligent and have revealed them to infants;
Jesus does not despise learning; the learned are warned only when learning becomes pride. The Gospel is given to anyone with a humble and open heart.
for such was your gracious will.
Jesus accepts the Father’s way. Revelation is the Father’s gift, and he gives it as he chooses.
no one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son
The Son and the Father know each other completely. This is the heart of Jesus’ identity: he is not one prophet among others but the Son who alone can show us the Father.
ch: The Catechism quotes v. 27 to teach that Jesus revealed God as Father in an unheard-of sense, eternally Father in relation to his only Son (CCC 240). It also points to this prayer as the model of Jesus’ own thanksgiving to the Father (CCC 2603). The Church’s great teachers have often pointed to the “little ones” of this passage. St Thérèse of Lisieux, a Doctor of the Church, built her “little way” on the same trust: that God gives himself to the small and humble.

qa: Does Jesus say that education and learning are bad?

No. Jesus does not blame the wise and the intelligent for being learned; he warns against a pride that thinks it needs no one. The Church has always honored learning: many of its saints, such as Augustine, Thomas Aquinas and Edith Stein, were great scholars who approached God as little children.
study: God called Moses in the middle of his ordinary work. Where might God be calling me in the middle of mine?
Jesus rejoices that God reveals himself to the little ones. What would it mean for me to be “small” before God this week?

lead: Today’s readings are about a name and about rest. In Exodus Moses asks God for his name before he goes to the elders of Israel, and receives the great answer “I am who I am”. God makes himself known as the one who is, who was the God of the fathers, and who sees and will deliver. In the Gospel Jesus, the Son who alone knows the Father, speaks in his own person and says: “Come to me, all you that are weary… and I will give you rest.” The God who gave Moses his name now gives us himself, gentle and humble of heart. On this day the Church keeps the memorial of St Bonaventure, bishop and Doctor of the Church.

r.h: I AM has sent me to you
set: This is the second half of the scene at the burning bush. In vv. 1–12 God has called Moses and promised, “I will be with you.” Moses now raises a different difficulty. The Israelites in Egypt may ask which God has sent him, since the gods of Egypt were known by many names. Moses asks for the name that will make this God known.
str: v. 13: Moses asks what he is to say if they ask God’s name.
vv. 14–15: God gives the name, “I am who I am”, and tells Moses what to tell Israel; “This is my name forever.”
vv. 16–17: Moses is to assemble the elders and tell them of God’s visit and promise.
vv. 18–20: the elders and Moses will ask Pharaoh to let the people go three days’ journey to sacrifice; Pharaoh will not agree until God’s hand and wonders compel him.
kw: A Hebrew phrase that can also mean “I will be what I will be” or “I will be who I will be”. It is a name of presence, not of definition: God is the one who is there, who is with his people, and who cannot be reduced to an idol.

The four letters of the divine name, which sounds like the verb “to be”. Out of reverence the people of Israel do not pronounce it, and in reading Scripture they say Adonai, “Lord”. The Greek Old Testament puts Kyrios, “Lord”, and Christians follow the same practice.
God does not make a new beginning. He is the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, who kept the promises of old and will keep them now.
vv: God said to Moses, “I am who I am.”

The words are mysterious on purpose. God is not one being among many; he is the source of all being. The Greek Old Testament renders them “I am the One who is”, which later shaped Christian thought about God.
‘I am has sent me to you.’
The name is given for the sake of the people. They are not to be left with a distant power but with a God who is present and acts.
This is my name forever, and this my title for all generations.
The God who is with Moses is the same God who is with his people in every generation, including ours.
I know, however, that the king of Egypt will not let you go unless compelled by a mighty hand.
God does not hide the difficulty from Moses. He tells him in advance that Pharaoh will resist and that the deliverance will cost struggle.
ch: The Catechism teaches that in the revelation of the name God shows himself as the God who is always present, faithful and near, and that this name is mysterious and holy (CCC 205–206; 213). It notes also that the people of Israel do not pronounce the name out of reverence and that in the readings of Scripture the divine name is replaced by “Lord” (CCC 209). In the Gospel of John, Jesus speaks with the same words, “I am”, to reveal who he is (John 8:58; 18:5–6). Christian readers have long seen in the name an early announcement of the God of the Gospel, who is not a distant ruler but one who comes down to his people.

r.h: Come to me and I will give you rest
set: These three verses follow directly the thanksgiving of Jesus to the Father (11:25–27), where he says that the Son alone reveals the Father. Now the Son turns from the Father to the crowds. The Gospel of Matthew has just described cities that did not repent and people who found fault with both John and Jesus. In this setting Jesus makes his invitation without conditions: come.
str: v. 28: the invitation: come to me, you who are weary and heavy laden; I will give you rest.
v. 29: take my yoke and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; you will find rest for your souls.
v. 30: my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.
kw: Not only sleep, but refreshment and peace. Rest in the Old Testament is a gift from God (Exodus 33:14), and a promise for those who walk in the ancient paths (Jeremiah 6:16, the words “find rest for your souls”).

The wooden bar that joined two animals to pull together. Teachers of Israel spoke of the “yoke” of the Law and of wisdom, as in Sirach 51:26. Jesus offers his own yoke, not a heavier load, but a new way of walking with him.
The word means good, kind, well fitted. A yoke that is “easy” is one made to fit the animal, so that it does not rub. Jesus’ commandments are fitted to us by grace.
vv: Come to me, all you that are weary and are carrying heavy burdens, and I will give you rest.
The invitation is addressed to everyone. Jesus does not first ask for good works, but only that people come. He himself is the place of rest.
Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me; for I am gentle and humble in heart
Jesus is a teacher, and to take his yoke is to become a disciple who learns. What he teaches is gentleness and humility, and he teaches it by being so himself.
For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.

This does not mean that discipleship is without cost, for Jesus speaks elsewhere of the cross (16:24). It means that the one who carries it with Jesus is not alone and does not carry it by his own strength.
ch: The Catechism quotes v. 29 in teaching that Christ is the model of holiness: “Learn from me” (CCC 459). St Augustine’s famous words, “our heart is restless until it rests in you” (Confessions, book 1), are often read as a commentary on Jesus’ promise of rest (in substance). The Church also remembers that the easy yoke is made light by grace, because the Holy Spirit pours the love of God into our hearts (Romans 5:5) and makes the commandments a way of freedom and joy.

qa: Why do the Church’s Bibles write “the Lord” where the Hebrew has the divine name?

Jewish tradition does not pronounce the holy name, out of reverence, and the Greek and Latin translations, and the Church after them, follow this practice. The Church keeps this practice, out of respect for the Jewish people who first received the name from God, and replaces it with “Lord” in the readings of Scripture (CCC 209).
rite: St Bonaventure was born about 1217 in Bagnoregio in Italy and studied and taught at the University of Paris. He became a Franciscan, and in 1257 was elected Minister General of the Order. He wrote the Itinerary of the Mind into God and a Life of St Francis. In 1273 he was made a cardinal and bishop of Albano, and he died on 15 July 1274 while taking part in the Second Council of Lyons. He was declared a Doctor of the Church in 1588 and is called the Seraphic Doctor. His life shows how study and prayer belong together: he held that the mind grows by learning and the heart grows by love, and that both lead to the God who invites the weary to rest.
study: God gives Moses a name which means presence. When have I most felt that God is “with me”?
Jesus says, “I am gentle and humble in heart.” Where might I let him teach me gentleness this week?

lead: The first reading brings us to the night of the Passover: the lamb without blemish, the blood on the doorposts, the meal eaten in haste with sandals on the feet, and God’s promise, “When I see the blood, I will pass over you.” In the Gospel the disciples of Jesus pluck grain on the sabbath, and Jesus answers the objection with Scripture: God desires mercy and not sacrifice, and the Son of Man is lord of the sabbath. Both readings are about a feast and the meaning of keeping it: the Passover is a memorial that rescues, and the sabbath is a gift that serves life. Today is also the optional memorial of Our Lady of Mount Carmel; the readings of the Friday are kept.

r.h: When I see the blood, I will pass over you
set: Nine plagues have fallen on Egypt, and Pharaoh has refused to let Israel go. Chapter 11 closes with the summary of verse 10: Moses and Aaron have done all the wonders, and Pharaoh’s heart remains hard. Then comes the tenth announcement, the death of the firstborn, and the instructions for the Passover. These instructions are given before the event, so that Israel may keep the night every year for ever. The book of Exodus is written to be remembered and re-lived in worship.
str: 11:10: the summary: the wonders were done, but Pharaoh’s heart stayed hard.
12:1–2: the Lord gives the instructions in Egypt; this month will be the first month of the year.
12:3–10: the lamb, chosen on the tenth day, kept until the fourteenth, killed at twilight and eaten roasted with unleavened bread and bitter herbs.
12:11–13: how to eat it, hurriedly and ready to travel; the Lord will pass through Egypt; the blood on the houses is the sign.
12:14: the day is to be a remembrance and a festival for all generations.
kw: The name of the feast. Its root is explained here as God “passing over” the houses with the blood (v. 13); it may also carry the sense of protecting.
The word used for any offering to God. The lamb must be whole and perfect; Christian tradition sees in it the image of Christ.
In the Bible to remember is not only to think but to make present again. The Jewish family at table still says that each generation is to see itself as brought out of Egypt.
vv: the Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart,

The Bible says both that Pharaoh hardened his own heart (8:15, 32) and that the Lord hardened it. The Hebrew way of speaking sees God’s hand even in the working out of human refusal. Pharaoh is never presented as a puppet; he is responsible for his choices.
Your lamb shall be without blemish, a year-old male;
The best is given. The family does not give what it can spare but a lamb of the first quality, and it keeps it from the tenth day, so that it comes to know it.
your loins girded, your sandals on your feet, and your staff in your hand;
The meal is a night of departure. Those who eat are already on the road, ready to leave a land of slavery.
when I see the blood, I will pass over you,
The blood on the doorposts is a sign of faith and obedience, and God’s promise is attached to the sign. The people are saved by God’s mercy through what he has told them to do.
This day shall be a day of remembrance for you.
The Passover is not only an event of the past but a feast. In keeping it Israel has remembered its liberation in every generation.
ch: From the New Testament onward the Church has read this night in the light of Christ. Paul says, “Christ, our paschal lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7), and John presents Jesus as the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29). The Catechism teaches that by celebrating the Last Supper with the apostles during the Passover meal Jesus gave the Jewish Passover its definitive meaning (CCC 1340), and that the Eucharist is the memorial in which his Passover becomes present (CCC 1363–1364). The Church honors the Jewish people, who have kept this feast through every century, and says of them that they are beloved by God for the sake of the fathers (Nostra Aetate 4).

r.h: I desire mercy and not sacrifice
set: Chapter 12 begins a series of conflicts over the sabbath. Jesus is walking through the grainfields with his disciples. The law of Moses allowed a traveler to pluck ears of grain by hand in a neighbor’s field (Deuteronomy 23:25), but forbade harvesting on the sabbath (Exodus 34:21). The question raised by some Pharisees is therefore a real one: is this plucking a kind of reaping? The debate is a debate within Judaism about how best to honor the sabbath; Jesus and the Pharisees both loved it. Jesus does not deny the sabbath but shows what it is for.
str: vv. 1–2: the hungry disciples pluck grain; some Pharisees object.
vv. 3–4: first answer: David and his companions, hungry, ate the bread of the Presence.
vv. 5–6: second answer: the priests work on the sabbath in the Temple and are blameless; something greater than the Temple is here.
vv. 7–8: Hosea 6:6: mercy over sacrifice; the Son of Man is lord of the sabbath.
kw: Twelve loaves set before the Lord in the sanctuary each sabbath, for the priests alone to eat (Leviticus 24:5–9). David took it for his hungry men when he fled (1 Samuel 21:1–6).
Hosea’s word ḥesed means loyal love, the faithful kindness that God shows and asks of his people. Matthew’s Greek eleos renders it.
The sabbath is God’s gift. Jesus claims for himself, as Son of Man, authority over the day that belongs to God.
vv: they began to pluck heads of grain and to eat.
The disciples are hungry, and the need is real. Jesus does not treat hunger as a small thing.
something greater than the temple is here.
In the sabbath debate, Jesus declares that with him the greatest holy thing is present: he is the place where God dwells with his people.
I desire mercy and not sacrifice
Jesus quotes Hosea 6:6, as he did in 9:13. Hosea does not reject sacrifice; he says that sacrifice without love misses its purpose.
the Son of Man is lord of the sabbath.
The sabbath was made for human beings, as Mark adds (Mark 2:27). The one who is Lord of the sabbath is the one who knows best how to keep it.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus never fails to respect the holiness of the sabbath, but gives it its authentic and divine meaning: “the sabbath was made for man”; Christ is the Lord of the sabbath (CCC 2173). Because the Lord rose on the first day, Christians keep the Lord’s Day, and the Church asks that works of charity and rest from unnecessary work mark the day (CCC 2184–2186). The Church has always seen that mercy is not opposed to worship but is its fruit. St Augustine is often quoted as teaching that true sacrifice is every work done to unite us to God in holy fellowship (City of God 10.6, in substance).

qa: How are we to read the death of the firstborn of Egypt?

It is a hard text, and we should not read it lightly. The book of Wisdom reads it as an answer to Pharaoh’s decree to kill the infants of Israel (Wisdom 18:5; compare Exodus 1:22). The Church takes no joy in anyone’s death, and the Passover tradition itself carries sorrow: in the Jewish Passover meal a little wine is spilled for each plague, remembering the suffering of the Egyptians. The text tells us above all that God will not let oppression stand and that he saves his people.
rite: The optional memorial of Our Lady of Mount Carmel recalls the Carmelite family, which took its name from Mount Carmel in the Holy Land, where the prophet Elijah worshipped the Lord (1 Kings 18). It has been kept in the Roman calendar since 1726. According to Carmelite tradition the Virgin Mary gave the scapular as a sign of her protection, and the Church sees in the scapular a sign of devotion to Mary and of a life lived in her care. In Kerala the Carmelite family is well known, and St Kuriakose Elias Chavara, who founded the Carmelites of Mary Immaculate, is honored in many parishes. Today’s Gospel fits Mary’s own way: she kept the feasts of her people faithfully, and her heart was full of mercy.
study: The Israelites ate the Passover “with sandals on the feet”, ready to leave. What am I being asked to leave behind in order to follow God?
Jesus answers a question about the sabbath with mercy. Is there a rule I keep strictly in my family or parish while forgetting the person it was made to serve?

lead: After the Passover night comes the departure. The first reading tells of Israel marching out of Egypt with unleavened dough on their backs, and calls the night a vigil kept for the Lord for all generations. In the Gospel the Pharisees plot against Jesus after the sabbath healing, and he quietly withdraws, healing all who follow him. Matthew sees in this gentleness the Servant of Isaiah, who will not break a bruised reed or quench a smoldering wick. Both readings show God’s way of saving: not with noise and force of arms, but in a night of watching and in a quiet service of the weak.

r.h: A night of vigil
set: Yesterday’s reading (Exodus 11:10–12:14) gave the instructions for the Passover; today’s tells of the departure itself. The night of the tenth plague has passed, and Pharaoh has let Israel go (12:29–32). The people leave in haste from Rameses, the royal city in the eastern delta, and make their first stop at Succoth. The passage is a short narrative summary, written with a liturgical tone, and its last verse turns from the past to the feast kept for ever.
str: v. 37: the march from Rameses to Succoth, with six hundred thousand men on foot, besides children.
v. 38: a mixed crowd and great flocks and herds go with them.
v. 39: unleavened cakes baked from the dough, because there was no time to prepare.
vv. 40–41: the time in Egypt: four hundred and thirty years, ending exactly on that day.
v. 42: it was a night of vigil for the Lord, to be kept by all the Israelites for ever.
kw: Other peoples, probably slaves and poor workers of different origins, joined Israel in its going out. The people of God has always been open to those who attach themselves to it (compare Exodus 12:48–49).
Bread made without yeast, because there was no time to wait for it to rise. Israel keeps this bread each year as a reminder of the haste of the deliverance.
Literally “a night of keeping” or “watching”. God kept watch to bring them out, and Israel is to keep watch in return. The word suggests both God’s care and the people’s attention.
vv: about six hundred thousand men on foot, besides children.

The number is very large, and scholars debate how to understand it (some think the Hebrew word translated “thousand” may also mean a clan or military unit). What the verse says for sure is that the whole people went out, as one people.
A mixed crowd also went up with them,
From the very beginning those who join Israel are among the people God leads out. Salvation is not shut to any who come with them.
because they were driven out of Egypt and could not wait,
The people did not plan their own liberation. God’s act came suddenly, and they had to follow.
That was for the Lord a night of vigil, to bring them out of the land of Egypt.
The night of the exodus is a night when God was watching over his people, and every year those who keep it watch with him.
ch: The Church remembers this night every year at the Easter Vigil, the “mother of all vigils”, which begins in the dark and reads the story of the exodus. The Exsultet, the great proclamation of Easter, sings in substance that this is the night when God first saved our fathers and delivered the children of Israel from slavery in Egypt. The Church reads the Passover as the great type of Christ’s own passing from death to life, and it also honors the Jewish people who have kept the vigil of Passover through every century. Paul recalls the 430 years when he explains that the promise to Abraham came long before the law (Galatians 3:17).

r.h: He will not break a bruised reed
set: The passage follows the sabbath healing of the man with the withered hand (12:9–13). Some Pharisees are angered and plan how to destroy Jesus. The Pharisees were a lay movement of devout Jews; Matthew names those in this scene, not the whole group and certainly not the Jewish people. Jesus does not answer with a counter-attack. He withdraws, and he goes on healing, and Matthew finds in this the first Servant Song of Isaiah (Isaiah 42:1–4).
str: v. 14: the plot of the Pharisees.
vv. 15–16: Jesus withdraws; the crowds follow; he heals them all and asks that he not be made known.
vv. 17–21: Matthew’s quotation of Isaiah 42:1–4: the chosen servant, filled with the Spirit, brings justice to the nations without quarrel or noise, and the Gentiles will hope in his name.
kw: The Greek word can mean both. It renders the Hebrew ʿebed, the servant who belongs to the Lord and does his will. At the baptism of Jesus the Father’s voice uses the same words of love (3:17).
The right order God brings to the world, especially in defense of the poor and the wronged. The servant brings it “to victory”, not by force but by faithful gentleness.
A reed already cracked, which any pressure would snap. The picture is of something weak and damaged, and the servant treats it with care.
vv: the Pharisees went out and conspired against him, how to destroy him.
The sabbath healing, an act of mercy, is the occasion of the plot. Here begins the road that leads to the Cross.
he cured all of them,
Jesus does not withdraw to rest alone. Even when he leaves the scene of conflict, he serves those who follow.
he ordered them not to make him known.
Jesus does not wish to be known first as a wonder-worker or as a political figure. He lets his mission unfold in its own way, as that of a servant who will suffer.
Here is my servant, whom I have chosen, my beloved,
The words recall the voice at the baptism, “This is my beloved Son” (3:17). Matthew shows that the Son is also the Servant.
He will not break a bruised reed or quench a smoldering wick until he brings justice to victory.
This is the heart of the passage: strength is shown in gentleness. Jesus will not crush those who are weak in faith or in strength.
in his name the Gentiles will hope.
The scene of conflict with some of his own people ends with a word of hope for the nations. Matthew’s Gospel, written for a community of Jewish and Gentile believers, holds both.
ch: The Catechism points to the Servant of Isaiah as one of the ways the Spirit prepared the coming of the Messiah (CCC 713). The Church sees in the bruised reed and smoldering wick the way Jesus meets sinners and the weak: he calls them, forgives them, and does not break them. Pastors and confessors are asked to imitate this gentleness. The Church recalls too that the Servant’s mission is to bring justice to the nations, which is why the Gospel is preached to all peoples.

qa: Does this Gospel say that the Pharisees as a group wanted to kill Jesus?

No. Matthew speaks of some Pharisees in this scene. In the Gospels other Pharisees invite Jesus to dinner and warn him of danger (Luke 7:36; 13:31), and Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea, who were of the leading class, honor him at the end. The Church teaches that what happened to Jesus in his Passion cannot be blamed on all the Jews of that time, nor on the Jews of today (Nostra Aetate 4).
study: The Israelites left Egypt in haste, with only dough and a mixed crowd. When has God asked me to move before I felt ready?
Jesus will not break a bruised reed. Whose weakness do I treat roughly, in my family or parish, and how could I treat it with his gentleness?

lead: Today’s readings are about the shepherd. In Jeremiah God speaks against the shepherds, the kings of Judah, who have scattered his flock, and promises to gather the remnant himself, to give them shepherds who will care for them, and to raise up a righteous Branch of David whose name is “The Lord is our righteousness.” In the Gospel Jesus sees a great crowd, like sheep without a shepherd, and is moved with compassion; he begins to teach them. The promise of Jeremiah is being fulfilled before the eyes of the apostles.

Psalm 23, “The Lord is my shepherd, I shall not want,” is the people’s answer: the flock that is led to green pastures and still waters, that fears no evil in the darkest valley, and that dwells in the house of the Lord. The second reading, from Ephesians, shows what the Shepherd’s work achieves: he has made those who were far off and those who were near into one new people, and has given both access in one Spirit to the Father. Next Sunday the Lectionary turns from Mark to John 6 for five weeks; today’s Gospel is the introduction to the feeding of the five thousand that follows it.

r.h: I will raise up shepherds over them
set: Jeremiah was a priest of Anathoth who was called as a young man in 627 before Christ and prophesied through the last decades of the kingdom of Judah until after the fall of Jerusalem in 587. Chapters 21–23 are a collection of sayings about the kings of Judah, who failed to lead the people in justice. In the ancient Near East a king was called the shepherd of his people, so to speak of “shepherds” was to speak of the rulers.

Background. The kings of Jeremiah’s day were Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin and Zedekiah. Under them the people were scattered, first by the exile of 597 and then by the destruction of Jerusalem in 587. This passage looks both back at the failure and forward to God’s own rescue.
str: vv. 1–2: woe to the shepherds who scatter the flock; God will “attend” to their evil doings.
v. 3: God himself will gather the remnant from all the lands and bring them back.
v. 4: he will set up shepherds who will really shepherd them, and no one will be missing.
vv. 5–6: the promise of a righteous Branch of David, who will reign wisely; his name, “The Lord is our righteousness.”
kw: Kings, princes and leaders. A shepherd leads, feeds, protects and searches for the lost. The prophets measure rulers by these tasks (Ezekiel 34).

The same verb is used twice in v. 2: “you have not attended to them” and “I will attend to you for your evil doings”. The shepherds did not visit the flock, so God will visit them. The verb can mean care or judgment, depending on what is found.
The shoot that comes from a stump. After the fall of the royal line, God promises a new growth from the root of David (compare Isaiah 11:1).
vv: Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture!
The flock is God’s: “my pasture”, “my flock”. Those who lead have been given a trust and are answerable to the owner.
you have not attended to them. So I will attend to you for your evil doings,
Neglect is a sin. The shepherds are not accused only of cruelty but of not caring at all.
Then I myself will gather the remnant of my flock out of all the lands
God does not wait for better shepherds before saving his people. He acts himself, and brings them back to their fold, with the promise that they will be fruitful and multiply.
I will raise up shepherds over them who will shepherd them, and they shall not fear any longer,
God does not abolish leadership. He promises leaders who truly lead, so that the flock lives without fear and no one is lost.
when I will raise up for David a righteous Branch,
The hope of Israel is bound to the house of David. Jeremiah’s promise is the root of the later Jewish expectation of the Messiah, and Christians have read it as fulfilled in Jesus.
“The Lord is our righteousness.”

The Hebrew is YHWH ṣidqēnû. It is a wordplay on the name of Zedekiah, the last king, whose name means “my righteousness is the Lord”. The true king will live up to the name that the last king failed to honor.
ch: The Church reads this oracle as a promise of the Messiah, the true Shepherd from David’s line. The Catechism teaches that the Church is the sheepfold whose one door is Christ, and the flock of which God himself foretold that he would be the shepherd (CCC 754; Lumen Gentium 6). Jesus names himself the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11). The Church then asks its pastors to share in his care: the Second Vatican Council says that bishops are to be shepherds who serve and do not rule for themselves (Lumen Gentium 27), and the Church prays that God will give his people shepherds after his own heart, as he promised through Jeremiah (3:15). St Augustine, in his sermon on the shepherds (Sermon 46), reminded the bishops of his time that the flock belongs to Christ and not to them (in substance).

r.h: He is our peace
set: The Letter to the Ephesians was written in the name of Paul, and the Church receives it as his. Many scholars think that it was composed by a disciple of Paul who wrote in his name soon after his death, and that it was meant as a circular letter for several churches in the region of Ephesus; this does not change its authority in the Church. Its first three chapters praise God’s plan: to unite all things in Christ.

Background. In chapter 2 the writer speaks to Gentile Christians, who once were “aliens from the commonwealth of Israel” (2:12), and says that in Christ they have been brought near. The picture is of a great Temple court, with a low wall that separated the court of the Gentiles from the holy places beyond it. Notices on that wall warned Gentiles not to go farther, on pain of death. Many commentators think this wall stands behind the image of the “dividing wall” in v. 14.
str: v. 13: those who were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ.
v. 14: Christ is our peace; he made both groups one and broke down the dividing wall.
v. 15: he abolished the law with its commandments and ordinances, to create one new humanity.
v. 16: he reconciled both groups to God in one body through the cross.
vv. 17–18: he proclaimed peace to those far and near; through him both have access in one Spirit to the Father.
kw: The Greek word for peace, with the Hebrew šālôm behind it: wholeness, harmony with God and with one another. Here it is a person: “he is our peace”.
Literally “middle wall”. The writer does not say that Israel was a wall, but that the separation between Jew and Gentile was a wall that Christ has taken down.
The word for being brought into the presence of a king, introduced at court. Through Christ, both Jew and Gentile are brought into the presence of the Father.
vv: you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ.
The Gentiles who were far have been brought near, not by their own effort, but by the blood of Christ. The language of near and far is that of the prophets (Isaiah 57:19).
For he is our peace; in his flesh he has made both groups into one and has broken down the dividing wall,
Peace is not first a treaty or a feeling but a person. The reconciliation was made in his flesh, in the body that was given on the cross.
He has abolished the law with its commandments and ordinances,

This does not mean that the law of Moses was bad. The writer means that the observances that set Israel apart and divided Jew from Gentile no longer divide them in Christ. Paul himself says that the law is holy (Romans 7:12), and Jesus did not come to abolish it but to fulfil it (Matthew 5:17).
one new humanity in place of the two,

The new humanity is not the Gentile Church replacing Israel but a new people in which Jews and Gentiles share in one body. Paul says elsewhere that Gentiles are grafted into the olive tree of Israel (Romans 11:17–24).
reconcile both groups to God in one body through the cross,
The reconciliation has two directions: of the two groups with each other, and of both with God. The cross is the place where hostility is put to death.
through him both of us have access in one Spirit to the Father;
This verse is a short summary of the Trinity at work in our prayer: through the Son, in the Spirit, we come to the Father.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Christ’s peace is the foundation of all true peace among peoples, and that it is the gift of the reconciling cross (CCC 2305). The Second Vatican Council quotes this passage in its teaching on the Jewish people: Christ, through his cross, reconciled Jews and Gentiles and made both one in himself (Nostra Aetate 4). The same document recalls that the Jews remain dear to God, who does not repent of the gifts he has made, and the Catechism teaches that the Old Covenant has never been revoked (CCC 121; 839). The Church sees in v. 18 the shape of all Christian prayer, and of the Mass itself, which is offered to the Father, through Christ, in the Holy Spirit.

r.h: Like sheep without a shepherd
set: The Twelve have just been sent out two by two to preach repentance, cast out demons and anoint the sick (6:7–13). Between their sending and their return Mark has placed the story of the death of John the Baptist (6:14–29), so that the reader feels the cost of the mission. Now the apostles come back. They are tired, and so is Jesus: the shadow of John’s death lies on them.

Background. The scene is by the Sea of Galilee. Jesus and the apostles cross by boat to a deserted place, probably on the north-east shore near Bethsaida. In the verses that follow the Lectionary’s reading (6:35–44) the feeding of the five thousand takes place there.
str: v. 30: the apostles return and tell Jesus all they have done and taught.
v. 31: Jesus invites them to come away and rest; there are too many people for them even to eat.
vv. 32–33: they go by boat to a deserted place; the crowds see them and run ahead by land.
v. 34: Jesus goes ashore, sees the crowd, has compassion because they are like sheep without a shepherd, and begins to teach.
kw: “Those sent out”. Mark uses this title here at the moment when they come back from being sent. The Church first reports to the one who sent her.
In Mark the desert is a place to meet God (1:12–13; 1:35). It is also where Israel was shepherded by Moses, and so a fitting place for the Shepherd to feed his flock.

From the Greek word for the inner organs, the seat of deep feeling. In the Gospels it is used only of Jesus and of figures in his parables who show God’s mercy (Mark 1:41; 8:2; Luke 15:20). His compassion is not a passing sympathy but moves him to act.
vv: told him all that they had done and taught.
The apostles bring their work back to Jesus. In pastoral work, prayer and report to the Lord go together with work for the people.
“Come away to a deserted place all by yourselves and rest a while.”
Jesus does not ask the apostles to work without rest. He gives rest because he loves them; and he wants them near him. Rest in his company is part of ministry.
they hurried there on foot from all the towns and arrived ahead of them.
The crowd’s hunger was greater than the apostles’ tiredness. Plans for rest met people’s need; Jesus lets the need change his plan.
he had compassion for them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd;

The phrase recalls Moses’ prayer in Numbers 27:17, when he asked God to give the people a leader so that they would not be like sheep without a shepherd. God named Joshua, whose name in Greek is Jesus.
and he began to teach them many things.
The first gift of the shepherd is the word. Only afterwards does he feed them with bread (6:35–44). Word and bread belong together.
ch: The Church sees in this scene the figure of her own life: the apostles are sent, return to the Lord, rest in him, and are drawn again into the needs of the crowd. The Catechism teaches that the Church has always venerated the Scriptures as she venerates the Body of the Lord, and that at Mass she receives from the one table the bread of life from both the word of God and the Body of Christ (CCC 103; Dei Verbum 21). The Church also offers the Lord’s Day as a time for rest and for works of mercy (CCC 2184–2186). Pope St John Paul II took the title of his letter on the priesthood from Jeremiah’s promise, “I will give you shepherds after my own heart” (Pastores Dabo Vobis, 1992, quoting Jeremiah 3:15).

qa: Does “he has abolished the law” mean that the Old Testament is no longer important?

No. The Church teaches that the Old Testament is the word of God, and that the covenant God made with Israel has never been revoked (CCC 121; Romans 11:29). In Ephesians, what ends is the law as a barrier between Jews and Gentiles: the observances that marked Israel as God’s own people no longer divide those who belong to Christ. Jesus said that he did not come to abolish the law but to fulfil it (Matthew 5:17), and the Church still reads the Ten Commandments and the whole Old Testament as the word of God for us.
Is it right to rest when so many people need help?

Jesus himself said, “Come away… and rest a while.” Even when the crowd was waiting, he knew that those who serve need rest, prayer and friendship with him. Rest is not selfish; it makes love last. The Church’s teaching about the Lord’s Day, as a day of worship, rest and charity, is meant to protect this balance (CCC 2184–2186).
