At the same time Jesus did not send the crowd away; his compassion led him to teach and to feed them.
What should we do when those who lead the Church fail?

Jeremiah and Jesus both show that God sees the failures of shepherds and that the flock is his, not theirs. The Church asks her pastors to serve and to be accountable; the people of God are asked to pray for them, to speak the truth with love, and to take their own part in the Church’s mission. We trust, above all, not in any person but in Christ, the Good Shepherd, who promises that he will not leave his flock (John 10:11–16).
rite: In the Latin Church the Sundays of Ordinary Time in Year B follow Mark’s Gospel; from next Sunday the Lectionary reads John 6, the Bread of Life discourse, for five weeks, and today’s verses prepare for it. The image of the shepherd is also close to the Church’s liturgy: the bishop carries a crosier, the shepherd’s staff, as the sign of his ministry, and the Church prays at every Mass for the Pope and the bishop by name. In Kerala many families pray for their parish priests and for vocations. Today’s readings invite the faithful to take part in that prayer and in the care of one another, since all share in the shepherd’s work of looking after those who are tired, lost or alone.
study: Jeremiah says that God will attend to those who did not attend to the flock. Who in my family, parish or work depends on me to “attend” to them?
Jesus invites his tired apostles to rest with him. What would real rest “with Jesus” look like for me this week?
Ephesians says that Christ is our peace and has broken down the dividing wall. What wall in my family, parish or village could I help take down?
Psalm 23 says, “you are with me; your rod and your staff, they comfort me.” When have I known the Shepherd’s presence in a dark valley?

lead: These weeks the first reading follows the Exodus. Today Pharaoh changes his mind and chases the people to the edge of the sea. Trapped between the water and the chariots, they cry out in fear, and Moses answers: “Do not be afraid, stand firm, and see the deliverance that the Lord will accomplish for you today.” In the Gospel some scribes and Pharisees ask Jesus for a sign, and he points them to Jonah, and to “something greater than Jonah”. Both readings speak of God who saves when every road seems closed. The responsorial psalm is the song of Moses that follows the crossing (Exodus 15).

r.h: Stand firm and see the Lord’s deliverance
set: Israel has left Egypt after the death of the firstborn, led by the pillar of cloud and fire (13:17–22). God has told Moses to turn back and camp by the sea, so that Pharaoh will think the people are lost in the wilderness (14:1–4). The reading begins when Pharaoh hears that they have gone and regrets it. The places named, Pi-hahiroth and Baal-zephon, cannot be located with certainty today. What the story wants the reader to feel is plain: the people are cornered, with the sea in front and the army behind.
str: vv. 5–9: Pharaoh’s change of heart; he gathers six hundred picked chariots and overtakes the camp.
vv. 10–12: the people cry out to the Lord, then turn on Moses and say it was better in Egypt.
vv. 13–14: Moses answers: do not be afraid; the Lord will fight for you.
vv. 15–18: the Lord tells Moses to go forward, to lift his staff over the sea, and promises glory over Pharaoh.
kw: In v. 8 the Lord “hardened” Pharaoh’s heart. The Hebrew verb means to make firm or strong, and in the Exodus story Pharaoh’s own stubbornness and God’s hand are both spoken of (compare 8:15). The Church reads it as a mystery of human responsibility, not as God forcing a person to sin.
From the same root as the name Jesus (Yeshua). Moses promises that the people will “see” it. Here the word means rescue from an enemy; the New Testament will give it its widest meaning.
In v. 14 the people are told they “have only to keep still”: not to do nothing, but to stop panicking and let God act, while v. 15 at once tells them to go forward.
vv: Was it because there were no graves in Egypt that you have taken us away to die in the wilderness?
Fear speaks bitterly. The people forget the slavery they cried out against and remember only that Egypt was familiar. The same temptation returns again and again in the wilderness.
Do not be afraid, stand firm, and see the deliverance that the Lord will accomplish for you today;
Moses gives three commands in a row: do not fear, stand firm, look. Faith here is trust before any proof appears.
The Lord will fight for you, and you have only to keep still.
Israel is not asked to defeat Pharaoh. The victory belongs to the Lord, and a saying from Israel’s tradition of the Lord’s battles becomes here a saying of trust.
Why do you cry out to me? Tell the Israelites to go forward.
Prayer is not enough on its own at this moment. God asks the people to take the step, and then he opens the way. Trust and action go together.
ch: The Church reads the crossing of the sea in the light of Baptism. The Catechism teaches that the passage of the Red Sea, which was literally Israel’s liberation from the slavery of Egypt, announces the liberation wrought by Baptism (CCC 1221). St Paul already says that our ancestors “were all baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Corinthians 10:1–2). For this reason the Exodus crossing is always read at the Easter Vigil. The text also speaks to every believer who stands between a danger and a sea: God does not remove the sea, but he opens a way through it.

r.h: The sign of Jonah
set: Jesus has just healed a man who was blind and mute, and some Pharisees have said he drives out demons by the prince of demons (12:22–37). Now some scribes and Pharisees (not all of them, as Matthew writes “some”) ask for a sign. Jesus has done many signs already. What they want is one that settles the question on their terms, and he refuses it.

Matthew’s Gospel is addressed first to a community of Jewish followers of Jesus, and its sharp words against his opponents belong to a family argument inside Israel. They are not a verdict on the Jewish people, then or now (CCC 597).
str: vv. 38–39: the request for a sign; Jesus calls this generation “evil and adulterous” and promises only the sign of Jonah.
v. 40: Jonah’s three days and nights, and the Son of Man in the heart of the earth.
v. 41: the people of Nineveh repented; something greater than Jonah is here.
v. 42: the queen of the South came to hear Solomon; something greater than Solomon is here.
kw: In Matthew a sign is not a wonder that forces belief but a pointer that asks for faith. The sign Jesus gives is his own death and rising.

In the prophets, such as Hosea, Israel’s unfaithfulness to the Lord is called adultery, because Israel was bound to him by covenant as a bride. Jesus uses that language of unfaithful hearts; it is not about the sin of any particular person.
The Greek is neuter: not “someone” but “something” greater. Jesus claims more than a prophet and more than a king: he himself is the place where God’s word and wisdom are present.
vv: An evil and adulterous generation asks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah.
The sign is Jonah’s deliverance from the sea monster, which Jesus applies to his own death and rising. It is a sign given by God, not at the demand of the questioners.
so for three days and three nights the Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth.
“Three days and three nights” is a way of speaking of a short time counted inclusively, as in Esther 4:16 and 5:1, and agrees with the Church’s teaching that Christ rose on the third day.
because they repented at the proclamation of Jonah, and see, something greater than Jonah is here!
The Gentiles of Nineveh listened to a reluctant prophet. How much more should God’s own people listen to the one who is more than a prophet.
because she came from the ends of the earth to listen to the wisdom of Solomon,
The queen of the South is the Queen of Sheba (1 Kings 10:1–10). She travelled a long way for wisdom. Jesus says that the Wisdom of God stands here, and the people can hear him without any journey.
ch: The Fathers saw in Jonah’s three days in the fish a figure of the burial and resurrection of Christ, and Jesus himself offers this reading here. The Church carries the same pattern into Baptism: going down into the water and rising to new life, as the Catechism says of the sacrament (CCC 1214, 1227). At every Mass the Church also proclaims the death and rising of the Lord as the one sign given to the world. The sharp words of this Gospel are a warning to every believer who asks for proof instead of trust, not a condemnation of a people.

qa: Why did God harden Pharaoh’s heart, and was Pharaoh responsible for his own choice?

The book of Exodus speaks in two ways: Pharaoh hardens his own heart, and the Lord hardens it. Many commentators read this as the Bible’s way of saying that God is sovereign even over human refusal, while the refusal remains Pharaoh’s own. The Church teaches that God never causes sin and that every person is responsible for his or her own choices. The story’s main point is not Pharaoh’s fate but that the Lord, not Egypt’s army, decides Israel’s future.
study: Moses told the frightened people, “Do not be afraid, stand firm.” Where in my life do I need to stand firm and also to take the next step?
Jesus is the “something greater” than Jonah and Solomon. What do I still look for before I am ready to trust him?

lead: The story of the sea continues. Yesterday the people stood trapped; today the waters divide, Israel walks through on dry ground, and the Egyptian army is swallowed up at dawn. “Thus the Lord saved Israel that day,” and the people “believed in the Lord and in his servant Moses”, and break into song. In the Gospel, when Jesus’ mother and brothers wait outside, he points to his disciples and says that whoever does the will of his Father is his brother and sister and mother. The Church may also remember St Apollinaris, first bishop of Ravenna, a martyr.

r.h: Through the sea on dry ground
set: This is the moment toward which the whole book has been moving: the liberation from Egypt. The account joins what scholars often see as older and later strands, and the result is a story told in two ways: a strong east wind driving the sea back all night (v. 21), and the waters standing like a wall (vv. 22, 29). The Bible does not choose between them. It wants the reader to see that the event was both natural in its means and wholly the Lord’s work.
The sea is called yam sûf in Hebrew, usually translated “Sea of Reeds”; the Greek Old Testament calls it the Red Sea, and that is how tradition has named it. The exact place is unknown.
str: vv. 21–23: Moses stretches out his hand; the wind drives the sea back; Israel goes through; the Egyptians follow.
vv. 24–25: in the morning watch the Lord looks down and throws the Egyptian army into panic; their wheels clog.
vv. 26–29: Moses stretches out his hand again; the waters return and cover the army; Israel walks on dry ground.
vv. 30–31, 15:1: the Lord saves Israel that day; the people fear the Lord and believe; Moses and Israel begin to sing.
kw: Many readers hear an echo of creation (compare Genesis 1:9, where dry land appears as the waters are gathered, though the Hebrew word there is different): the waters are driven back so that a people can stand on dry ground.
In v. 31 the people “feared the Lord and believed in the Lord and in his servant Moses.” Faith here is born after seeing the deliverance. The fear is reverence, not terror.
Chapter 15 begins with a song, the oldest long poem in the Bible according to many scholars. The deliverance is not only told; it is sung. Praise is the natural answer to rescue.
vv: The Israelites went into the sea on dry ground, the waters forming a wall for them on their right and on their left.
The sea that threatened them becomes a protecting wall. The verse is repeated in v. 29, as if the storyteller cannot stop marvelling.
At the morning watch the Lord in the pillar of fire and cloud looked down upon the Egyptian army,

The same pillar that led and sheltered Israel now stands between them and Pharaoh. The “morning watch” is the last part of the night, just before dawn, the hour in the Bible when God so often comes to help.
Thus the Lord saved Israel that day from the Egyptians;
One sentence gives the heart of the Old Testament’s faith: Israel was saved by the Lord. Later prophets and psalms keep returning to this day.
Then Moses and the Israelites sang this song to the Lord:
From the shore, the story turns to worship. The responsorial psalm of this Mass takes its words from this song.
ch: The Church sees in this event a sign of Baptism and of Easter. The Catechism speaks of the passage through the sea as announcing the liberation wrought by Baptism (CCC 1221). At the Easter Vigil the Church sings the same song of Moses, so that the newly baptized may hear in it their own deliverance. Christians do not read this as a story against Egypt’s people, but as a story of how the Lord rescues the oppressed; and we pray for those who suffer in many lands today, and for those who wrong them.

r.h: My mother and my brothers
set: Jesus is teaching the crowds in a house or courtyard, probably in Capernaum, when word comes that his mother and brothers are outside. Mark tells the same scene (3:31–35). In Matthew the scene follows the hard words about this generation (12:38–45) and is a short lesson on who belongs to Jesus’ true family.

In the Semitic world “brothers” was a wide word for close relatives. The Church has always taught that Mary remained a virgin, and that these “brothers” are relatives of Jesus, not other children of Mary (CCC 500).
str: vv. 46–47: his mother and brothers stand outside, wanting to speak to him.
v. 48: Jesus asks, “Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?”
vv. 49–50: pointing to his disciples, he says that whoever does the will of his Father is his brother and sister and mother.
kw: Greek adelphos is used in the Septuagint for close kin of several kinds, because Hebrew and Aramaic had no common single word for cousin (compare Genesis 13:8, where Abram calls his nephew Lot his kinsman). The Church reads it of relatives.
“The will of my Father” is the heart of Matthew’s teaching (6:10; 7:21; 26:42). To be family to Jesus is to do what the Father wants, and it is open to everyone.
Jesus does not push away his family. He stretches out his hand toward his disciples and opens the family to all who follow him.
vv: Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?
The question is not cold. It opens the door of Jesus’ family wider than blood and home.
Here are my mother and my brothers!
The disciples are named first, and the family grows from hearing and doing.
For whoever does the will of my Father in heaven is my brother and sister and mother.

Jesus names three kinds of relationship, and all of them are open to the obedient. Mary herself is the first to belong to him in this way, since she said “let it be with me according to your word” (Luke 1:38).
ch: The Second Vatican Council teaches that in the course of Jesus’ preaching Mary received the words in which he put the kingdom above the ties of flesh and blood, and faithfully kept them, advancing in her pilgrimage of faith (Lumen Gentium 58, in substance). Luke’s parallel says the same: “Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and obey it” (Luke 11:28). This Gospel therefore does not lower Mary; it shows why she is the first of the disciples, and the Church honours her as mother and model of all who hear the Word and keep it. Baptism makes every believer a brother or sister of Christ, and the Eucharist builds up that family.

rite: St Apollinaris is, by tradition, the first bishop of Ravenna in northern Italy, probably in the second century, and died a martyr. Little is known for certain about his life. The great basilica of Sant’Apollinare in Classe, built in the sixth century near Ravenna’s ancient harbour, holds his relics and is known for its mosaics. His memorial on 20 July is optional in the Roman calendar.
study: After the rescue the people sang. When did God last bring me through something, and did I stop to give thanks?
Jesus says that those who do the Father’s will are his family. What is one thing the Father is asking of me this week?

lead: A month or so after leaving Egypt the people are hungry, and they grumble against Moses and Aaron. God’s answer is bread from heaven: manna each morning, quail each evening, enough for each day. In the Gospel Jesus sits beside the sea and tells the parable of the sower: the seed falls on the path, on rock, among thorns and, at last, on good soil, where it yields a hundredfold. In both readings God gives generously, and the question is how we receive it. Psalm 78 recalls the manna: “The Lord gave them bread from heaven.” Today the Church may also remember St Lawrence of Brindisi, a great preacher of the Word.

r.h: Bread from heaven
set: The people have been out of Egypt for about a month. They have crossed the sea and sung the song of Moses (15:1–21), and they have come to the wilderness of Sin, a desert region between Elim and Sinai. Here the food they brought is running out. The story that follows is the first of several “murmuring” stories in the wilderness (compare 15:22–24; 17:1–7; Numbers 11).
The reading leaves out vv. 6–8 and 10–11, which tell how Moses and Aaron answered the complaint and how the glory of the Lord appeared in the cloud.
str: vv. 1–3: the whole congregation complains; they remember the fleshpots of Egypt.
vv. 4–5: the Lord promises bread from heaven, a daily portion, and a double portion on the sixth day; it is a test.
vv. 9–12: Aaron summons the congregation; the glory of the Lord appears in the cloud; the Lord has heard and promises meat at twilight and bread in the morning.
vv. 13–15: quail cover the camp; in the morning a fine flaky substance lies on the ground; the people ask “What is it?”; Moses says it is the bread the Lord has given.
kw: The name comes from the people’s question in v. 15, “What is it?” (mān hû). It is thus a gift so strange that the people have to ask what it is. Scholars note that wilderness insects can produce a sweet substance on desert shrubs, but the story speaks of the sign that no natural account fully explains: the daily portion, and the double portion on the sixth day.
In v. 4 God says he will test the people “whether they will follow my instruction or not”. The test is simple: to take only what they need for each day, and trust that tomorrow’s bread will come.

The people’s complaining, repeated in this chapter, is turned by Moses in vv. 7–8: it is not against us, but against the Lord. Hunger is real; the problem is that they forget the God who rescued them.
vv: If only we had died by the hand of the Lord in the land of Egypt, when we sat by the fleshpots and ate our fill of bread;
Memory has become selective. They remember the pots and the bread, and forget the slavery. Hunger can do this to anyone.
I am going to rain bread from heaven for you,
The Lord answers complaint with a gift. Bread “from heaven” will become a great biblical picture, taken up in Psalm 78 and John 6.
and each day the people shall go out and gather enough for that day.
Daily bread means daily trust. The people may not store up, because the gift comes again each morning.
In the evening quails came up and covered the camp;
Meat in the evening, bread in the morning, exactly as promised. God’s word is fulfilled even in the wilderness.
“What is it?” For they did not know what it was.
The people receive what they cannot name. Faith often begins with a gift we do not yet understand.
ch: The Fathers and the Church read the manna as a sign of the Eucharist. The Lord himself draws this line in the Gospel of John, saying that the true bread from heaven is not what Moses gave but what the Father gives, and “I am the bread of life” (John 6:32–35); that discourse will be read from next Sunday. The Our Father also asks for “daily bread”, and the Catechism teaches that this petition is a petition for the bread of every day and for the Bread of life (CCC 2828–2837, in substance). The manna teaches the Church two things: that God feeds his people in the wilderness, and that we are to receive his gifts with trust and thanks, not with grumbling.

r.h: A sower went out to sow
set: With chapter 13 begins the third of the five great speeches of Matthew’s Gospel, the “parables of the kingdom”. Jesus has just spoken of true family (12:46–50). Now he leaves the house, sits in a boat beside the Sea of Galilee, and teaches the crowd on the shore. The sower’s picture was familiar to every farmer in his audience. Seed was scattered by hand over the field and ploughed in afterward, so some inevitably fell on the path at the edge, on rocky ground where the limestone lay close under the soil, or among thorn roots.
This is the first parable in the chapter. On Friday the Mass gives Jesus’ own explanation of it (13:18–23).
str: vv. 1–3a: Jesus teaches the crowd from a boat, speaking in parables.
vv. 3b–7: the seed falls on the path, on rocky ground and among thorns, and fails.
v. 8: the seed on good soil yields a hundredfold, sixty and thirty.
v. 9: “Let anyone with ears listen!”
kw: From the Greek verb “to throw alongside”. In Hebrew māshāl is any wise saying or comparison. A parable puts something known beside something new, so that the listener must think and choose. The Catechism notes that parables invite us to enter the kingdom (CCC 546).
The point of the story is the harvest. Fruit is a favourite word of Matthew for a life changed by the Word (compare 3:8, 7:16–20).
To “have ears” is to be ready to hear. In the Bible hearing means obeying: the word must be received with the whole person.
vv: Listen! A sower went out to sow.
The parable begins with a call to attention. The sower is generous, scattering seed generously, and the seed is good.
Other seeds fell on rocky ground, where they did not have much soil,
Many things start well and die when the sun rises. Faith that has no depth cannot meet trouble or time.
Other seeds fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up and choked them.
The thorns are not wicked: they are only other growing things. Good things, crowded, can choke the best thing.
Other seeds fell on good soil and brought forth grain, some a hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty.
A hundredfold was an extraordinary harvest in Galilee. The surprise of the parable is the harvest: the sower’s labour is not wasted, and the Word bears fruit beyond measure.
Let anyone with ears listen!
Jesus does not say that only some can hear. He invites everyone to hear the Word and let it take root.
ch: The Church has always read this parable as a picture of how the Word of God is received. The Catechism teaches that, as the sower scatters the seed, so Christ teaches in parables, and the kingdom grows in the hearts of those who accept the word with a good heart (CCC 546, 543, in substance). The lesson is not discouragement at the three failures, but wonder at the harvest, and an invitation to examine our own ground. At every Mass the Church makes ready the soil in two ways: the Liturgy of the Word, where the seed is sown, and the Eucharist, which strengthens us to bear fruit.

rite: St Lawrence of Brindisi (1559–1619) was an Italian Capuchin friar, a preacher and a linguist who knew several languages, including Hebrew and Greek, and was so steeped in the Bible that he could, it is said, quote it almost by heart. He served his order as a superior and was sent on diplomatic missions by the Popes. In 1959 Pope St John XXIII declared him a Doctor of the Church. His memorial on 21 July is optional in the Roman calendar. The sower who scatters the Word without counting the cost is a fitting picture of him.
study: The Israelites remembered only the food of Egypt, not its slavery. When have I remembered the past in a way that hid the truth from me?
Which of the soils in the parable is closest to my own heart today: the path, the rock, the thorns or good soil? What is one small step to give the Word more room?

lead: Today the Church keeps the feast of St Mary Magdalene, the first witness of the Resurrection. The two readings sing one longing. In the Song of Songs a woman searches the city by night for the one her soul loves, asks the watchmen, and at last finds him and holds him. In John’s Gospel Mary Magdalene comes to the tomb in the dark, weeps outside it, does not recognise Jesus until he speaks her name, and is sent to tell the disciples, “I have seen the Lord.” Seeking in love, being found by name, and being sent: these are the three movements of today’s feast. Psalm 63, “My soul is thirsting for you, O Lord my God,” gives the same longing a prayer.

r.h: I sought him whom my soul loves
set: The Song of Songs is a collection of love poems, in which a woman and a man speak and sing of one another, with a chorus of friends, the “daughters of Jerusalem”. The Church receives it as inspired Scripture and has always read it on two levels: as a celebration of faithful human love, and as a picture of the love between God and his people, between Christ and the Church, and between God and each soul. The Mass reads it on this feast because Mary Magdalene’s search at the tomb recalls the lover’s search in the night.

This passage is the first of the Song’s two searches (the second is in 5:2–8). It is partly a dream or a night-time scene, told in the lover’s own voice: the empty bed, the empty streets, the watchmen who meet her on their rounds. The Mass reading stops at the finding in v. 4a; the text goes on to say that she holds him until she brings him to her mother’s house.
str: v. 1: by night in her bed she seeks him; she does not find him; she calls and he gives no answer.
v. 2: she resolves to rise and search the city, in the streets and the squares.
v. 3: the sentinels find her, and she asks if they have seen him.
v. 4a: scarcely has she passed them when she finds him; she holds him and will not let him go.
kw: Nefesh means breath, life, the whole person with its desires, more than the “soul” as we now say. The lover loves with her whole self and seeks with her whole self.
The verb “seek” comes four times in vv. 1–2. In the Bible, seeking God is a great theme (Psalm 63:1; Isaiah 55:6; Jeremiah 29:13). Here it is the language of love.

The verb means to grasp, to take hold. It meets its answer in John 20:17, where Jesus says to Mary, “Do not hold on to me”; the same pattern of finding and holding returns, but now love must learn to let the Lord ascend.
vv: Upon my bed at night I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him, but found him not; I called him, but he gave no answer.
Love’s first experience here is absence. Christian spiritual writers have long seen in it the “night” of the soul that seeks God and does not yet feel him near.
“I will rise now and go about the city, in the streets and in the squares; I will seek him whom my soul loves.”
Longing will not stay in bed. She rises and goes into the dark streets. Love moves.
The sentinels found me, as they went about in the city. “Have you seen him whom my soul loves?”
She asks the watchmen of the city. They give no answer in the text, and she finds him soon after, as if the asking itself had brought her close.
Scarcely had I passed them, when I found him whom my soul loves. I held him, and would not let him go
Here is the end of the search. The joy is in the finding, and in the clinging, and in the wish to bring him home.
ch: The Fathers of the Church read the Song in the light of Christ and the soul. St Gregory the Great, in a homily on the Gospel for this feast, quotes this Song when speaking of Mary Magdalene: she seeks the Lord who is gone, and her love will not let her rest (in substance). Hippolytus of Rome, in one of the oldest commentaries on the Song, already links the women at the tomb with the Bride of the Song, and calls them apostles to the apostles (in substance). Today’s pairing follows them. The Church, too, is the Bride who searches for her Lord in the night of the world; and each Christian is invited to seek him with the whole heart (compare CCC 2560–2565 on prayer as thirst for God, in substance).

r.h: I have seen the Lord
set: John’s Resurrection chapter begins in darkness. All four Gospels name Mary Magdalene among the women who went to the tomb on the morning after the Sabbath; John tells only of her, and in his account she is the one who finds the stone removed and runs to tell Peter and the disciple whom Jesus loved. The reading skips vv. 3–10, the race of the two disciples to the tomb and the first faith of the beloved disciple. It then returns to Mary, who has come back, or has stayed, weeping at the entrance.

Who is she? The Gospels introduce her as Mary “called Magdalene”, that is, of Magdala, a town on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee. Luke 8:2 says seven demons had gone out of her, and that she followed Jesus and supported his ministry with other women. She stood at the cross with Jesus’ mother (John 19:25). The Gospels do not say she was a prostitute. She is not the sinful woman who anoints Jesus’ feet in Luke 7:36–50, and she is not Mary of Bethany, the sister of Martha and Lazarus. These identifications came from later centuries and have no support in the Gospel texts.
str: vv. 1–2: the stone is removed; Mary runs to Peter and the beloved disciple: “They have taken the Lord.”
vv. 11–13: Mary weeps outside; she sees two angels; they ask why she weeps.
vv. 14–15: she turns and sees Jesus, but does not recognise him; he asks why she weeps and whom she seeks; she thinks he is the gardener.
v. 16: he says her name, “Mary!”, and she answers, “Rabbouni!”
vv. 17–18: “Do not hold on to me.” He sends her to his brothers; she announces, “I have seen the Lord.”
kw: An Aramaic word, a more personal form of “Rabbi”: “my master”. John says the language was “Hebrew”, as he uses the word for the Jewish language of Jesus’ day. She recognises his voice before his face.
do not hold on to me

The Greek present imperative can mean “stop clinging to me”. Mary’s embrace (compare Matthew 28:9, where the women take hold of his feet) is not forbidden as sinful. Jesus is telling her that the relationship has changed: she must not try to keep him as he was, because he is ascending to the Father, and will be present in a new way, in the Spirit and in the Church.

The verb used of Mary in v. 18 is the verb for an announcement from a messenger. She is the first to bring the news of the Resurrection to the disciples. Over centuries, Christians have called her the “apostle to the apostles”, since she was sent to the apostles with the news.
vv: Early on the first day of the week, while it was still dark, Mary Magdalene came to the tomb
The “first day of the week” is the Day of the Lord, the day of new creation. Darkness is both the hour and the state of her heart.
“They have taken the Lord out of the tomb, and we do not know where they have laid him.”
“We” suggests she was not alone, as the other Gospels say. Her first thought is not of resurrection but of theft: love will not accept that the body is lost.
“Woman, why are you weeping?” She said to them, “They have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him.”
The angels ask what Jesus will ask. Her tears show love which has not yet understood. Notice “my Lord”: the love is personal.
Jesus said to her, “Mary!” She turned and said to him in Hebrew, “Rabbouni!”
The whole scene turns on one word. Jesus had said in the Good Shepherd discourse that the sheep hear his voice and he calls his own by name (John 10:3–4). She is found by name.
“Do not hold on to me, because I have not yet ascended to the Father.
Easter is not a return to the earlier life. The Risen Lord is going to the Father, and the disciples will have to learn to be with him in faith.
Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples, “I have seen the Lord”;
The first words of the Church’s preaching are: “I have seen the Lord.” They are spoken by a woman, and the disciples hear them from her.
ch: The Catechism says that Mary Magdalene and the holy women, who had come to finish anointing the body of Jesus, were the first to encounter the Risen One, and so women were the first messengers of Christ’s Resurrection for the apostles themselves (CCC 641). Jesus’ words “my Father and your Father” show that he is the Son of God in a way no disciple is, and also that he makes his disciples sharers in his filial life (CCC 443, in substance). St Thomas Aquinas, commenting on John, calls Mary the apostle to the apostles (in substance), and Gregory the Great, preaching on this Gospel, sees in her tears the love that seeks and does not give up (in substance). On 3 June 2016, the Congregation for Divine Worship, with the approval of Pope Francis, raised her memorial to the rank of feast in the Roman calendar, so that she may be honoured as the apostle of the apostles.

qa: Was Mary Magdalene a sinful woman? Was she Jesus’ wife?

The Gospels say she was a woman from whom seven demons had gone out (Luke 8:2), a disciple and a witness of the cross and the empty tomb. They never say she was a prostitute, and they do not identify her with the woman of Luke 7. That identification goes back to a sermon of Pope Gregory the Great in the sixth century and shaped art and preaching for a long time, but the Church’s own liturgy no longer makes it. As for the claim that she was Jesus’ wife, no Gospel, and no ancient Christian tradition of the first centuries, says so. It comes from much later writings and from modern fiction, and has no support in the Scriptures the Church receives.
Why does Jesus say “Do not hold on to me”, when he later lets Thomas touch his wounds?

Both are true to the Gospel of John. The words to Mary are not a rebuke but a change of relation: she is not to cling to the earlier way of being with him, for he is ascending to the Father. The invitation to Thomas is a different moment, for a different need, to bring a doubting disciple to faith (John 20:27). Jesus is the same in both, risen with a true, glorified body (CCC 645). In both cases the answer is the same: believe and go and tell.
Is it right to call a woman an “apostle”? Does it change the apostolic ministry of the Twelve?

In the early Church “apostle” has more than one use. In its strictest meaning it names the Twelve and Paul, chosen by Christ to be witnesses and the foundation of the Church’s ministry, and bishops are their successors. In a wider sense it means “one who is sent”, and Mary Magdalene was sent by the Risen Lord himself to the disciples. The title “apostle of the apostles”, used by Hippolytus and Aquinas, honours that mission without changing the Church’s teaching on the apostolic ministry.
rite: Until 2016 the Roman calendar kept 22 July as an obligatory memorial. By decree of the Congregation for Divine Worship and the Discipline of the Sacraments, on 3 June 2016, it became a feast, in the same rank as the feasts of the other apostles. The Mass, with the Gloria, has its own Preface, which praises her as the one sent by the Risen Christ as apostle to the apostles. The Mass readings are the Song of Songs 3 (or 2 Corinthians 5:14–17) and John 20. In Latin art she is often shown with a jar of ointment, as one of the women who came to anoint the Lord. Her name, “of Magdala”, reminds us that in Galilee, a town beside the lake was the home of the first witness of the Resurrection.
study: Mary kept looking for the Lord even when she found only an empty tomb. When has my search for God felt like an empty place, and what kept me going?
Jesus called her by name, and she knew him. Where do I hear God calling me by name: in prayer, in Scripture, in a person who needs me?
“Do not hold on to me”: what in my faith do I try to keep unchanged, when the Lord is leading me on?
Mary became the first to say, “I have seen the Lord.” To whom am I being sent this week with good news?

lead: Three months after leaving Egypt, the people stand at Mount Sinai, and God speaks the Ten Commandments. They begin not with a demand but with a reminder: “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.” The law is given to a people already rescued. In the Gospel Jesus explains the parable of the sower to his disciples, naming the path, the rock, the thorns and the good soil, and showing what hinders the Word and what lets it bear fruit. Both readings are about hearing God’s word and doing it. Psalm 19 praises the law: “The decrees of the Lord are sure, making wise the simple.” The Church may also remember St Bridget of Sweden.

r.h: The ten words
set: Israel has come to Sinai in the third month (19:1). Moses has gone up and down the mountain, and the people have been told to prepare. Now, in the hearing of the whole people, God speaks. The Decalogue is the heart of the covenant at Sinai. The book of Exodus places it before the longer collection of laws (chapters 21–23), and the covenant is sealed in chapter 24, which the Mass reads tomorrow.

The Ten Commandments appear twice in the Bible, here and in Deuteronomy 5:6–21, with small differences, such as the reason given for the Sabbath. The Hebrew Bible calls them the “ten words” (34:28). Different traditions divide them in different ways. The Catholic Church follows the numbering of St Augustine, as the Catechism notes (CCC 2066): the first commandment forbids other gods and idols together (vv. 2–6), and the ninth and tenth are the two commandments against coveting (v. 17).
str: vv. 1–2: God speaks, and introduces himself by what he has done: he brought them out of slavery.
vv. 3–6: no other gods; no idols; the Lord is a jealous God, whose mercy reaches to the thousandth generation.
v. 7: the name of the Lord is not to be misused.
vv. 8–11: remember the Sabbath day and keep it holy, because God rested on the seventh day.
vv. 12–17: honour father and mother; do not murder, commit adultery, steal, bear false witness, or covet.
kw: I am the Lord your God
The Ten Words begin with a statement of who God is and what he has done, before they say what he asks. Obedience is the answer of a rescued people.

In Hebrew this word means a passionate love that will not be shared, like that of a husband for his wife (compare Hosea 2). It is not envy. The punishment that “reaches the third and fourth generation” is set beside mercy that reaches “the thousandth”, so mercy is far greater. Ezekiel 18 later makes clear that each person answers for his or her own sin.

The verb names the unlawful killing of a person, not every taking of life (see, for example, the laws of war and of the court in Exodus 21–22). The Church understands the commandment as a strong protection of every human life (CCC 2258, in substance).
vv: I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery;
The law is rooted in grace. God does not first give commands and then rescue those who keep them; he rescues, and then gives the commands as the way of life for those he has rescued.
you shall have no other gods before me.
The first commandment asks for the whole heart. “Before me” can also be heard as “in my presence”: there is no place where another god may stand.
but showing steadfast love to the thousandth generation of those who love me and keep my commandments.
The last word of the first table is mercy. The Hebrew ḥesed is the covenant love that does not fail.
Remember the sabbath day, and keep it holy.
The Sabbath is a gift of time to be with God. The Church, in memory of the Lord’s Resurrection on the first day of the week, keeps Sunday as the Lord’s Day (CCC 2174).
Honor your father and your mother, so that your days may be long in the land that the Lord your God is giving you.
This commandment stands at the hinge between the two tables, between God and neighbour. The family is where we first learn what it is to be loved and to owe love.
You shall not covet your neighbor’s house;
The last commandments look into the heart: wrongdoing begins as desire. Jesus will say the same in the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5:21–30).
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Decalogue means literally “ten words” and that God revealed these words to his people on the holy mountain (CCC 2056). When a rich young man asked what he must do, Jesus answered, “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments” (Matthew 19:17; compare CCC 2053), and he sums them up in the double commandment of love of God and neighbour (Matthew 22:37–40). The ban on images does not forbid the Christian veneration of holy images, which honours the person they represent, and the Incarnation of the Son of God has changed what may be shown (CCC 2131–2132, in substance). In the New Covenant the law is written on the heart by the Holy Spirit; it is not set aside. Christians share this reading with the Jewish people, for whom the Ten Words are also a gift, and we honour that bond.

r.h: The sower explained
set: After the parable of the sower (13:1–9) Jesus explained to his disciples why he spoke in parables (13:10–17). Now he explains this parable itself. It is the first of three parables of this chapter that he explains, the others being the weeds (13:36–43) and the net (13:49–50). The reading is the heart of the chapter: how does the Word of God meet different hearers?

Many scholars see in the explanation the early Church’s way of applying the parable, shaped by its own experience of preaching; the Church receives it as part of the inspired Gospel, in which Jesus himself teaches how the word is received (compare Mark 4:13–20 and Luke 8:11–15).
str: v. 18: “Hear then the parable of the sower.”
v. 19: the seed on the path: the word is heard but not understood, and the evil one snatches it away.
vv. 20–21: the seed on rocky ground: received with joy, but with no root, it falls away in trouble or persecution.
v. 22: the seed among thorns: the cares of the world and the lure of wealth choke it.
v. 23: the seed on good soil: the one who hears and understands, and bears fruit, a hundredfold, sixty or thirty.
kw: Matthew uses it twice in this passage (vv. 19, 23). In the Bible, to understand is more than knowing facts: it is to take the word to heart, so that it shapes the life. The fruit grows from that understanding.

The one on rocky ground “falls away” (literally “is made to stumble”) in trouble or persecution. Matthew’s community knew such pressure. The word names a failure of endurance, not a hatred of the word.
“Cares of the world” and “the lure of wealth” are the thorns. The Greek word for “lure” can also mean deceit: wealth promises security, and does not keep the promise.
vv: When anyone hears the word of the kingdom and does not understand it, the evil one comes and snatches away what is sown in the heart;
The seed that is not understood has no defence. The Word needs the effort of the mind and the opening of the heart.
yet such a person has no root, but endures only for a while,
Joy is a good beginning, but without root, in prayer, the sacraments and the community, it cannot meet hardship.
but the cares of the world and the lure of wealth choke the word, and it yields nothing.
The Word is not driven out by great sins but crowded out by many small cares. Ordinary anxieties and the love of money can leave a good heart without fruit.
this is the one who hears the word and understands it, who indeed bears fruit
The good soil is not a perfect heart but one that hears, understands and bears fruit. Fruit comes in different measures: a hundred, sixty or thirty, and each is a harvest.
ch: The Church sees in this explanation a call to hear the Word of God with faith and to put it into practice. The Second Vatican Council teaches that the Church has always venerated the Scriptures as she has venerated the Lord’s Body, and urges all the faithful to read them with prayer (Dei Verbum 21–25, in substance). The Catechism teaches that in Baptism the Word is sown in the heart, and that perseverance in faith needs prayer, the sacraments and the support of the community (compare CCC 162, in substance). The four soils are not four kinds of people fixed for ever; most of us are all four at different times, and the Church offers her help, in Word and sacrament, to deepen the soil.

rite: St Bridget of Sweden (about 1303–1373) was a noblewoman, the wife of Ulf Gudmarsson, and the mother of eight children, among them St Catherine of Sweden. After her husband’s death she gave herself to prayer and penance and founded the Order of the Most Holy Saviour, the Brigittines, at Vadstena. She spent her last decades in Rome, from 1349, and made a pilgrimage to the Holy Land in 1372. She died in Rome on 23 July 1373. Her visions were gathered in the Revelations; the Church leaves such private revelations to the judgement of faith and does not require belief in them. In 1999 Pope St John Paul II named her, with St Catherine of Siena and St Teresa Benedicta of the Cross, a co-patroness of Europe.
study: God began by reminding the people what he had done for them, and then he gave the commandments. How does remembering what God has done for me change the way I keep his law?
Which “thorn” most often crowds out the Word in my life: anxiety, work, money, or something else? What could I do this week to give the Word more room?

lead: Today’s first reading is the sealing of the covenant at Sinai. Moses tells the people all the words of the Lord, and they answer with one voice, “All the words that the Lord has spoken we will do.” Then he builds an altar, offers sacrifice and sprinkles the blood: half on the altar, half on the people. “See the blood of the covenant that the Lord has made with you.” In the Gospel Jesus tells the parable of the wheat and the weeds, in which the owner will not pull up the weeds early, “for in gathering the weeds you would uproot the wheat along with them.” Both readings speak of God’s patient dealing with his people and of the day of harvest. The Church may also remember St Sharbel Makhluf, a hermit of Lebanon.

r.h: The blood of the covenant
set: Chapters 20–23 gave the Ten Commandments and the “Book of the Covenant”, a collection of laws for life in the land. Now the covenant is formally made. In the ancient world a covenant between a ruler and a people was sealed with an oath and a ritual. At Sinai the sealing has three parts: the people hear the words and promise obedience; an altar is built with twelve pillars for the twelve tribes; and the blood of the sacrifice is shared between God and the people.

The reading leaves out nothing important in the sealing. The verses that follow (vv. 9–11) tell how Moses, Aaron and the elders go up the mountain and eat and drink in God’s presence: the covenant ends in a meal. The sacrifices are offered by “young men”, because the priesthood of Aaron has not yet been established (compare 28:1).
str: v. 3: Moses tells the people all the words and ordinances; they answer, “All the words that the Lord has spoken we will do.”
v. 4: he writes down the words, builds an altar at the foot of the mountain and sets up twelve pillars.
v. 5: young men offer burnt offerings and offerings of well-being.

vv. 6–8: Moses puts half the blood in basins and dashes half against the altar; he reads the book of the covenant; the people promise to obey; he sprinkles the people with the blood: “See the blood of the covenant.”
kw: A covenant is a solemn bond, more than a contract. In it God binds himself to the people, and the people bind themselves to him. It is the basic word of the Old Testament. The New Testament speaks of the “new covenant” in Christ’s blood (Luke 22:20).

In Israel’s understanding the life of a living creature is in its blood (Leviticus 17:11). The blood on the altar and on the people shows that one life now joins God and the people. The act is a sign of binding union, not of violence.
we will do and we will hear

In v. 7 the people say they “will do” and “will be obedient” (literally, “will hear”, and in Hebrew hearing means obeying). Their promise is generous and sincere. Chapter 32 will show how quickly it is tested, which is why the covenant rests on God’s mercy too.
vv: All the words that the Lord has spoken we will do.
The people speak with one voice. God has given the commandments to a rescued people, and they accept them willingly. The covenant is not forced on them.
Moses wrote down all the words of the Lord.
God’s word is written down. This is the beginning of Scripture as the Church receives it: a book that keeps the covenant, and is read to the people.
Moses took half of the blood and put it in basins, and half of the blood he dashed against the altar.
The altar represents God. The blood shared between altar and people shows that the two parties are joined by one life.
Then he took the book of the covenant, and read it in the hearing of the people;
The covenant is sealed by reading and hearing, as at every Liturgy of the Word. The people respond only after they have heard.
“See the blood of the covenant that the Lord has made with you in accordance with all these words.”
These words are echoed at the Last Supper. The covenant of Sinai is the pattern, and Jesus takes it to its fulfilment.
ch: The Church hears in Moses’ words the foreshadowing of the Last Supper. Jesus says over the cup, “This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many” (Mark 14:24; compare Matthew 26:28, Luke 22:20, 1 Corinthians 11:25), and the Letter to the Hebrews draws the comparison in full (Hebrews 9:18–22). The Catechism teaches that Christ’s death is the sacrifice of the New Covenant, which restores us to communion with God through the “blood of the covenant” (CCC 613). At every Mass, the Liturgy of the Word, with its reading and its “Amen”, and then the sacrifice and the meal, follows the pattern of Sinai: God speaks, the people respond, and the blood of the covenant is shared. The first covenant, never revoked (Romans 11:29), remains the root, and Christians honour it.

r.h: The wheat and the weeds
set: This is the second parable of Matthew 13, after the sower. It is found only in Matthew. Jesus tells it to the crowds beside the sea; later, in the house, he explains it privately to his disciples (13:36–43). The picture is one a Galilean farmer knew well. The “weeds” are probably darnel, a grass that looks very like wheat until the ear forms, and whose roots can tangle with those of the wheat, so that one cannot easily be pulled up without the other.
The parable answers a question that every generation asks: if the kingdom of heaven is God’s field, and the seed is good, why is there evil in it, even within the community of believers?
str: vv. 24–26: a man sows good seed; while everyone sleeps, an enemy sows weeds; both come up.
vv. 27–28: the servants ask where the weeds came from; the master says an enemy did this; they ask if they should gather them.
vv. 29–30: the master says no, lest the wheat be uprooted; let both grow together until the harvest, when the reapers will separate them.
kw: The Greek word names the darnel that grows in grain fields. To the eye, until the harvest, it is hard to tell from wheat. This is why no one can be sure who is wheat and who is weed.
The weeds are not the farmer’s mistake but the work of an enemy. In the explanation Jesus names him as the devil (13:39). Evil is real, and it is not from God.
In the Old Testament and the Gospels the harvest is the time of God’s final judgment (compare Joel 3:13; Revelation 14:15). The parable moves the sorting out of human hands and into God’s.
vv: while everybody was asleep, an enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat, and then went away.
The enemy works in secret and leaves. The weeds are noticed only when the plants have grown.
‘An enemy has done this.’
The master does not blame his servants or his seed. Evil has an enemy’s hand behind it, and it is not part of the good God has sown.
‘No; for in gathering the weeds you would uproot the wheat along with them.
The servants’ zeal is natural, but they cannot see well enough. Judging and uprooting by human hands risks harming the good.
Let both of them grow together until the harvest;
This is God’s patience. It gives time for repentance, since the weeds of today may still turn, by grace, to wheat. It is not indifference to evil.
but gather the wheat into my barn.
The parable ends with the gathering of the good. God’s purpose is the harvest, and the barn is the sign of what the whole field is for.
ch: The Church has always read this parable as a teaching about patience and the final judgment. St Augustine used it against the Donatists, who wanted a Church of the pure only: on earth, he said, the Church holds good and bad together until the harvest (in substance). The Catechism teaches that the Church is “at once holy and always in need of purification”, embracing sinners in her bosom, and that all her members, ministers included, must acknowledge that they are sinners (CCC 827, in substance). The parable does not forbid correction or discipline: Jesus himself teaches how to correct a brother (Matthew 18:15–17). It forbids hasty judgment of persons, which belongs to God, who alone sees the heart. Meanwhile, it calls each of us to examine our own field, and to pray for the conversion of those who do wrong.

qa: If God is patient with evil, does that mean we should do nothing about it?

No. The parable speaks of what the servants must not do: uproot persons by their own judgment before the harvest. It does not tell the Church to ignore sin. Jesus tells his disciples to correct a brother who sins (Matthew 18:15–17), to love enemies, to feed the hungry, and to work for justice. The parable asks us to resist evil with patience and mercy, and to leave to God the final separation, because he alone knows who will bear fruit and who may yet repent.
rite: St Sharbel Makhluf (1828–1898) was a Maronite monk and priest of Lebanon. Born Youssef Makhlouf in a mountain village, he entered the monastery of St Maron at Annaya in 1851, took the name Sharbel, and was ordained priest in 1859. In 1875 he withdrew to the hermitage of Saints Peter and Paul above the monastery, where he lived for twenty-three years in prayer, poverty and obedience. He died on 24 December 1898, eight days after a stroke suffered while celebrating the Divine Liturgy, and his tomb at Annaya has drawn pilgrims of many faiths. Pope St Paul VI canonised him in 1977. The Maronite Church, in full communion with Rome, belongs to the Syriac tradition, a heritage shared by the Eastern Churches of Kerala, and devotion to him has spread far beyond Lebanon. His memorial on 24 July is optional in the Roman calendar.
study: The people said, “We will do,” and later they failed. How can I keep my own promises to God, knowing my weakness, by relying on his mercy?
At Mass I hear the Word, answer “Amen” and receive the Lord’s Body and Blood. How can I take the “blood of the covenant” more seriously the next time I am there?
In the parable, patience is not indifference. Whom am I tempted to “uproot” in my judgment, and how might God be patient with them, and with me?

lead: The Seventeenth Sunday of Year B opens five Sundays in which the Roman Lectionary pauses Mark and reads John 6, the chapter of the bread. Today is the sign itself: Jesus takes five barley loaves and two fish from a boy, gives thanks, and feeds about five thousand, with twelve baskets left over. The first reading gives the pattern in miniature: the prophet Elisha feeds a hundred people with twenty barley loaves, and the Lord says, “They shall eat and have some left.” Psalm 145 sings the same trust: “You open your hand, satisfying the desire of every living thing.”

The second reading, from Ephesians, seems to change the subject, but it names what the bread builds: one body, one Spirit, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all. The bread that Christ gives is not only for each person; it gathers a people into unity.

r.h: They shall eat and have some left
set: The story belongs to the cycle of Elisha, the prophet who took up the work of Elijah in the northern kingdom of Israel in the ninth century before Christ. Just before this scene the sons of the prophets are hungry because of a famine in the land, and Elisha has made a poisoned stew safe to eat (4:38–41). Bread is scarce, and a man brings the first of his harvest to the “man of God”.

The gift comes from Baal-shalishah, a place in the hill country of Ephraim whose exact site is not certain. Under the Law the firstfruits were holy to the Lord and were given to his priests and ministers (Numbers 18:13; Deuteronomy 18:4). Here the man brings them to the prophet, and the prophet gives them away.
str: v. 42: a man brings twenty barley loaves and fresh grain from the first fruits; Elisha says, “Give it to the people and let them eat.”
v. 43: the servant objects that it cannot feed a hundred; Elisha repeats the command and gives God’s word: “They shall eat and have some left.”
v. 44: the servant sets it before them; they eat and have some left, “according to the word of the Lord”.
kw: The first and best of the crop, offered to God in thanks. The loaves are therefore holy bread, yet Elisha does not keep them for himself or for the prophets; he gives them to the hungry.
The word of the Lord is a promise of enough and more than enough. The same two verbs close the story, so that the event matches the word exactly.
The usual title for a prophet who speaks and acts for God. The miracle is done by God’s word through his messenger, not by the prophet’s own power.
vv: Give it to the people and let them eat.
The command is simple and generous. The firstfruits, given to God, become food for his hungry people.
How can I set this before a hundred people?
The servant speaks honestly about the numbers. The story gives his doubt its place: the miracle begins where human resources end.
thus says the Lord, ‘They shall eat and have some left.’
Elisha does not argue about arithmetic; he repeats what God has said. Obedience to the word comes first, and then the loaves are enough.
He set it before them, they ate, and had some left, according to the word of the Lord.
The story ends with the word fulfilled. John does not name Elisha, but the barley loaves, the doubt about the numbers and the leftovers make the echo hard to miss.
ch: The Church reads this story as a sign pointing forward to the Gospel, as the Lectionary does by placing it before John 6. The Catechism teaches that the Old Testament prepares what Christ fulfils, and that the miracles of the multiplication of the loaves foretell the greater bread of the Eucharist (CCC 1335). What Elisha does for a hundred, Christ does for five thousand; what Elisha does by a word received, Christ does by his own word, since he is the Word. The Church also keeps the thought of the firstfruits: in the Mass the bread and wine are offered in thanks to God, and returned to his people as the Body and Blood of Christ.

r.h: One Lord, one faith, one baptism
set: The letter to the Ephesians is traditionally ascribed to St Paul, writing as a prisoner. Many scholars think it was written by a close disciple of Paul after his death, in his name and from his thought; the Church receives it as inspired Scripture and as Paul’s teaching either way. The words “in Ephesus” (1:1) are missing from some of the oldest manuscripts, and many think the letter was meant for several churches in the region, not for one community only.

Chapters 1–3 praise what God has done in Christ: Jews and Gentiles, once divided, are made one in Christ’s body. Chapters 4–6 turn to how that unity is to be lived. Our reading opens the second half with the word “therefore”: because of what God has done, live in a way that fits it.
str: v. 1: “I… beg you to lead a life worthy of the calling to which you have been called.”
v. 2: the attitudes that make unity possible: humility, gentleness, patience, love.
v. 3: the effort to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
vv. 4–6: the creed of unity in seven “ones”: body, Spirit, hope, Lord, faith, baptism, God and Father of all.
kw: Literally “to walk in a way worthy of”. In Scripture the Christian life is a way along which one walks day by day, not only a belief held.
The word means eagerness and diligence. Unity is a gift of the Spirit, yet it asks effort from us; Paul says to “maintain” it, not to create it.
A ligament, something that binds parts together. The unity is held together by peace, as the body is held together by its ligaments.
vv: I therefore, the prisoner in the Lord, beg you
Paul writes from prison and has no earthly power. He begs, and his chains give weight to his words.
with all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love,
Unity is not first an organisation but a way of treating one another. Christians are different from each other, and love means bearing with the difference.
making every effort to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
The Spirit gives the unity; Christians must protect it. The goal is not sameness but peace among those who are different.
one Lord, one faith, one baptism,
Many scholars think Paul, or his disciple, is quoting here a very early summary of the faith: one Lord confessed, one faith professed, one baptism by which believers are joined to him.
one God and Father of all, who is above all and through all and in all.
The list ends with the Father, source of everything. The Trinity is in the background: one Spirit (v. 4), one Lord (v. 5), one God and Father (v. 6).
ch: The Catechism says that the Church is one because of her source, the unity of the Trinity (CCC 813), and that baptism is the foundation of the communion among all Christians (CCC 1271). It teaches that the Eucharist makes the Church: those who share one bread are one body (CCC 1396). The wounds of division among Christians are real, and the Church prays and works for the unity Christ wills. The seven “ones” are also the foundation of ecumenical dialogue: Catholics, Orthodox and many other Christians share one Lord, one baptism and a great part of the one faith.

r.h: Jesus took the loaves, gave thanks, and distributed them
set: John calls the miracles of Jesus “signs”, and this is one of the best known. Apart from the Resurrection, it is the only miracle that all four Gospels record. John sets it by the Sea of Galilee, also called the Sea of Tiberias, a name taken from the city Herod Antipas built there and named for the emperor.

John places it near Passover, “the festival of the Jews” (v. 4). He writes for readers who may not know the feast, and he does not mean it as blame: Jesus and his disciples are Jews keeping a Jewish pilgrimage season. The mention of Passover tells the reader that the bread of this chapter will be linked to the new Passover. After the sign Jesus teaches in the synagogue of Capernaum about the bread of life (6:22–59), and the Lectionary reads it across the next Sundays.
str: vv. 1–4: the crowd follows him because of his signs; Jesus goes up the mountain; Passover is near.
vv. 5–9: Jesus asks Philip where to buy bread, to test him; Philip counts the cost; Andrew finds a boy with five barley loaves and two fish.
vv. 10–11: the people sit on the grass; Jesus takes the loaves, gives thanks, and distributes them, and the fish also.
vv. 12–13: “Gather up the fragments”; twelve baskets are filled.
vv. 14–15: “This is indeed the prophet”; Jesus withdraws from those who would make him king.
kw: John calls miracles “signs”: acts that show who Jesus is. The multiplication points to the one who is himself the bread of life.
The verb from which “Eucharist” comes. John uses it of Jesus’ prayer over the loaves (vv. 11 and 23), and the Church has always heard the Mass in it.
Broken pieces of bread. The same word appears in the early Christian eucharistic prayer of the Didache, which speaks of the broken bread scattered on the hills and gathered into one.
vv: Where are we to buy bread for these people to eat?
Jesus asks the question himself and does not wait to be asked. John says that he already knew what he would do (v. 6).
There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish. But what are they among so many people?
Only John mentions the boy and the barley, the bread of the poor. Andrew’s question is honest. Jesus does not dismiss the small gift; he takes it.
Then Jesus took the loaves, and when he had given thanks, he distributed them to those who were seated;

The actions, take, give thanks, distribute, are those the Gospels and St Paul record at the Last Supper (compare Luke 22:19; 1 Corinthians 11:23–24). John does not tell the Supper in this way, so he lets the sign carry the meaning here.
Gather up the fragments left over, so that nothing may be lost.
Jesus is generous and not wasteful. The word “lost” will come again in the discourse: “that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me” (6:39).
he withdrew again to the mountain by himself.
The people want a king who will feed them. Jesus will be a king, but on the cross, not by force. He withdraws to pray, as in other Gospels.
ch: The Catechism says that the miracles of the multiplication of the loaves, when the Lord said the blessing, broke and gave the loaves through his disciples, prefigure the superabundance of the one bread of the Eucharist (CCC 1335). Many of the Fathers loved the details (in substance): they took the twelve baskets as a sign of the twelve apostles, through whom the bread is given to the world, and some heard in the gathered fragments a lesson of reverence for what has been consecrated. The Church has never turned this Gospel into a lesson about food alone: it is about the one who feeds, and about the bread which, in the next verses of the chapter, he will say is his flesh for the life of the world.

The reading also teaches generosity. Jesus used a boy’s small gift; the Church reads in it the call to bring what we have, however little, and to trust that Christ can use it. The Church has always taught that charity toward the hungry is not optional. Those who share the one bread at the altar must not leave others without bread (CCC 1397).

qa: Was the miracle only a miracle of sharing, as some say?

The Church reads the Gospel as it was written: Jesus multiplied the loaves. John calls it a sign, and signs in his Gospel are real acts that point beyond themselves. Sharing is part of the lesson, since the boy gave and the people received, yet the Gospel does not reduce the miracle to sharing. The one who made bread from five loaves is the one who will give himself as bread.
Why do we read John on the Sundays of Mark’s year?

Mark’s Gospel is short, and in Year B the Lectionary reads it through; but it has no long account of the bread. So for five Sundays, from today to the Twenty-first Sunday, the Church reads John 6. This lets the whole chapter be heard in order: the sign, the discourse on the bread of life, and the response of faith or refusal.
Why does Jesus withdraw when the people want to make him king?

Because they want the wrong kind of king, one who gives food without asking for conversion. Jesus is the Messiah, but his kingdom is not won by force or by giving away bread. The same temptation was put to him in the wilderness (Matthew 4:3–4), and he refused it. His kingship will be shown on the cross.
rite: In 2021 Pope Francis established the World Day for Grandparents and the Elderly, to be kept on the Sunday closest to the memorial of Saints Joachim and Anne, whom the Church honours tomorrow as the parents of the Blessed Virgin Mary. Many parishes remember the elderly and the lonely today. The five Sundays of John 6 are also a good time to teach about the Mass: the Eucharistic Prayer follows the same movement as the Gospel, taking bread, giving thanks, breaking and giving. The feast of St James the Apostle, usually kept on this date, gives way to the Sunday.
study: Elisha trusted God’s word when the arithmetic was against it. Where in my life am I counting only what I have and forgetting what God has said?
Paul begs the Ephesians to “maintain the unity of the Spirit”. In my family, parish or workplace, which of the four attitudes, humility, gentleness, patience or love, do I most need to ask for today?
Andrew brought a boy with five loaves to Jesus, though it seemed too little. What small gift of time, skill or money can I bring to Christ this week?
Jesus gave thanks before he broke the bread. How does thanksgiving shape the way I come to Mass and the way I eat at home?

lead: Moses comes down from Sinai carrying the tablets and finds his people dancing round a golden calf. He breaks the tablets, destroys the calf, and then climbs the mountain again to plead for the people, even offering his own name for theirs. In the Gospel Jesus gives two short parables of the kingdom: the mustard seed, smallest of seeds and greatest of shrubs, and the yeast hidden in three measures of flour. One reading shows how great a sin can be, the other how quietly grace works. Today the Church also keeps the memorial of Saints Joachim and Anne, the parents of the Blessed Virgin Mary. The proper readings of the memorial (Sirach 44:1, 10–15 and Matthew 13:16–17) may be used instead of these.

r.h: Alas, this people has sinned a great sin
set: Moses has been on Mount Sinai for forty days receiving the law and the pattern of the tabernacle. At the foot of the mountain the people grew impatient, and Aaron made a calf of gold from their earrings (32:1–6). God told Moses what was happening and threatened to destroy the people, and Moses interceded (32:7–14). Our reading begins as he comes down the mountain.

A calf, or young bull, was a symbol of strength and fertility in the religions around Israel. The people probably meant the calf as a throne or pedestal for the Lord (Aaron proclaims “a festival to the Lord,” 32:5), not as another god, yet the First Commandment forbids making any image of him. The story is the first great test of the covenant just sealed in Exodus 24.
str: vv. 15–16: Moses carries the tablets, the work of God, written on both sides.
vv. 17–18: Joshua hears a noise of war; Moses hears the sound of singing.
vv. 19–20: Moses sees the calf and the dancing, breaks the tablets, destroys the calf and makes the people drink the powder.
vv. 21–24: Moses questions Aaron; Aaron blames the people and says the calf “came out” of the fire.
vv. 30–32: the next day Moses goes back up to the Lord and asks for forgiveness, offering to be blotted out himself.
vv. 33–34: the Lord says that those who sin will be blotted out, yet tells Moses to lead the people on; punishment will come “when the day comes”.
kw: A young bull. The word is used for the idol again in Psalm 106:19 (the psalm used today) and Nehemiah 9:18. In 1 Kings 12:28 Jeroboam makes two golden calves for the northern kingdom, and later writers see in them the same sin.

From the verb kipper, to cover over or make amends. Moses does not claim to take away the sin by himself; he says “perhaps”. Atonement is God’s gift, and the same root names the Day of Atonement (Yom Kippur).
The book that God has written, the list of the living. Moses is ready to be struck from it for the sake of the people. Similar images are found in Psalm 69:28, Daniel 12:1 and Revelation 3:5.
vv: The tablets were the work of God, and the writing was the writing of God, engraved upon the tablets.
The reader is told twice how holy the tablets are before Moses breaks them. The people have shattered what God gave long before Moses does.
it is the sound of revelers that I hear.
The sound of singing: no war, no victory, only noise of feasting round the calf. The text moves slowly toward the scene, and the reader waits with Moses.
So I said to them, ‘Whoever has gold, take it off’; so they gave it to me, and I threw it into the fire, and out came this calf!
Aaron’s excuse is almost comic. He describes the calf as if it appeared on its own. He cannot hide his part (32:2–4), and Scripture does not hide it for him.
blot me out of the book that you have written.
The sentence breaks off before its second half, as though Moses cannot finish it. His love for the people is greater than his concern for himself.
Nevertheless, when the day comes for punishment, I will punish them for their sin.
Forgiveness is not cheap. God keeps his promise to lead them, but sin still has consequences.
ch: Moses is the pattern of the intercessor in Scripture. The Catechism says that his prayer is the typical example of intercessory prayer, which will be fulfilled in Jesus Christ, the one mediator between God and men (CCC 2577). It also teaches that idolatry is not confined to ancient paganism; it remains a constant temptation to faith, whenever a person honours and reveres a creature in place of God (CCC 2113). St Paul’s own wish to be accursed for the sake of his people (Romans 9:3) shows the same love, and the Church sees in Moses’ offer a foreshadowing of Christ, who actually became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13) so that sins might be forgiven.

r.h: The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed … like yeast
set: Matthew 13 is the third great discourse of the Gospel and gathers parables of the kingdom. Jesus has just told the sower and the weeds; now he gives two short parables about growth, one from the field and one from the kitchen. One image comes from a man’s sowing and the other from a woman’s baking, so that all his listeners may recognise their own daily work.

Both parables answer a question the disciples and crowds might ask: if the kingdom has come, why does it look so small? Jesus answers that it begins small and hidden, and grows by its own hidden power.
str: vv. 31–32: the mustard seed: smallest of seeds, greatest of shrubs, a home for the birds.
v. 33: the yeast a woman hid in three measures of flour until all was leavened.
vv. 34–35: Jesus speaks to the crowds only in parables, fulfilling the word of the prophet.
kw: The black mustard plant, whose seed is tiny, was proverbial for smallness, though it can grow to a height of a few metres. Jesus uses ordinary experience to make a point and does not teach botany.

Often a sign of corruption in Scripture (1 Corinthians 5:6–8), but here a sign of the kingdom’s hidden and spreading power. Jesus uses the same image in different senses elsewhere, which shows that a parable has one main point.
Three seah, a large quantity of flour, the amount Sarah used for her three visitors (Genesis 18:6). The yeast works on a great mass, so the kingdom is meant for a great many.
vv: it is the smallest of all the seeds, but when it has grown it is the greatest of shrubs and becomes a tree,
The contrast is the point: the very small becomes the very large. The tree where the birds come to nest echoes Ezekiel 17:23 and Daniel 4:12, where a great tree shelters the nations.
like yeast that a woman took and mixed in with three measures of flour until all of it was leavened.
The yeast is hidden, but it works from within. The kingdom does not begin with power or display but in a heart or a community, and changes the whole.
I will proclaim what has been hidden from the foundation of the world.
Matthew quotes Psalm 78:2, where the psalmist says he will tell the story of Israel in riddles. The hidden things are the mysteries of the kingdom, now made known in Jesus.
ch: The Council taught that the Church is, on earth, the seed and the beginning of the kingdom, and that this kingdom grows slowly through history (Lumen Gentium 5). Some of the Fathers heard in the mustard seed Christ himself, buried like a seed and rising as the great tree (in substance). These readings give the Church a calm patience: small beginnings and unseen work are the way of God.

rite: Joachim and Anne are the traditional names of the parents of the Blessed Virgin Mary. They are not named in the Gospels. The names come from an early Christian writing, the Protoevangelium of James, probably of the second century, which the Church does not count as Scripture but which has shaped devotion and art. Their joint memorial on this date has been kept in the Roman calendar since its reform in 1969. The Church honours them as grandparents of Jesus according to the flesh and as the first teachers of Mary in the faith of Israel. The Mass today may therefore be a prayer for grandparents and for the transmission of faith in families.
study: Moses went back up the mountain for a people who had wronged God. For whom, even someone who has hurt me, can I plead in prayer this week?
The yeast is hidden but changes all the dough. What small, hidden thing, a kind word or a daily prayer, might change my home from within?

lead: After the sin of the golden calf, the first reading shows what remained between God and Moses: a tent outside the camp where the Lord spoke to him “face to face, as one speaks to a friend”, and a mountain where the Lord passed before him and proclaimed his name, merciful and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love. Moses’ prayer, “pardon our iniquity and our sin”, is answered with a renewed covenant. In the Gospel the disciples ask Jesus to explain the parable of the weeds, and he describes the harvest at the end of the age, when the righteous will shine like the sun. In both readings the patience of God is the ground of hope, and his justice is not forgotten.

r.h: The Lord used to speak to Moses face to face
set: The two passages come from after the golden calf (Exodus 32). God has said that his angel, but not he himself, will go with the people (33:2–3), and the people mourn. The “tent of meeting” described in 33:7–11 is not the grand tabernacle, which has not yet been built; it is a simple tent that Moses pitches outside the camp, a place of prayer and of seeking the Lord’s will.

Chapter 34 tells of the renewal: Moses cuts two new tablets and goes up the mountain again, and the Lord comes down in the cloud. The words proclaimed in verses 6–7 are among the most quoted in the Old Testament, repeated in Numbers 14:18, Nehemiah 9:17, Psalm 103:8, Joel 2:13 and Jonah 4:2.
str: 33:7–8: Moses’ tent outside the camp; the people watch him go.
33:9–11: the pillar of cloud, the Lord speaking with Moses face to face; Joshua stays.
34:5–7: the Lord descends, proclaims his name and his merciful character.
34:8–9: Moses bows and prays for forgiveness and for the Lord to go with them.
34:28: forty days and forty nights; the words of the covenant written on the tablets.
kw: A place where God and his people meet. Because it is outside the camp, the people must go out from their own tents to seek the Lord, and everyone who seeks him may go (33:7).

A Hebrew idiom for direct and friendly speech. The Lord says a little later in the same chapter that no one can see his face and live (33:20), so “face to face” describes closeness, not sight of God’s being.
The first two of the attributes of the Lord that the Jewish tradition calls the thirteen attributes of mercy. “Merciful” is from the word for womb, reḥem: the tenderness of a mother.
Faithful, covenant love that does not give up. It is the quality in God that most often makes the covenant possible after the people’s failure.
vv: Thus the Lord used to speak to Moses face to face, as one speaks to a friend.
This is the phrase that gives Moses his place among the prophets. In Numbers 12:8 the Lord says of Moses that he speaks with him directly, not in riddles.
