The Lord, the Lord, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness,
God defines himself. He begins with mercy, not with power. This description is the foundation of the whole Old Testament’s hope in forgiveness.
keeping steadfast love for the thousandth generation,
God’s love reaches to a thousand generations, while his visiting of sin reaches only to three or four (v. 7). The balance is on the side of mercy.
Although this is a stiff-necked people, pardon our iniquity and our sin, and take us for your inheritance.

God had called them a stiff-necked people (33:3, 5), and Moses uses the same word as a reason for God to go with them: because they are so weak they need God more. He includes himself in the sin: “our iniquity”.
ch: The Church reads God’s self-description in Exodus 34 as the root of everything she says about divine mercy. The Catechism presents Moses, who spoke to the Lord face to face as to a friend, as a model both of contemplative prayer and of intercession (CCC 2576–2577). It treats this same self-revelation of the Lord as “merciful and gracious” when it speaks of God’s mercy and love (CCC 210–211).

r.h: Explain to us the parable of the weeds of the field
set: Jesus has told the parable of the weeds sown among the wheat (13:24–30): the householder’s servants want to pull up the weeds, but he says to let both grow together until the harvest. Now Jesus leaves the crowds, goes into the house, and explains it privately to his disciples. This is the second parable in the chapter with an explanation, after the sower (13:18–23).

The weeds were probably darnel, a plant that looks like wheat until it ripens. The parable answers a question early Christians asked and we still ask: if the kingdom has come, why is there still evil in the field?
str: v. 36: the disciples ask for an explanation.
vv. 37–39: the interpretation of each figure: the sower, the field, the good seed, the weeds, the enemy, the harvest and the reapers.
vv. 40–42: the end of the age: the Son of Man sends angels to collect the causes of sin and the evildoers.
v. 43: the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father.
kw: A weed that looks like wheat. Pulling it up early would destroy the wheat. The point is patience, not indifference to evil.
Literally “stumbling blocks”. They are removed from the kingdom, not individual weak people, but the things that make others fall.
The close of the present age, when God’s purpose is completed. The expression is characteristic of Matthew (13:39, 40, 49; 24:3; 28:20).
vv: the field is the world,
The field is the world, not only the Church. Jesus sows his Word in the whole world, and the good seed is “the children of the kingdom”.
Just as the weeds are collected and burned up with fire, so will it be at the end of the age.
Judgment belongs to God and comes at the end. Until then the disciples’ task is not to uproot the weeds but to grow as good wheat.
Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father.
An echo of Daniel 12:3, where those who lead many to righteousness shine like the stars. The end of the story is light, and the Father’s kingdom is home.
ch: The Catechism teaches that in every member of the Church, the weeds of sin are still mixed with the good wheat of the Gospel until the end of time (CCC 827). It adds that the Church is therefore holy, yet always in need of purification, and follows the way of penance and renewal (CCC 827). The Church’s teaching on the last things quotes the same Gospel: Jesus solemnly proclaims that he will send his angels, and they will gather all who do evil (CCC 1034). St Augustine used the parable to teach that in this age the good and the bad are mixed in the Church and in the world (in substance); only God can sort them, and so we are to judge no one beforehand.

qa: Does God punish children for the sins of their parents (Exodus 34:7)?

No. The Bible itself corrects this reading. Ezekiel 18 says plainly that the child will not bear the guilt of the parent, and Deuteronomy 24:16 forbids it in the courts. Exodus 34:7 means that sin has long consequences in families and communities, as hatred, violence and addiction pass from one generation to the next. It also says that God’s love reaches a thousand generations, far beyond the reach of sin.
study: God describes himself first as “merciful and gracious”. When I think of God, do I begin with mercy or with fear?
Jesus teaches patience with the weeds. Where in my family or parish am I tempted to “pull up the weeds” instead of praying and waiting?

lead: Moses comes down from Sinai with a shining face and does not know it: he has been talking with God, and the light has stayed on him. The people are afraid to come near, so he veils his face when he speaks with them and takes the veil off when he goes in before the Lord. In the Gospel Jesus tells two short parables of the kingdom: a hidden treasure and a pearl of great price, each found and bought at the cost of everything. Psalm 99 repeats, “Holy is the Lord our God.”

Today is the memorial of St Alphonsa of the Immaculate Conception, a Franciscan Clarist sister of Kerala who died on 28 July 1946 after a short life of great suffering, and who in 2008 was canonised, the first woman of India raised to the altars. These readings are the weekday readings; the prayers of the Mass may be taken from the Common of Virgins. Her life is a living commentary on both: a face that shone without her knowing it, and a heart that gave everything for the treasure.

r.h: Moses did not know that the skin of his face shone
set: Moses has come down Sinai for the second time, carrying the new tablets after the golden calf. For forty days and nights he has been in the presence of the Lord (34:28), and the people see the mark of it on him.

The passage is the end of a long section about the renewal of the covenant. It also prepares the building of the tabernacle in the last chapters of Exodus: the people have a mediator who goes in before the Lord and comes out to tell them what he has been commanded.
str: v. 29: Moses comes down with the tablets, his face shining; he does not know it.
v. 30: Aaron and the people see the light and are afraid.
vv. 31–32: Moses calls them; the leaders and then all the people come near, and he gives them the Lord’s commands.
vv. 33–35: Moses puts a veil on his face when he has finished speaking, and removes it each time he goes in to speak with the Lord.
kw: the skin of his face shone

The verb qāran is related to qeren, “horn” or “ray”. Moses’ face sent out rays of light. St Jerome’s Latin translation understood “horned”, and for this reason Moses is painted and carved with horns in much medieval art, as in Michelangelo’s statue.
A covering used only in this passage in the Old Testament. Moses wears it when speaking to the people and removes it before the Lord.
Aaron and the people are afraid to come near. Holiness both attracts and frightens, and the one who has been with God carries something of it.
vv: Moses did not know that the skin of his face shone because he had been talking with God.
The most beautiful thing about the verse is what it says of Moses: he does not know. Holiness does not look at itself. The glory is the result of being with God, not of trying to shine.
they were afraid to come near him.
The people who sinned with the calf cannot bear the sight of the light. The light of God shows what is in us, and Moses must call them to come near.
Moses called to them;
The mediator does not leave the people afraid. He calls them, and they come. The one who has been with God brings others near and does not keep them at a distance.
whenever Moses went in before the Lord to speak with him, he would take the veil off,
Before the Lord there is no veil. Moses speaks with God unhidden, and then returns to the people who need the veil.
ch: St Paul reads this passage in 2 Corinthians 3:7–18. The glory on Moses’ face was real and was fading; the glory of the new covenant is greater and lasting, and Christians, with “unveiled faces”, are transformed from glory to glory by the Spirit. This is not a rejection of Moses or of the Old Covenant, which remains God’s gift (Romans 11:29); it is a statement that the light of the Law finds its fulfilment in Christ. The Church also reads the shining face of Moses in the light of the Transfiguration, where Moses and Elijah appear with Jesus and the face of Jesus shines like the sun (Matthew 17:2–3). The Catechism teaches that the saints share in the light of Christ and that by their lives the Church recognises the power of the Spirit of holiness within her (CCC 828). The saints are those whose faces shine because they have been with God.

r.h: In his joy he goes and sells all that he has
set: These are the shortest parables in the chapter. They are spoken to the disciples in the house, after Jesus has explained the weeds (13:36–43), and they come in a pair, as the mustard seed and the yeast did: a man and then a merchant.

The treasure is found by chance; the pearl is found after a search. In both cases the discovery is followed by a decision, and the decision is joyful. They tell us what the kingdom is worth, and how the one who finds it should act.
str: v. 44: the treasure hidden in a field; the finder hides it again, and in his joy sells all that he has and buys the field.
vv. 45–46: the merchant looking for fine pearls finds one of great value, sells all that he has and buys it.
kw: Money or valuables, often buried in a field for safety, since there were no banks. A man who finds one has found more than he could ever earn.
The joy that causes the man to sell everything. The cost is not a grim obligation but the natural response of one who has seen the value.
Pearls were the most prized of jewels in the ancient world. The merchant knows pearls, which is why he recognises this one as worth everything.
vv: The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field,
The kingdom is already present but hidden. It must be found, and when found, it is worth more than everything else.
then in his joy he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field.
The finder is not forced to sell; he sells in joy. For the one who has seen what the kingdom is, giving up other things no longer feels like loss.
on finding one pearl of great value, he went and sold all that he had and bought it.
The merchant sells all for one pearl. The Church has always seen in these words the way of those who give everything to Christ, as martyrs, religious and all who put him first.
ch: The Catechism says that, in the parables, Jesus invites people to enter the kingdom, and that to enter it one must make a radical choice, selling all that one has (CCC 546). Many Fathers and saints read the pearl as Christ himself (in substance), and the kingdom as his own presence in the soul. In the Church’s tradition the vows of poverty, chastity and obedience are one way to “sell all” for the kingdom, but the parable speaks to every Christian: whoever has found Christ is asked to prefer nothing to him, and to do it in joy. This is why the Church keeps the memorials of the saints: they show what this looks like in a real life.

qa: What is a memorial, and why does the Church keep St Alphonsa’s today?

A memorial is the lowest of the three ranks of feasts in the Roman calendar, below a solemnity and a feast. Memorials are obligatory or optional. For the Church in India, St Alphonsa’s is an obligatory memorial on 28 July, the day of her death. Her prayers at Mass may be taken from the Common of Virgins, but the readings are the weekday readings, which is why we hear Moses and the parables today.
Is it healthy to speak of offering one’s suffering to God?

Yes, when it is understood rightly. The Church never says that suffering is good in itself or that God wants people to suffer. Christ has given suffering a new meaning: it can unite us to his redemptive Passion (CCC 1521). The Church also asks us to relieve suffering by every means, and the sick have a right to treatment and care. The saints did both: they sought relief where it could be had, and offered with Christ what could not be removed.
Why is she called “of the Immaculate Conception”?

Religious often take a name that places them under the protection of a mystery of faith or of the Blessed Virgin. Alphonsa received the name when she was given the habit as a Franciscan Clarist sister in 1928. The Immaculate Conception, defined in 1854, is the teaching that Mary was preserved from original sin from the first moment of her existence, by a singular grace of God and in view of the merits of Christ (CCC 491). Devotion to Mary was part of her spirituality.
rite: St Alphonsa was born Annakutty on 19 August 1910 at Kudamaloor in Kerala, in the Syro-Malabar Church. Her mother died soon after her birth, and she was raised by relatives. Accounts of her life tell of a severe burn to her feet in her girlhood, at a time when a marriage was being arranged for her, and of her wish to belong to Christ alone. She entered the Franciscan Clarist Congregation at Bharananganam in 1927, received the habit in 1928, made her first vows in 1931 and her perpetual profession in 1936. Her life was marked by illness, and she died at Bharananganam on 28 July 1946, at the age of thirty-five. She was beatified by Pope John Paul II in Kottayam in 1986 and canonised by Pope Benedict XVI in Rome on 12 October 2008, the first woman of India raised to the altars. Her tomb at Bharananganam is a place of pilgrimage for people of every faith, and every Christian can pray for the sick through her intercession. The Latin Church in India keeps her memorial today, and she is honoured above all by her own Syro-Malabar Church. The Gospel today fits: she is remembered as one who gave everything, quietly and in joy, for the treasure.
study: Moses did not know that his face shone. What might others see in me that I cannot see myself, and how can I stay close enough to God to carry his light?
The people were afraid, yet Moses called them near. Who is afraid to come near to God or to the Church, and how can I call them, as Moses did?
The finder of the treasure sold all “in his joy”. What would I give up if I truly saw the worth of the kingdom, and what stops me from doing it joyfully?
St Alphonsa offered her suffering with Christ. For whom can I offer something small and hidden today, a pain, a tiredness or a patience?

lead: The book of Exodus ends with a house for God. Moses sets up the tabernacle exactly as the Lord commanded, and the cloud covers it and the glory of the Lord fills it, so that even Moses cannot enter. God has come to live among his people and to travel with them. In the Gospel, on the memorial of Martha, Mary and Lazarus, Martha goes out to meet Jesus on the road to Bethany, speaks honestly of her grief, and is brought to the great confession: “I believe that you are the Messiah, the Son of God, the one coming into the world.” Jesus’ own word to her, “I am the resurrection and the life,” is at the heart of Christian hope.
The Gospel is the proper one for today. The Church also allows Luke 10:38–42, the visit to Martha and Mary, in its place: Martha welcomes Jesus, and Mary sits at his feet.

r.h: The glory of the Lord filled the tabernacle
set: The last chapter of Exodus closes the story that began with slavery in Egypt. After the instructions for the tabernacle (chapters 25–31) and the golden calf (chapter 32), the craftsmen have made everything (chapters 35–39), and now Moses sets it up. The date given, the first day of the first month of the second year, is almost one year after the Exodus, which began in the same first month (12:2).

The chapter repeats the phrase “as the Lord had commanded Moses” again and again (40:16, 19, 21, 23, 25, 27, 29, 32). The point is obedience: the house of God is built according to his word and not according to human invention.
str: vv. 16–19: Moses sets up the tabernacle, its frames and its covering, as the Lord commanded.
vv. 20–21: he puts the tablets in the ark, places the mercy seat above it and screens the ark with the curtain.
vv. 34–35: the cloud covers the tent of meeting; the glory of the Lord fills it; Moses cannot enter.
vv. 36–38: when the cloud lifts, the people set out; by day it is a cloud, by night a fire, before the eyes of all Israel.
kw: From the verb šākan, “to dwell”. The tabernacle is God’s dwelling among his people, a movable tent for a people on the move.
From a root meaning “heavy”. God’s glory is his weighty, real presence, the sign that he is here. It fills the tabernacle (40:34–35), and later Solomon’s temple (1 Kings 8:10–11).
The verb used for the cloud “settling” on the tent (v. 35). Later Jewish writers used the related word Shekinah for God’s dwelling presence, though the noun does not appear in the Bible itself.
vv: Moses did everything just as the Lord had commanded him.
The opening line of the chapter sets its tone. Moses is faithful, and what he builds is what God has asked.
Then the cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the glory of the Lord filled the tabernacle.
God answers. The house is not complete when it is built; it is complete when God fills it. A building becomes a dwelling by his presence.
Moses was not able to enter the tent of meeting because the cloud settled upon it,
Even Moses, who spoke to God face to face, cannot enter when the glory fills the tent. Nearness to God does not remove reverence.
For the cloud of the Lord was on the tabernacle by day, and fire was in the cloud by night,
The book ends with the guiding cloud and fire, the same presence that led Israel out of Egypt. God is with his people at every stage of their journey.
ch: The New Testament takes up the language of this passage. St John says that the Word became flesh and “lived among us” (John 1:14); the Greek verb means “pitched his tent”. St Luke says that the power of the Most High “overshadowed” Mary (Luke 1:35), using the verb the Greek Old Testament uses for the cloud over the tent (Exodus 40:35). The Catechism points to the cloud that covered the tent of meeting as an image of the Holy Spirit who comes down on the Virgin Mary and overshadows her (CCC 697). In the same way the Church sees in her churches, and above all in the tabernacle where the Blessed Sacrament is kept, a dwelling of God among his people.

r.h: I am the resurrection and the life
set: Lazarus of Bethany, the brother of Martha and Mary, has died, and Jesus has delayed two days before going to him (11:6). When he arrives, Lazarus has been in the tomb four days (11:17). Bethany is a village about two miles from Jerusalem (11:18), so many friends and neighbours have come to console the sisters.

John says that “many of the Jews” had come to Martha and Mary. Here the phrase simply means Judeans, the people of the area, and they come with kindness; there is no blame in it. The Gospel is the proper one for the memorial of the three friends of Jesus, and it is also read at the funerals of many Christians.
str: vv. 19–20: mourners at the house; Martha goes out to meet Jesus while Mary stays at home.
vv. 21–22: Martha’s words: “if you had been here,” and her trust: “even now I know that God will give you whatever you ask”.
vv. 23–24: Jesus says Lazarus will rise; Martha answers with the faith of her people in the last day.
vv. 25–26: “I am the resurrection and the life”; “Do you believe this?”
v. 27: Martha’s confession of faith.
kw: The solemn “I am” of John’s Gospel, echoing the divine name revealed to Moses (Exodus 3:14). Jesus uses it with a predicate seven times in the Gospel (the bread of life, the light of the world, the door, the good shepherd, the resurrection and the life, the way, the truth and the life, the true vine).

Literally “standing up again”. Martha believes in a general resurrection on the last day, a hope held by many Jews of her time (Daniel 12:2). Jesus gives that hope a face: the resurrection is a person.
The verb of John’s Gospel, often followed by “into” or “in” someone. Faith is trust in a person, here in Jesus.
vv: Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.
A cry of grief, and also of faith: she knows that his presence would have made a difference. Her sister says the same words in verse 32. Honest grief is not lack of faith.
I know that he will rise again in the resurrection on the last day.
Martha answers with the faith she was taught. It is true, but it is far away and cold. Jesus takes her from “the last day” to a person standing in front of her.
I am the resurrection and the life. Those who believe in me, even though they die, will live,
Resurrection is not only an event at the end of time; it is Jesus himself. Whoever is joined to him by faith lives with the life that death cannot end.
Yes, Lord, I believe that you are the Messiah, the Son of God, the one coming into the world.

Martha’s confession is among the fullest in the Gospels, with that of Peter (Matthew 16:16). It names Jesus as Messiah, Son of God and the one who was to come, and she says it with a dead brother in the tomb.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus links faith in the resurrection to his own person: “I am the Resurrection and the life” (CCC 994). The raising of Lazarus is a sign that announces his own Resurrection, and the Church uses these words at the funeral of her children. Martha’s confession is the faith of the Church. The Church honours Martha, Mary and Lazarus together as friends of Jesus and as a family that shows faith, service and listening to his word, as the other Gospel suggests (Luke 10:38–42). Contemplation and service belong together; neither is complete without love.

qa: Is Mary of Bethany the same person as Mary Magdalene?

No. Mary of Bethany, the sister of Martha and Lazarus, is a different person from Mary Magdalene, who is named separately in the Gospels (Luke 8:2; John 19:25; 20:1). Old traditions in the West combined several women, but the Church has not taught that they are one, and the liturgy now keeps them apart: Mary Magdalene was celebrated on 22 July, and today the family of Bethany is honoured.
rite: Until 2021 the Roman calendar kept only St Martha on 29 July. By decree of the Congregation for Divine Worship, issued at the wish of Pope Francis, her sister Mary and her brother Lazarus were added, so that today it is the memorial of all three. The Gospel of Luke is also sometimes read on this day. The Church honours Martha as the patron of those who serve, in homes, hospitals and kitchens, and the sisters together as a sign that service and prayer are not rivals.
study: Martha spoke her grief to Jesus without hiding it. What do I need to say honestly to him today, even if it sounds like a complaint?
Jesus did not argue with Martha; he brought her from “the last day” to himself. What do I believe about the resurrection, and how does it change the way I face death?

lead: Leviticus now gives the calendar of Israel’s year: “These are the appointed festivals of the Lord, the holy convocations.” Time itself is made holy: Sabbath, Passover, the first fruits, the fifty days to the festival of Weeks, the Day of Atonement, and the festival of Booths. Each is a meeting with God at an appointed time. In the Gospel Jesus comes to his own hometown, Nazareth, and teaches in the synagogue. The people are astounded, then offended: they know his family and cannot see beyond it. One reading is about time that God makes holy; the other is about a familiar person in whom God was present, and was not recognised. The memorial of St Peter Chrysologus, bishop and Doctor of the Church, may be kept today.

r.h: These are the appointed festivals of the Lord
set: Chapter 23 belongs to the Holiness Code (Leviticus 17–26), laws that call Israel to be holy because the Lord is holy. After laws on sacrifice and purity, it turns to time. The chapter lists the weekly Sabbath and then the annual festivals, each with its date and its actions. Our reading takes some of the high points; today and tomorrow the Lectionary reads a few selected passages of the book.

The festivals are rooted in the agricultural year, with the barley harvest in spring, the wheat harvest in early summer, and the fruit harvest in autumn. They are also rooted in Israel’s history: Passover recalls the night of the Exodus, and Booths recalls the years in the wilderness (23:43). In this way the seasons of nature and the story of salvation are joined.
str: vv. 1–4: the Lord introduces the appointed festivals, the “holy convocations”.
vv. 5–8: Passover on the fourteenth day, followed by seven days of unleavened bread.
vv. 9–11: the first sheaf of the harvest is brought to the priest and waved before the Lord.
vv. 15–16: seven weeks are counted, fifty days, to a new offering of grain.
v. 27: the Day of Atonement on the tenth day of the seventh month.
vv. 34–37: the festival of Booths, seven days, with a solemn assembly on the eighth.
kw: From a root “to meet” or “to appoint”. A festival is an appointment with God. The “tent of meeting” has the same word.
A holy gathering, “called together”. God calls his people to assemble, and the people come.
The first bundle of barley cut at the start of the harvest and brought to the priest. It is waved before the Lord as a sign that the whole harvest belongs to him.
vv: These are the appointed festivals of the Lord, the holy convocations, which you shall celebrate at the time appointed for them.
The Lord, not the people, appoints the times. Israel does not choose when to meet God; God gives the times, and the community answers.
you shall bring the sheaf of the first fruits of your harvest to the priest.
Before the people eat any of the new harvest they give the first of it to God. The first fruits are a thanksgiving and a confession that the land is a gift.
You shall count until the day after the seventh sabbath, fifty days;
The fifty days between the sheaf and the new grain offering give the festival its later Greek name, Pentecost, “the fiftieth”. It is a time of counting, expectation and thanks.
you shall deny yourselves
The Day of Atonement is a day of fasting and repentance, the one day of the year when the whole people stands before God as sinners and asks forgiveness.
ch: The Church sees in these festivals the shadow of what Christ fulfils (Colossians 2:16–17), without denying their worth or rejecting the Jewish people who keep them still. The Catechism teaches that Jesus chose the time of Passover to institute the Eucharist (CCC 1340), and that Christian liturgy has roots in Jewish worship, for the Church’s feasts are connected to the same story of salvation (CCC 1096). St Paul calls Christ “the first fruits of those who have died” (1 Corinthians 15:20), and the fiftieth day, Pentecost, is when the Holy Spirit is poured out on the Church (Acts 2:1; CCC 731). The Church’s own year, with its appointed seasons, is the continuation of this idea: time is made holy by God’s works and by our meeting with him.

r.h: Prophets are not without honor except in their own country
set: After the parables of chapter 13, Jesus comes “to his hometown”, Nazareth, and teaches in the synagogue there. The people’s first reaction is astonishment at his wisdom and his deeds of power, which they have heard of from elsewhere.

The astonishment turns to offence when they think of his family. They know him as the carpenter’s son, and they know his mother and his relatives. Familiarity becomes a barrier: because they know where he came from, they cannot imagine who he is.
str: v. 54: Jesus teaches in the synagogue; the people are astounded.
vv. 55–56: “Where did this man get all this?” They name his family.
v. 57: “they took offense at him”; Jesus answers with a proverb about prophets.
v. 58: he did not do many deeds of power there, because of their unbelief.
kw: A craftsman who worked in wood and also in stone or metal. Jesus and Joseph were ordinary working people. The people of Nazareth see only the ordinary.
From skandalon, a stumbling block. The people stumble at the contrast between what they see and what he teaches. Faith needs openness to the unexpected.
The lack of trust that closes the door to God’s action. Jesus’ power is not lessened; it is the people’s closed hearts that limit what they receive.
vv: Is not this the carpenter’s son? Is not his mother called Mary?

The questions are ordinary, and they are true: Jesus is the son of a carpenter’s household and of Mary. The Church holds that this ordinary humanity is real, and also that there is more to him than they see.
Prophets are not without honor except in their own country and in their own house.
The proverb is true in the story of Israel too, for Jeremiah and other prophets were rejected by their own. Jesus says it with sadness; he takes it as the lot of a prophet.
And he did not do many deeds of power there, because of their unbelief.
Mark says even more strongly that he “could do no deed of power there” (Mark 6:5). Faith does not force God’s hand, but where there is no faith, there is no opening for the gift.
ch: The Catechism says that during the greater part of his life Jesus shared the condition of most human beings: a daily life without evident greatness, a life of manual labour (CCC 531). That the people of Nazareth found this hard to reconcile with his teaching is a warning to everyone who has grown used to him. The “brothers and sisters” named here are, in the Catholic understanding, near relatives of Jesus and not children of Mary, who remained a virgin; the Greek and Hebrew words cover cousins and other relatives (CCC 500). The Church also teaches that faith is a gift that must be welcomed willingly, and that one can close the door by refusing to listen.

qa: Who are the “brothers and sisters” of Jesus?

The Gospels use the word adelphoi, which in the Greek of the Septuagint, and in the Hebrew word behind it, can mean brothers but also cousins and other close relatives. The Catholic Church holds that Mary remained a virgin all her life and that these were near kinsmen of Jesus (CCC 500). Mark and Matthew also name a different Mary at the cross as mother of James and Joseph (Matthew 27:56), which suggests that at least some of these were children of another woman.
rite: St Peter Chrysologus (about 380–450) was bishop of Ravenna, then the capital of the Western Roman Empire. His name, “golden-worded”, was given later in recognition of his preaching. His sermons are short, vivid and practical; many speak of the Gospel, of prayer and fasting, and of Mary. He was declared a Doctor of the Church in 1729. His memorial may be kept today, and the Gospel suits him: he preached to ordinary people in their own language and in familiar images.
study: Israel kept holy times: Sabbath, Passover, Booths. What are the holy times in my own week and year, and do I keep them or let them be crowded out?
The people of Nazareth could not see past what they knew. Whom do I take for granted, in my family, in the parish or in Christ himself, and how might I look again?

lead: The first reading gives the law of the Jubilee. After seven times seven years, on the Day of Atonement, a trumpet sounds through the whole land, and the fiftieth year is holy: liberty is proclaimed, each family returns to its property, the land rests, and no one is to cheat a neighbour. In the Gospel, a different kind of power appears: Herod, who has imprisoned John the Baptist for telling him “It is not lawful for you to have her,” gives in to a dancing girl and her mother and has John beheaded. The jubilee is a year of release; Herod’s court is a place of fear and bondage, and John, in prison, is the one truly at liberty. The memorial of St Ignatius of Loyola, whose proper readings (1 Corinthians 10:31–11:1 and Luke 14:25–33) may be used instead, is kept today.

r.h: You shall return, every one of you, to your property
set: Leviticus 25 is part of the Holiness Code. It begins with the sabbatical year, in which the land rests every seventh year (25:1–7), and then gives the law of the Jubilee: after seven sabbaths of years, forty-nine years, the fiftieth year is a year of release. The word “Sinai” in verse 1 recalls that these are laws given by God to Israel at the mountain.

The law rests on the conviction that the land belongs to God (25:23): Israel’s families are tenants and stewards, not absolute owners. If poverty forced a family to sell its land or itself into service, the jubilee returned them to their inheritance. Scholars debate how fully the jubilee was kept in ancient Israel, but the prophets and the Gospels hold it up as an ideal of what God wants.
str: v. 1: the Lord speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai.
vv. 8–9: seven weeks of years; on the Day of Atonement the trumpet sounds throughout the land.
vv. 10–12: the fiftieth year is holy; liberty is proclaimed; each returns to his property and family; the land is not sown.
v. 13: “you shall return, every one of you, to your property”.
vv. 14–17: honest dealing: prices fixed by the number of harvests until the next jubilee; “you shall not cheat one another, but you shall fear your God”.
kw: Originally the ram’s horn that was blown to announce the year. The Latin iubilaeum, “jubilee”, comes from it, though it later came to be associated with iubilare, “to rejoice”.
The word for the freedom proclaimed in the year of jubilee, found again in Isaiah 61:1 and Jeremiah 34:8. Jesus quotes the Isaiah text in the synagogue of Nazareth (Luke 4:18).
From the verb yānâ, “to oppress, to wrong”, used in verses 14 and 17 (“you shall not cheat one another”). The jubilee law forbids it, and verse 17 grounds the prohibition in the fear of God.
vv: you shall proclaim liberty throughout the land to all its inhabitants.

The liberty is for all the inhabitants of the land. These words were later carved on the Liberty Bell in Philadelphia, but their first meaning is the release of the poor and the return of families to their land.
you shall return, every one of you, to your property and every one of you to your family.
Property and family go together. The jubilee guards both the means of life and the bond of kinship, so that no family is cut off for ever.
you shall eat only what the field itself produces.
The year of rest is a year of trust. The land is not worked, and the people depend on what God gives without their labour.
You shall not cheat one another, but you shall fear your God;
The law of the market is joined to the fear of God. Honest dealing is not only a matter of law but of reverence for the Lord who sees.
ch: The Church reads the jubilee in the light of Jesus’ first sermon at Nazareth, where he reads from Isaiah 61, “to proclaim release to the captives… to proclaim the year of the Lord’s favor,” and says that it is fulfilled today (Luke 4:16–21). Since 1300 the Church has also celebrated Holy Years, as times of pilgrimage, conversion and mercy; Pope John Paul II linked them expressly with Leviticus 25 (Tertio Millennio Adveniente 11–13). The Catechism teaches the universal destination of goods: God gave the earth to the whole human race, and private property does not remove the claim of the poor on what is superfluous (CCC 2402–2403). The jubilee is a standing reminder that every possession is held in trust.

r.h: Herod sent and had John beheaded in the prison
set: The account follows the rejection of Jesus at Nazareth. Herod “the ruler” is Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, who governed Galilee and Perea as tetrarch from 4 BC until AD 39. Matthew has just told that Jesus’ fame was spreading, and now Herod hears of it and fears that John the Baptist, whom he killed, has been raised.

The story is a flashback: Matthew tells how John came to die. Herod had married Herodias, the wife of his brother Philip; John said that this was not lawful, as the Law of Moses forbids a man to marry his brother’s wife while the brother is alive (Leviticus 18:16; 20:21). Matthew’s account is brief; the historian Josephus also tells of John’s death and says that Herod put him to death at the fortress of Machaerus.
str: vv. 1–2: Herod hears of Jesus and thinks he is John raised from the dead.
vv. 3–5: the flashback: John imprisoned for saying “It is not lawful”; Herod wants to kill him but fears the crowd.
vv. 6–11: Herod’s birthday, the dance, the oath, the request for John’s head, and the beheading.
v. 12: John’s disciples bury him and tell Jesus.
kw: Literally “ruler of a fourth part”. Matthew calls Herod “the ruler”, and in v. 9 “the king”, as he was called by courtesy though Rome had not given him the title.
Herod binds himself by an oath, and the oath becomes his excuse. Jesus teaches elsewhere that his disciples should not swear at all (Matthew 5:33–37), and this story shows why.
A flat dish for food. The head on a platter is the grim reversal of a banquet, where the guests are fed and a prophet is killed.
vv: It is not lawful for you to have her.
John is not afraid of a king. He speaks the truth about marriage and the Law and he pays for it. The same word “lawful” is used of the Sabbath and divorce elsewhere in Matthew.
Though Herod wanted to put him to death, he feared the crowd,
Herod’s fear of the crowd restrains him for a while. Later, fear of the guests and of his own oath moves him in the other direction. A man who fears people and not God can be led anywhere.
The king was grieved, yet out of regard for his oaths and for the guests, he commanded it to be given;
The most tragic line of the story: he is sorry, and he does it. Regret that does not turn into action is no protection.
His disciples came and took the body and buried it; then they went and told Jesus.
The disciples of John give him a burial and take the news to Jesus. With this, John’s story passes into Jesus’ story: the forerunner’s death foreshadows his own (Matthew 17:12).
ch: The Church honours John the Baptist as the forerunner who prepared the way, and as a martyr for the truth: his death is kept on 29 August as the Passion of St John the Baptist. The Catechism teaches that martyrdom is the supreme witness given to the truth of the faith (CCC 2473), and it presents John as the one who goes before the Lord “in the spirit and power of Elijah” (CCC 523). His death is a sign for every Christian who speaks the truth where it is unwelcome. Herod’s story is the other side: one who knew John was a holy man (Mark 6:20) and still chose to protect his own position.

rite: St Ignatius of Loyola (1491–1556) was born into a Basque noble family. As a soldier he was wounded at Pamplona in 1521, and while he recovered at Loyola he read the lives of Christ and the saints, and his life turned. After a year of prayer at Manresa he wrote the first notes of the Spiritual Exercises, a month of guided prayer that has shaped countless lives. In 1540 Pope Paul III approved his Society of Jesus. Its motto, “for the greater glory of God”, is the thread of the proper readings: “whatever you do, do everything for the glory of God” (1 Corinthians 10:31) and the cost of following Christ (Luke 14:25–33). He died in Rome on 31 July 1556 and was canonised in 1622.
study: The jubilee returns each family to its land and each person to freedom. Is there a debt, a grievance or an old wrong that I can release this week?
Herod grieved, and yet obeyed his oath and his guests. When have I done something I knew to be wrong because of what others would think, and what would have helped me to stand firm?
